193:
## Aṅguttara Nikāya
## Aṭṭhaka Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One.
## 1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka
## 1. Mettā Vagga
## 1. Mettā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta, 'āsevitāya' means because it has been cultivated with respect. 'bhāvitāya' means because it has been developed. 'bahulīkatāya' means because it has been practiced frequently. 'yānikatāya' means because it has been made like a well-yoked vehicle. 'vatthukatāya' means because it has been made like a foundation, in the sense of being a basis. 'anuṭṭhitāya' means because it has been firmly established by repeatedly attending to the object. 'paricitāya' means because it has been accumulated and consolidated from all sides. 'susamāraddhāya' means because it has been well-undertaken and well-performed. 'āniśaṃsā' means the benefits. Regarding the matters mentioned in the phrases such as "one sleeps happily," I shall explain them in the Ekādasaka Nipāta.

'appamāṇaṃ' means immeasurable by way of pervasion. "For one who sees, the fetters are thinned as the substrate is exhausted" means that for one who reaches Arahantship—known as the exhaustion of substrates—through the sequence of insight (vipassanā) which has loving-kindness as its proximate cause, the ten fetters are abandoned. Alternatively, "the fetters are thinned" means that aversion and the fetters associated with aversion are weakened. "For one who sees the exhaustion of substrates" means for one who sees by way of attaining loving-kindness, which is called the exhaustion of the substrates of defilements. "He becomes meritorious by that" means he becomes meritorious through that practice of loving-kindness. 'sattasaṇḍaṃ' means filled with the assembly called beings, or crowded with beings. 'vijetvā' means having conquered by Dhamma alone, without punishment or weapons. 'rājisayo' refers to righteous kings who are like seers. 'yajamānā' means giving gifts. 'anupariyagā' means they wandered about.

In the passage beginning with 'assamedha,' it is said that in the time of ancient kings, there were four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu): sassamedha, purisamedha, sammāpāsa, and vācāpeyya, by which kings supported the people. Among these four, taking one-tenth of the harvested crops is called 'sassamedha.' It means being wise in the abundance of crops. Providing six months' rations to the soldiers is called 'purisamedha.' It means being wise in supporting the employees. Lending money interest-free for three years to the poor, marking it in their hands, is called 'sammāpāsa.' It means binding them well like a snare; by such binding, the mind is gladdened. Speaking gentle words is called 'vācāpeyya,' which is simply speaking endearing words. Thus, a country supported by these four bases of sympathy...
194: ...kings supported the world. Among those four, taking a tenth part of the produced crops is called 'sassamedha,' meaning wisdom in the production of crops. Giving six months' worth of rations and wages to great warriors is called 'purisamedha,' meaning wisdom in supporting people. Taking a signed bond from poor people and giving them wealth of about one or two thousand without interest for three years is called 'sammāpāsa.' This is called 'sammāpāsa' because it binds people well, as if tying them to the heart. Speaking gentle words such as "father" or "uncle" is called 'vācāpeyya,' meaning pleasant speech. A kingdom supported by these four bases of social integration becomes prosperous, flourishing, abundant in food and drink, safe, and free from strife. People live happily, making their young children dance on their chests, with their house doors left open. This is called 'niraggala' (unbolted) because of the absence of door-bolts at the house entrances. This was the ancient tradition.However, in later times, during the reign of King Okkāka, the Brahmins altered these four bases of social integration and this prosperity of the kingdom, turning them upside down, and established five sacrifices (yañña) such as assamedha and purisamedha. Among those sacrifices, it is called 'assamedha' because a horse (assa) is killed (medhanti) in this sacrifice. This is the name of a sacrifice that is to be offered with two peripheral sacrifices, having twenty-one sacrificial posts, involving the terrifying slaughter of five hundred and ninety-seven animals on the final day alone, and where all remaining wealth and possessions are given as a sacrificial gift, excluding only the land and the people. It is called 'purisamedha' because a human (purisa) is killed in this sacrifice. This is the name of a sacrifice to be offered with four peripheral sacrifices, where the wealth mentioned in the assamedha is given along with the land. It is called 'sammāpāsa' because a peg (samma) is thrown (pāsanti) in this sacrifice. This is the name of a sacrificial session (sattrayāga) to be offered by throwing a peg called 'samma,' which is a rod inserted into a yoke-hole every day, making an altar at the spot where that rod falls, and proceeding upstream with portable sacrificial posts and so forth, starting from the place where the Sarasvatī River disappears. It is called 'vācāpeyya' because vāja (clarified butter) is drunk (pivanti) in this sacrifice. This is the name of a sacrifice to be offered with one peripheral sacrifice and seventeen animals, having a sacrificial post made of wood-apple (beluva), and seventeen sacrificial gifts. It is called 'niraggala' because there is no bolt (aggaḷa) in this sacrifice. This is the name of a variation of the assamedha sacrifice, also called 'sabbamedha,' to be offered with nine peripheral sacrifices, where the wealth mentioned in the assamedha is given along with the land and the people.
195:
All those great sacrifices, because of the greatness of the fruit of a single thought of loving-kindness, do not equal a sixteenth part, nor do they reach a sixteenth portion. "na jināti" means he himself does not cause the defeat (or ruin) of another. "na jāpayeti" means he does not cause another to cause the defeat of another. "mettāṃso" means having a portion of the mind that develops loving-kindness. "sabbabhūtānaṃ" means towards all beings. "veraṃ tassa na kenaci" means that person has no unwholesome enmity or personal enmity with anyone.

## 2. Paññā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "ādibrahmacariyikāya" means being the beginning of the holy life of the Path. "paññāya" means through insight wisdom. "garuṭṭhāniyaṃ" means being a cause for respect, worthy of esteem. "tibbaṃ" means intense or strong. "paripucchati" means he inquires about the meaning, the Pali, the connection, and the sequence. "paripañhati" means he poses questions, thinking "I will ask this and that." "dvayena" means in two ways. "anānākathiko" means he is one who does not speak diverse words. "atiracchānakathiko" means he does not speak various kinds of animal talk (low talk contrary to the Path). In the phrase "ariyaṃ vā tuṇhībhāvaṃ," noble silence refers to the fourth jhāna; attending to other meditation subjects is also appropriate. "jānaṃ jānāti" means he knows the Dhamma that should be known. "passaṃ passati" means he sees the Dhamma that should be seen. "piyattāya" means for the sake of being loved. "garuttāya" means for the sake of being esteemed. "bhāvanāya" means for the sake of development (or for honoring with virtues). "သာမညာယ" (sāmaññāya) means for the sake of the ascetic life. "ekībhāvāya" means for the sake of being continuous (without interruption).

## 3-4. Appiya Sutta Dvaya Vaṇṇanā
3-4. In the third sutta, "appiyapasasī" means one who praises the unloved, speaking words of their virtues. "piyagarahī" means one who blames or disparages the loved. In the fourth sutta, "anavaññattikāmo" means one who desires not to be looked down upon by others, thinking "Oh, may others not know me as inferior." "akālaññū" means he does not know the time for speech and speaks at the wrong time. "asuci" means one who is endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth.

## 5. Paṭhamalokadhamma Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "lokassa dhammā" means worldly conditions. There is no one who is free from these worldly conditions; they occur even to the Buddhas. Therefore, it is said: "lokaṃ anupariyavattanti" (they follow the world). It means they follow along (anubandhanti).
196:
It means they do not give up, they do not depart from the world of beings. 'The world also follows the eight worldly conditions' means this world follows these eight worldly conditions; it does not give them up, it does not depart from those things.

'Gain and loss' (lābho alābho) means it should be understood that when gain comes, loss also surely comes. The same method applies to disrepute (ayasa) and so on. 'Contemplates things that have the nature of change' means contemplating thus: 'These things have the nature of change.' 'Vidhūpitā' means destroyed, dispelled. 'Having known Nibbāna' means having known Nibbāna which is to be attained through the knowledge of the Path and the Fruit. 'One who has reached the further shore of existence knows well' means one reaches the further shore of existence and attains the completion and the summit; having known Nibbāna, one knows distinctly the state of having reached that shore. In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 6. Dutiyalokadhammasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'What is the distinction?' means what is the special reason. 'What kind of effort is there?' means what kind of superior effort is there. 'Pariyādāya' means having taken, having completed. In this sutta also, only the round of suffering and the cessation of the round are taught.

## 7. Devadattavipattisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'Not long after he had departed' means not long after he had departed after causing a schism in the Saṅgha. 'Ārabbha' means on account of, with reference to. 'One's own failure' means one's own deviation, the manner of failure. The same method applies to the remaining words. 'Abhibhuyya' means having overcome, having crushed.

## 8. Uttaravipattisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'At the Vaṭajālikā monastery' means in the monastery of this name. It is said that the monastery came to be called Vaṭajālikā because it was situated in a banyan grove (vaṭavana). 'Became manifest' means he went and became manifest with the intention, 'I will report this matter to the King of Devas.' 'Ādibrahmacariyaka' means one who is the beginning of the holy life of the entire Dispensation, which includes the three trainings.

## 9. Nandasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'A son of good family' means a son of a high-born family. 'Balavā' means one endowed with strength. 'Pāsādika' means one who inspires confidence due to physical beauty. 'Tibbarāga' means one who has intense passion. In the words 'Kimanyatra' and so on, the meaning is: what benefit would there be by another reason...
197:
Because it is spoken with reason: "This Nanda is one who guards the doors of his senses, knows moderation in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, and is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension." For these reasons, Nanda is able to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) in its fullness and purity. If he were not endowed with these reasons, he would not be able to do so. "Itiha tattha" means "thus in that place." In this sutta, only the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) is spoken of.

## 10. Kāraṇḍavasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "aññenāññaṃ paṭicarati" means covering up one reason or word with another reason or word. "Bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti" means introducing another external, extraneous conversation. "Apanejjeyyaso" means this person should be removed or expelled. "Samaṇadūsī" means a corrupter of recluses. "Samaṇapalāpo" means a "chaff-recluse," being without essence among recluses, just like chaff is without essence among grains of rice. "Samaṇakāraṇḍavo" means recluse-rubbish. "Bahiddhā nāsentī" means they expel him outside. "Yavakaraṇe" means in a barley field. "Phuṇamānassa" refers to the condition of one standing in a high place and winnowing in a strong wind. "Apasammajjanti" means they repeatedly sweep or strike to separate the essential grains from the weak grains; or they remove them with a winnowing basket or a cloth that catches the wind, which is called "striking." "Daddaraṃ" refers to a thudding sound like "daddara."

"Saṃvāsāyaṃ" means this person is to be known through living together. "Vijānātha" means you should know. "Santavāco" means one who has gentle speech. "Janavatī" means being in the midst of a crowd of people. In the phrase "raho karoti karaṇaṃ," "karaṇaṃ" is said to be an evil deed; he performs that evil deed in secret, being hidden. "Saṃsappī ca musāvādī" means one who speaks falsely while trembling; the meaning is that when speaking falsely, one trembles or quivers. In this sutta, after speaking only of the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), the round and the cessation of the round (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) are spoken of in the verses.

## First is the Mettā Vagga.
## 2. Mahā Vagga
## 1. Verañjasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second vagga, the words beginning with "abhivādeti" should be connected according to the method stated in the phrase "na samaṇo gotamo," and the meaning should be understood thus: (He does not pay homage, does not rise from his seat, nor does he invite them, saying, "Sirs, please sit here"). Thus the meaning should be understood. Indeed, in this context, the word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of clarification (vibhāvana), as in "rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā" (Is form permanent or impermanent?) and so forth. Seeing the Blessed One who did not perform acts such as paying homage even though he had arrived at his presence, he said: "O Gotama, it is just as I have heard; my hearing and my seeing coincide and agree; they become one in meaning. For Master Gotama does not... nor does he invite with a seat." Thus, concluding what he had heard with what he saw, he spoke disparagingly: "O Gotama, this is not complete (not proper)," meaning that the failure to perform acts such as paying homage is indeed improper.
198:
It should be understood thus: "He does not pay homage, nor does he rise from his seat, nor does he invite them with a seat, saying, 'Sirs, please sit here.'" Here, the word "vā" is used in the sense of clarification, as in "Is form permanent or impermanent?" and so forth. Having spoken thus, and seeing the Blessed One not performing acts such as paying homage to him, he said: "This is just so, Master Gotama." He meant: "It is exactly as I have heard; my hearing and my seeing coincide; they agree and become one in meaning. For Master Gotama does not... nor does he invite with a seat." Thus, concluding what he had heard with what he saw, he spoke disparagingly: "O Gotama, this is not complete (not proper)," meaning that the failure to perform acts such as paying homage is indeed improper.

Then the Blessed One, without falling into the faults of self-exaltation and disparaging others, and wishing to dispel that ignorance with a heart cooled by compassion and to show the proper state, spoke the words beginning with: "Brahmin, I am not like that." The summary of the meaning is this: "Brahmin, even when I look with the unimpeded eye of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), I do not see any person in this world with its devas and so forth whom I should pay homage to, or rise for, or invite with a seat. It is not surprising that I, having attained omniscience today, do not see such a person worthy of such respect. Furthermore, even when I was just born and went seven steps facing the north and looked at the entire ten thousand world systems, even then I did not see any person in this world with its devas and so forth to whom I should show such respect. At that time, even the Great Brahma, a non-returner (khīṇāsava) with a lifespan of sixteen thousand aeons, with joined palms, paid respect with a joyful heart, saying: 'You are the Great Man in the world; you are the foremost, the eldest, and the best in the world with its devas; there is no one superior to you.' Even then, seeing no one superior to myself, I uttered the Lion's Roar: 'I am the foremost of the world, I am the eldest of the world, I am the best of the world.' If even at birth there was no person worthy of receiving homage from me, now that I have attained omniscience, whom should I pay homage to? Therefore, Brahmin, do not expect such supreme respect from the Tathāgata. For, Brahmin, if the Tathāgata were to pay homage to any person... or invite them with a seat, the head of that person would, at the end of the night, be severed from the neck and fall suddenly to the ground, like a ripe palm fruit loosened from its stalk."
199:
Even when spoken to in this way, the Brahmin Verañja, due to his lack of wisdom, could not recognize the Blessed One’s status as the foremost in the world. Merely unable to endure those words, he said, "Master Gotama is one who is tasteless (arasarūpa)." This was his intended meaning: in the world, the acts of bowing, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, and paying respect are called "sāmaggirasa" (the essence of harmony). These acts do not exist in Master Gotama. Therefore, Master Gotama is one who is tasteless, of a tasteless nature, and of a tasteless character. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to soften the Brahmin’s mind and avoiding direct confrontation, showed the meaning of those words in another way regarding himself, saying, "There is indeed a way (pariyāya), Brahmin, [by which one could say...]" and so on.

In that passage, "atthi khvesa" means "atthi kho esa." "Pariyāya" means reason or method. The meaning is this: "Brahmin, there is indeed a reason by which a person, in saying 'Master Gotama is tasteless,' would be speaking rightly and would be considered a speaker of truth. And what is that reason? Brahmin, those delights in forms (rūparasa)... and so on... delights in tangibles (phoṭṭhabbarasa), those have been abandoned by the Tathāgata." What is meant by this? There are delights in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, known as the delight in sensual pleasure, which arise for worldlings—even those considered noble by birth or rebirth—who enjoy, delight in, and are attached to sense objects like forms. These delights pull at this world as if binding it by the neck. Because they arise from the harmony of the physical base and the object, they are also called "sāmaggirasa" (the essence of harmony). All these delights have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Although he should have said, "They have been abandoned by me," he taught the Dhamma without exalting himself with the notion of "I," or perhaps this is the elegance of the Tathāgata's teaching (desanāvilāsa).

In that context, "pahīna" means gone from the mental continuum, or abandoned. In this sense, the genitive case "tathāgatassa" should be understood in the instrumental sense (abandoned by the Tathāgata). Because the root of these delights, consisting of craving and ignorance, has been cut off by the weapon of the Noble Path, they are called "ucchinnamūla" (uprooted). Because the basis of those delights has been made like the site of a palm tree, they are called "tālāvatthukata." Just as when a palm tree is pulled up by the roots and only the site remains, that palm tree can never grow again; likewise, when the delights in forms and so on are uprooted by the weapon of the Noble Path, leaving only the site in the mental continuum as a state of having previously existed, all those are called "tālāvatthukata." Or, because they are of a nature not to grow again, like a palm tree with its head cut off, they are called "tālāvatthukata." Since they have been made "tālāvatthukata" in this way, they have reached the state of non-existence (anabhāvaṅkata)...
200:
(Those delights in forms, etc.) are made in such a way that they do not occur again. Therefore, they are called "anabhāvaṅkata" (rendered non-existent). "Āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā" means they are of a nature not to arise in the future.

"No ca kho yaṃ tvaṃ sandhāya vadesi" means: "But it is not for the reason you have in mind." The Brahmin meant that Master Gotama is "arasarūpa" (tasteless) because he lacks the harmonious delight of bowing to elders and so on; the Buddha meant that this reason does not apply to him. Here, one might ask, "If someone possesses sāmaggirasa (the essence of harmony), does it not mean they admit to having that taste?" But that is not so. Only if a person is fit to perform that sāmaggirasa but does not do so, would they deserve to be called "arasarūpa" due to its absence. The Blessed One, however, is no longer fit to perform such acts. Therefore, wishing to show his unfitness for such acts, he said, "The reason you have in mind is not to be said of us." It means, "The reason for which you call me 'arasarūpa' is not applicable to us."

In this way, the Brahmin, unable to establish the "arasarūpa" quality he intended, then spoke other words such as "nibbhoga" (without enjoyment). In all these instances, one should understand the sequence of application and the intended meaning according to the method already mentioned. The Brahmin, considering the acts of bowing to elders in the world as "sāmaggiparibhoga" (harmonious enjoyment), called the Blessed One "nibbhoga" and so on because of the absence of those acts. The Blessed One, seeing in himself the absence of "chandarāgaparibhoga" (enjoyment through desire and lust) with which beings enjoy forms and so on, admitted to it by another reason.

Again, the Brahmin, seeing that the Blessed One did not perform the customary acts of bowing to elders that worldly people do, called him an "akiriyavāda" (proponent of non-action). The Blessed One, however, because he teaches the non-doing of bodily misconduct and so on, saw that state of "akiriyavāda" in himself and admitted to it by another reason. In that context, excluding bodily misconduct and so on, the remaining unwholesome states should be understood as various types of evil, unwholesome states.

Again, the Brahmin, not seeing those acts of bowing and so on in the Blessed One, thought, "Because of this man, the continuity of the world (lokapaveṇī) will be cut off," and called him an "ucchedavāda" (proponent of annihilation). The Blessed One, however, teaches the annihilation of lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure and the hatred associated with the two types of unwholesome consciousness by means of the Path of Non-returning. As for delusion, which is the source of all unwholesome states, [he teaches its annihilation] by means of the Path of Arahantship...
201:
The Blessed One teaches the annihilation of unwholesome states. Setting aside those [three views], he teaches the total destruction of the remaining evil, unwholesome states through the four paths as appropriate. Therefore, seeing that the nature of annihilating (ucchedavāda) those unwholesome states exists within himself, he acknowledged it in a different sense.

Again, the Brahmin, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama likely loathes the traditional customs of the clans, such as paying homage to those senior in age, and thus he does not perform those acts," addressed the Blessed One as "one who is loathsome (jegucchī)." The Blessed One, however, loathes bodily misconduct and the like. Whatever unwholesome and base states there are, including the cultivation of, the attainment of, and the possession of bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct—he loathes them all, just as a man who is fond of adornment loathes excrement; he is repelled by them. Therefore, seeing that the nature of loathing (jegucchita) such unwholesome states exists within himself, he acknowledged it in a different sense. In that context, in the words beginning with "kāyaduccaritena," the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of the accusative (the object).

Again, the Brahmin, not seeing those acts such as paying homage in the Blessed One, thought, "This person destroys the acts performed for the elders in the world," or else, "Because this person does not perform these acts of respect, he is one who should be disciplined or suppressed," and thus addressed the Blessed One as "a destroyer or one to be disciplined (venayika)." The meaning of that term is: he is "vinaya" because he destroys; it means he causes destruction. The word "vinaya" itself is "venayika." Alternatively, he is "venayika" because he deserves discipline (niggaha). The Blessed One, however, is called "venayika" because he teaches the Dhamma for the discipline (vinaya) and the stilling of lust and other defilements. This alone is the intended meaning here—he is "venayika" because he teaches the Dhamma to destroy lust, etc. The usage of the taddhita suffix is indeed diverse. Seeing that the state of being a "venayika" who destroys lust and so on exists within himself, he acknowledged it in a different sense.

Again, the Brahmin considered, "Those who perform acts of respect such as paying homage to elders please them and make them joyful; those who do not, however, cause them distress, harass them, and cause them mental displeasure." Since the Blessed One does not perform those acts, the Brahmin thought, "This person causes distress to the elders." Or, because he is devoid of the conduct of virtuous men, thinking, "This is a miserable man (kapaṇapurisa)," he addressed the Blessed One as "tapassī." The meaning of that term is: it is "tapa" because it causes distress; it means it harasses. This is a designation for not performing acts of respect. He is "tapassī" because he has such distressing conduct. In the second alternative meaning, without analyzing the syllables, a miserable man in the world is called "tapassī." ... Setting aside those three ...
202:
is called "tapassī." The Blessed One, however, is known as "tapassī" because he has abandoned those unwholesome states which are called "tapanīya" because they burn (torment) the world. Therefore, seeing that the state of being a "tapassī" (one who has burned away defilements) exists within himself, he acknowledged it in a different sense. The etymological meaning here is: they are "tapa" because they burn; this is a designation for unwholesome states. He is "tapassī" because he has abandoned, discarded, and destroyed those "tapa" (unwholesome) states.

Again, the Brahmin, thinking that the act of paying homage and so on leads to the attainment of the celestial womb (gabbhasampatti) and the acquisition of rebirth in the deva world, and seeing the absence of such acts in the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as "apagabbha" (one without a womb). Or, out of anger, wishing to point out a fault in the Blessed One's conception in his mother's womb, he spoke thus. The etymological meaning here is: he is "apagabbha" because he is away from the womb (gabbha), meaning he is unfit to reach rebirth in the deva world. Or, he is "apagabbha" because he has a low (hīna) womb. It means that because he is excluded from the celestial womb, he will be a partaker of a low rebirth in the future. Or, it means his dwelling in his mother's womb was low. For the Blessed One, however, since future gestation in a womb is gone, seeing that state of being free from the womb (apagabbhatā) within himself, he acknowledged it in a different sense. In that context, the meaning of the words, "Brahmin, for whom future gestation in a womb and rebirth in a new existence are abandoned," should be understood thus: "Brahmin, for whichever person future gestation in a womb and rebirth in a new existence are abandoned because their causes have been destroyed by the unsurpassed Path of Arahantship." Here, by the term "gabbhaseyya" (gestation in a womb), womb-born (jalābuja) birth is taken; by the term "punabbhavābhinibbatti" (rebirth in a new existence), the other three types of birth, such as moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneous (opapātika), are also taken.

Alternatively, the lying down of an embryo is called "gabbhaseyya." Since becoming again is itself the new arising, it is called "punabbhavābhinibbatti"; thus should the meaning be understood. Just as when "viññāṇaṭṭhiti" (station of consciousness) is mentioned, there is no station other than consciousness itself, so too here, no lying down other than the womb itself should be understood. As for "arising" (abhinibbatti), it can be either that which constitutes a new existence (punabbhava) or that which does not. Since in this context, the arising in a new existence is intended, it is said: "Becoming again is itself the new arising (punabbhavābhinibbatti)."

From the time he arrived, even though the Brahmin was insulting him with the eight grounds of insult such as "arasarūpa" (tastelessness) and so on, the Tathāgata—the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma—looking at the Brahmin with a cool eye of compassion, having penetrated the Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) known as the Knowledge of Omniscience, reached the perfection of the beauty of teaching.
203:
Furthermore, there is a new arising that occurs without being a repeated birth. In this context, the arising in a new existence is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'Punabbhavo eva abhinibbatti punabbhavābhinibbatti' (Renewed existence itself is the arising). From this point onwards, the Blessed One—who is the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, and who came in the manner of former Buddhas such as Vipassī—having been abused by the Brahmin with the eight grounds of abuse such as 'arasarūpatā' (tastelessness), looked upon him with compassion through the cool eye of omniscience. Because He had thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) known as omniscient knowledge, He attained the splendor of teaching. Like the full moon in a cloudless sky or the sun in the autumn season, He desired to dispel the darkness of the Brahmin's heart. By showing the very grounds of that abuse to beings in a different manner, He once again demonstrated the expansion of His compassion, the characteristic of that quality obtained by being unshaken by the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma), the state of having a mind like the earth (pathavīsama-citta), and the nature of being unshakeable by anger.

Thinking, "This Brahmin perceives his seniority only by his grey hair, broken teeth, and wrinkled skin. He does not know himself to be followed by birth, pursued by old age, overwhelmed by disease, and struck down by death; that having died today, he will tomorrow again reach the state of an infant capable only of lying on its back. However, he has come to me with great effort; let his coming be fruitful," the Blessed One, desiring to show His own peerless seniority in this world, expanded the Dhamma teaching to the Brahmin with the method beginning with "Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa" (Just as, Brahmin).

In those words beginning with "Seyyathāpi," the meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated below. This, however, is the distinction—to elaborate further, according to the method stated below, those chicks come out flapping their wings and chirping according to that moment. Among those chicks coming out in this way, the one that comes out first is called the 'eldest.' Therefore, the Blessed One, desiring to establish His own seniority through that simile, asked the Brahmin: "Among those chicks... what should he be called?"

In that Pali, "kukkuṭacchāpakānaṃ" means 'of the chicks.' "Kinti svāssa vacanīyo" means 'what should he be called?'—should he be spoken of as the eldest or the youngest?

"He should be called the eldest, Master Gotama," means 'Master Gotama, he should be spoken of as the eldest.' Why? Because he is the most senior among them. This is the meaning. Then, the Blessed One, completing the simile for him, said, "Even so" (evameva kho). Just as it is with that chick, so it is with Me. "Avijjāgatāya pajāya" (For the generation gone into ignorance)—ignorance (avijjā) refers to lack of knowledge; 'gone into' that. "Pajāya" is a designation for beings; it refers to beings who have entered inside the shell of ignorance. "Aṇḍabhūtāya" means 'become like an egg,' born or produced in an egg. Just as some beings produced in an egg are called 'egg-born' (aṇḍabhūta), so too these beings are called 'egg-born' because they are produced in the egg-shell of ignorance.
204:
Thus, all these beings are called 'egg-born' (aṇḍabhūta) because they are produced in the egg-shell of ignorance. 'Pariyonaddhāya' means enveloped, bound, or covered from all sides by that egg-shell of ignorance. 'Avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā' means having broken the egg-shell made of ignorance. 'Ekova loke' means that in the entire world of beings, I alone am the one without a second. 'Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho' means having penetrated and realized the unsurpassed, most excellent, and rightly self-awakened Enlightenment, or the praised and beautiful Enlightenment. This name 'Bodhi' is a name for the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa), as well as for the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Both are appropriate. If it is asked whether the path of Arahantship of other persons is the unsurpassed Enlightenment, the answer is 'no.' Why? Because it cannot bestow all virtues and qualities. Among them, the path of Arahantship of some gives only the fruit of Arahantship; for some, the three knowledges (vijjā); for some, the six higher powers (abhiññā); for some, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); and for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa). To Paccekabuddhas, it gives only the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. But the path of Arahantship of the Buddhas bestows the fulfillment of all qualities, just as the consecration of a king bestows sovereignty over the whole world. Therefore, the unsurpassed Enlightenment does not belong to any other person. 'Abhisambuddho' means known through higher knowledge, penetrated, reached, or attained.

Now, the comparison of the simile spoken by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with "Evameva kho" should be understood by comparing it with the meaning as follows: Just as that hen performs the three types of actions such as sitting on her eggs, even so the Blessed One, as a Bodhisatta seated on the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka), performed the three types of contemplation—impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta)—within His own continuity. Just as the eggs do not rot because the hen completes the three types of actions, so the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One as a Bodhisatta did not decline because He completed the three types of contemplation. Just as the moisture and viscosity of the eggs are exhausted by the hen performing the three types of actions, so the moisture of craving that follows through the three realms of existence was exhausted by the Blessed One as a Bodhisatta completing the three types of contemplation. Just as the egg-shells become thin by the hen performing the three types of actions, so the egg-shell of ignorance became thin by the Blessed One as a Bodhisatta completing the three types of contemplation. Just as the claws and beaks of the chicks become firm and hard by the hen performing the three types of actions, so the insight knowledge reached the state of being sharp, hard, clear, and courageous by the Blessed One as a Bodhisatta completing the three types of contemplation. Just as the time of maturity for the chicks arrives by the hen performing the three types of actions...
205:
For the Blessed One, while being a Bodhisatta, through the fulfillment of the threefold contemplation (anupassanā), it was the time of the maturation of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), the time of its growth, and the time of approaching the threshold of the Path. Just as a chick, through the hen's threefold action, pierces the eggshell with the tip of its claws or its beak and emerges safely, flapping its wings; so too, the Blessed One, by fulfilling the threefold contemplation, conceived the womb of insight knowledge, pierced the eggshell of ignorance (avijjā) with the Path of Arahantship attained in due order, flapped the wings of direct knowledge (abhiññā), and safely realized all the Buddha-qualities. This should be understood as that time.

"Brahmin, I am the eldest and the foremost in the world" means: Brahmin, just as among those chicks, the one that first pierces the eggshell and is born is the eldest; even so, among the generation fallen into ignorance, I am called the eldest and the most senior because I was born first through the noble birth (ariya-jāti), having pierced that eggshell of ignorance. And I am the foremost because I am peerless in all qualities.

Thus, the Blessed One, having revealed his peerless status as the eldest and foremost to the Brahmin, now began to show the practice by which he attained that state, starting from the preliminary stage, saying: "Brahmin, my energy was aroused," and so forth. In that passage, "Brahmin, my energy was aroused" means: Brahmin, I did not attain this peerless status as the eldest and foremost through laziness, lack of mindfulness, a restless body, or a distracted mind. On the contrary, for the sake of that attainment, my energy was indeed aroused. Sitting at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), I aroused energy consisting of the fourfold Right Efforts (sammappadhāna); it was upheld and exerted without slackening. Because it was so aroused, my energy was unshaken. Not only energy, but my mindfulness was also established, being directed towards the object; and because it was established, it was unconfused. "The calmed body was not restless" means that through the power of the tranquility of body and mind, my body also became tranquil. In this context, since the physical body (rūpakāya) is also tranquil when the mental body (nāmakāya) is tranquil, it is said "the calmed body" without distinguishing between the mental and physical bodies. "Not restless" means that because the body was tranquil, it was without agitation; it means it was free from distress.
206:
"The concentrated mind was one-pointed" means my mind was also well-composed, well-established, as if it had reached absorption (appanā). Because it was concentrated, it was one-pointed, unshaken, and motionless. By this much, the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) of jhāna is described.

Now, wishing to show the distinction starting from the first jhāna attained through this practice and ending with the threefold knowledge (tevijjā), he said: "That I," and so forth. Whatever should be said there by way of analytical method has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

In the words "Brahmin, this was my...", it is called "knowledge" (vijjā) in the sense of making things known. What does it make known? It makes known the previous existence (past lives). "Ignorance" (avijjā) is the delusion that covers it, in the sense of not making that same previous existence known. "Darkness" (tamo) is that same delusion, called darkness in the sense of covering. "Light" (āloka) is that same knowledge, called light in the sense of producing radiance. Here, "knowledge was attained" is the meaning; the rest are words of praise. The construction (yojanā) here is: "This knowledge was attained by me; for me who has attained knowledge, ignorance was destroyed, it perished." Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This same method applies to the other two pairs of terms.

In the phrase "yathā taṃ," "taṃ" is merely a particle. It means for one who is diligent because of the non-disappearance of mindfulness, who is ardent (ātāpī) because of the heat of energy, and who is resolute (pahitatta) because of having no regard for body or life and having sent the mind towards Nibbāna. This is what is meant: Just as for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, ignorance would be destroyed, knowledge would arise, darkness would be destroyed, and light would arise; even so, for me, ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, and light arose. I have obtained the fruit appropriate to that application of exertion.

"Brahmin, this was my first breaking out, like that of a chick from the eggshell" means: Brahmin, just as for a chick, piercing the eggshell with its beak or the tip of its claws and breaking out from that eggshell, emerging, is a rebirth in the species of fowl; so too, for me, piercing the eggshell of ignorance that covered the aggregates previously lived in with the beak of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa), it was the first breaking out, the first emergence, the first noble birth. This is the method regarding the talk on the recollection of past lives.
207:
In the discussion on passing away and rebirth (cutūpapāta), 'knowledge' (vijjā) refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). 'Ignorance' (avijjā) refers to the ignorance that veils passing away and rebirth. Just as it was stated in the discussion on the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa), 'Having broken the eggshell of ignorance that veils the aggregates previously lived in with the beak of the knowledge of recollection of past lives,' so too in this discussion on passing away and rebirth, it should be said: 'Having broken the eggshell of ignorance that veils passing away and rebirth with the beak of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth.'

Desiring to show the Brahmin the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khaya-ñāṇa), which is the fruit of Arahantship comprehended through the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), the Buddha said: 'Brahmin, this was my third knowledge,' and so forth. In that statement, 'knowledge' (vijjā) refers to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-vijjā). 'Ignorance' (avijjā) refers to the ignorance that veils the Four Noble Truths. In the statement, 'Brahmin, this was my third hatching,' it means: 'Brahmin, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that veils the Four Noble Truths with the beak of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, my third hatching, my third emergence, my third noble birth occurred.' It is like a young chick that breaks the eggshell with its beak or the tips of its claws, hatches from that shell, and is born into the flock of chickens.

What is shown by this? Brahmin, when that young chick breaks the eggshell and emerges from it, it is born only once. As for me, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that veils the aggregates previously lived in, I was first born through the knowledge of recollection of past lives. Then, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that veils the passing away and rebirth of beings, I was born for the second time through the knowledge of the divine eye. Again, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that veils the Four Noble Truths, I was born for the third time through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. Thus, I have been born three times through the three knowledges. This demonstrates that my birth is noble (ariya-jāti) and exceedingly pure. In showing this, he revealed the knowledge of the past through the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the knowledge of the present and future through the divine eye, and all mundane and supramundane qualities through the destruction of the taints. Thus, by manifesting all the qualities of an Omniscient Buddha through the three knowledges, he showed the Brahmin his status as the eldest and foremost by way of his noble birth.

When this was said, the Brahmin Verañja—since the Blessed One, out of compassion for the world and for the Brahmin, had preached the Dhamma revealing the three knowledges and his own supremacy as the eldest and foremost by way of his noble birth which is usually hidden—was filled with a sense of joy throughout his body and mind. Realizing the Blessed One's supremacy as the eldest and foremost by way of his noble birth, he thought, 'A person such as I...'
208:
...said of the Omniscient Buddha, who is the eldest in all the world and endowed with all qualities, that "He does not perform acts of respect and so forth toward others." Oh, how inappropriate is this ignorance!' Thus censuring himself, he reached the conclusion: 'Now, in this world, this Venerable Gotama is the eldest because he was born first by way of the noble birth, and he is the foremost because he is peerless in all qualities.' He then addressed the Blessed One: 'The Venerable Gotama is the eldest; the Venerable Gotama is the foremost.' Having said this, and again greatly rejoicing in the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma, he said: 'Excellent, Master Gotama!' and so forth. The meaning of those words is exactly as previously explained.

## 2. Sīhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'abhiññātā' means known, well-known, or famous. 'Santhāgāre' refers to an assembly hall built for the relaxation of the public. It is said that this assembly hall was in the center of the city and was clearly visible to those standing in the four directions. People coming from the four directions would first rest in that hall and then proceed to their respective convenient locations. Some also say it was a hall built for the Licchavi princes to manage the affairs of the state. Sitting there, the Licchavi princes would manage, execute, and deliberate on state affairs. 'Sannisinnā' means they were seated on expensive and excellent rugs and cushions specially prepared for their seating, under raised white umbrellas. 'Anekapariyāyena buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti' means that after deliberating on their duties in the royal house and their service to the world, they spoke of, praised, and illuminated the qualities of the Buddha in many ways.

Those princes were wise, endowed with faith, and were noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) who were Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), Once-returners (sakadāgāmi), or Non-returners (anāgāmi). All of them, having cut through the worldly entanglements, spoke in praise of the Triple Gem, beginning with the Buddha. In that context, the praise of the Buddha is threefold: praise of conduct (cariya-vaṇṇa), praise of the physical body (sarīra-vaṇṇa), and praise of qualities (guṇa-vaṇṇa). Among these three, the princes began by speaking of the praise of his conduct: 'Indeed, the Sammāsambuddha has performed what is difficult to perform! While fulfilling the thirty perfections—namely, the ten perfections (pāramī), the ten higher perfections (upapāramī), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī)—for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, he brought to perfection the three modes of conduct: conduct for the benefit of relatives, conduct for the benefit of the world, and conduct for the sake of Buddhahood, and he made the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga).' Thus, speaking of the Buddha's virtues through the five hundred and fifty Jātakas, they recounted his story up to his arrival in the Tusita heaven.
209:
When praising the virtues of the Dhamma, they spoke of the Dhamma's qualities according to its divisions, saying: "The Blessed One has well taught the Dhamma; by way of Nikāya, there are five Nikāyas; by way of Piṭaka, there are three Piṭakas; by way of Anga, there are nine Angas; and by way of Dhammakkhandha, there are eighty-four thousand Dhammakkhandhas."

When praising the virtues of the Saṅgha, they spoke of the Saṅgha's qualities by summarizing the act of renunciation, saying: "Noble sons who have gained faith after hearing the Teacher's Dhamma desanā, renounce their mass of wealth and circle of relatives. Without regard for positions such as the white parasol, the office of the crown prince, the general, the merchant, or the treasurer, they go forth and ordain in the Teacher's noble Dispensation. Even among those of royal birth who renounced the white parasol to ordain, such as King Bhaddiya, King Mahākappina, and King Pukkusāti, there were eighty thousand (80,000) during the Buddha's time. As for those like the noble son Yasa, the merchant's son Soṇa, and the noble son Raṭṭhapāla, who renounced wealth worth hundreds of millions to ordain, there is no limit to their number. Such noble sons as these ordain in the Teacher's Dispensation."

"Sīha Senāpati" refers to the commander of the army named Sīha. In the city of Vesālī, there were seven thousand, seven hundred and seven (7,707) kings. All of them assembled and, taking the consensus of all, said, "Search for one who is capable of administering the country." While searching, they saw Prince Sīha and, deciding "This prince will be capable," they gave him the general's parasol covered with a rug the color of a red ruby. It is in reference to his appointment as general that it is said, "Sīha Senāpati."

"Nigaṇṭhasāvaka" means a donor of the four requisites and a supporter of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta. On the surface of Jambudīpa, there were three chief supporters of the Nigaṇṭhas: the householder Upāli in Nālandā, the Sakyan Vappa in Kapilavatthu, and this General Sīha in Vesālī.

"Nisinno hoti" means that although seats were arranged among the assembly of the remaining kings, General Sīha sat in the center on a costly royal seat prepared for him. "Nissaṃsayaṃ" means without doubt, certainly, or surely. Indeed, they would not praise the virtues of someone with little influence in such a way with hundreds of reasons.

"Yena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto tenupasaṅkami" means that Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, thinking, "If this Sīha hears someone praising the virtues of the ascetic Gotama and goes to see him, it will be my loss..."
210:
...thinking, "It will be a loss for me," he had previously said to General Sīha: "General, in this world, many wander about saying, 'I am the Buddha, I am the Buddha.' If you wish to approach anyone for an audience, ask me. I will send you to the appropriate place and restrain you from the inappropriate place." The general, repeatedly reflecting on those words, thought, "If he sends me, I will go; if not, I will not go," and thus he approached Nigaṇṭha, the son of Nāṭa.

Then, upon hearing the general's words, Nigaṇṭha was overwhelmed by powerful grief as if pressed by a great mountain. Feeling displeased, he thought, "Now he desires to go to the very place where I do not want him to go; I am ruined!" and thinking, "I will find a way to prevent him," he said the words beginning with "But how can you..." In speaking thus, Nigaṇṭha destroyed the joy (pīti) that had arisen in Sīha, like one striking a wandering ox with a stick, or like one extinguishing a burning lamp, or like one overturning an alms-bowl filled with food. "Gamiyābhisaṅkhāra" refers to the effort or preparation made by way of arranging elephant-vehicles and so on, and taking perfumes, garlands, and so forth. "So paṭippassambhi" means that the effort subsided or was calmed.

"Dutiyampi kho" means for the second time. On this occasion as well, when the Licchavī princes praised the virtues of the Buddha, they spoke of the beauty of the body of the One of Ten Powers, defining it from the soles of the feet below to the tips of the hair above, from the time of the Tusita heaven until the seat of Great Enlightenment, by way of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, and the fathom-long aura. When praising the virtues of the Dhamma, they spoke of the Dhamma's qualities by way of its being well-proclaimed, saying, "There is no such thing as a slip even in a single word or a single syllable." When praising the virtues of the Saṅgha, they spoke of the Saṅgha's qualities by way of their practice, saying, "Those who renounce such glory, wealth, and prosperity to ordain in the Teacher's Dispensation are not of a lazy nature; rather, they fulfill the thirteen dhutaṅga qualities, strive in the seven types of contemplation (anupassanā), and make use of the thirty-eight varieties of meditation objects."

On the third occasion, however, the Licchavī princes praised the Buddha's virtues according to the Suttanta method, "Itipi so Bhagavā..." They praised the Dhamma's virtues according to the Suttanta method, "Svākkhāto Bhagavatā Dhammo..." and the Saṅgha's virtues as "Suppaṭipanno..."
211:
“The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples practices well,” and so on—in this manner of the Suttanta discourses, they spoke of the virtues of the Saṅgha. When they spoke thus, General Sīha thought: “Since the third day, these Licchavī princes have been speaking of the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and their mouths are not enough [to exhaust the praise]. Indeed, that Blessed One is endowed with unfailing virtues. Without letting go of this joy (pīti) that has now arisen, I shall see the Fully Enlightened One this very day.” Then the thought occurred to General Sīha: “What can the Nigaṇṭhas do to me?” In this context, “What can the Nigaṇṭhas do to me?” means “In what way can the Nigaṇṭhas affect me?” Whether I ask permission or not [makes no difference]. Indeed, even if asked, those Nigaṇṭhas cannot provide the success of vehicles and mounts, nor can they grant special authority; and even if I go without asking, they cannot prevent me. The meaning is that asking permission from these Nigaṇṭhas is fruitless.

In the phrase “He departed from Vesālī,” there is an analogy: just as when it rains in the summer, the water flowing down into a river travels only a little and then stops without continuing, so too was the time when the joy that arose in General Sīha on the first day, thinking “I will see the One of Ten Powers,” was obstructed by the Nigaṇṭha. Just as on the second day, when it rains, the flowing water enters the river, travels a little, and then stops upon hitting a mound of sand, so too was the time when the joy that arose in General Sīha on the second day, thinking “I will see the One of Ten Powers,” was obstructed by the Nigaṇṭha. Just as on the third day, when it rains, the flowing water enters the river, dragging along old leaves, dry sticks, wood, and rubbish, breaks through the sand mound, and flows inclining only towards the ocean, so too General Sīha, having heard the talk on the virtues of the Three Jewels on the third day, became filled with joy and gladness. Thinking, “The Nigaṇṭhas are fruitless, the Nigaṇṭhas are useless; what can these Nigaṇṭhas do to me? I will go to the presence of the Teacher,” he directed his mind and departed from Vesālī. While departing, he thought: “I have long desired to go to the presence of the One of Ten Powers; however, it is not fitting for me to go in an unrecognizable guise.” Having ordered, “Let all who wish to go to the presence of the One of Ten Powers come forth,” he had five hundred chariots harnessed. Mounting a noble chariot, surrounded by those five hundred chariots and a great assembly, and having perfumes, flowers, and aromatic powders brought along, he departed. “Divā divassa” means during the day, just after midday had passed.

When approaching the place where the Blessed One was, upon entering the monastery, he saw from afar the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide radiance, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the six-colored dense Buddha-rays. He thought: “I have lived so close to such a Great Man, yet for so long a time I did not see him!”
212:
Thinking, “I have indeed been deceived; I have indeed missed out on special benefits,” he approached the Blessed One with joy and gladness, like a poor man who has seen a great treasure. “Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākaronti” means they speak of a reason that is consistent with the reason taught by the Venerable Gotama. Here, the word “Dhamma” refers to “cause” or “reason,” as in “Knowledge of cause is the discrimination of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā).” In this context, “cause” refers to the meaning of the sound that has arisen, because it is the cause for the occurrence of that sound. Indeed, the use of sound is associated with the meaning. “Anukāraṇa” is that very reason as spoken by others. “Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo” means that your statement, being accompanied by reasons along with the reasons spoken by others, or any subsequent explanation of that statement, does not reach a point or cause that should be censured even slightly by the wise. The intended meaning is: “Is there no ground for censure in your statement in any way?” “Anabbhakkhātukāmā” means they do not wish to speak falsely. The meaning of “Atthi sīhapariyāyo” and so on should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Verañja section. “Paramena assāsena” means by the supreme consolation known as the four paths and four fruits. “Assāsāya dhammaṃ desemi” means “I teach the Dhamma for the sake of consolation and for the sake of stability.” Thus, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to General Sīha with eight factors.

“Anuviccakāraṃ” means “Do what should be done after knowing, reflecting, and weighing.” “Sādhu hoti” means “It is good.” For people like you, if they see you seeing me and going to me for refuge, or seeing a Nigaṇṭha and going to a Nigaṇṭha for refuge, the censure might arise: “Does this General Sīha go for refuge to whomever he happens to see?” Therefore, [the Buddha] shows that acting after investigation is good for people like you. “Paṭākaṃ parihareyyuṃ” means it is said that those Nigaṇṭhas, upon obtaining such a disciple, would raise a banner and wander about the city proclaiming: “Such a king, or a great royal minister, or a merchant has become a disciple who has gone to us for refuge.” Why do they wander so? Thinking, “In this way, our greatness will become manifest,” and also thinking, “If remorse should arise in him, thinking ‘Why did I go to these Nigaṇṭhas for refuge?’, he will not turn back, dismissing it with the thought, ‘Many people know that I have gone to these for refuge; it is difficult to turn back now.’” Therefore, He said, “They would carry a banner.” “Opānabhūtaṃ” means existing like a prepared well. “Kulaṃ” means your house. “Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsīti” means in the past, when ten, twenty, or sixty people arrived...
213:
(General Sīha, in the past, upon seeing the Nigaṇṭhas) used to give without saying "there is nothing." Now, the Buddha exhorted him: "Do not cut off the gifts to these Nigaṇṭhas merely because you have come to me for refuge; gifts should indeed be given to those who have arrived." Sīha replied, "Venerable Sir, I have heard that before." When asked from whom he had heard it, it was from the Nigaṇṭhas. Those Nigaṇṭhas used to boast in the houses of donors, saying: "We say that gifts should be given to anyone who arrives. But the ascetic Gotama says: 'Gifts should be given only to me, not to others; gifts should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others; only the gift given to me has great fruit, not that given to others; only the gift given to my disciples has great fruit, not that given to the disciples of others.'" It was in reference to such statements that General Sīha said, "I have heard that before."

The Gradual Discourse (Anupubbīkathā) refers to the teaching given in sequence: after Giving (Dāna), Virtue (Sīla); after Virtue, Heaven (Sagga); and after Heaven, the Path (Magga). Among these, the Discourse on Giving (Dānakathā) is as follows: This thing called giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, and the basis of wealth. It is the protection, the shelter, the resort, and the refuge for one who has fallen into ruin. In this world and the world beyond, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, resort, or refuge equal to giving. This giving is like a lion throne made of jewels because it is a support; it is like the Great Earth because it is a foundation; it is like a clinging rope because it is an object to hold onto. It is like a boat because it enables one to cross over suffering; it is like a brave soldier on the battlefield because it provides consolation; it is like a well-fortified city because it protects from danger; it is like a lotus because it is unstained by the impurities of stinginess; it is like fire because it burns away those impurities; it is like a cobra because it is unassailable; it is like a lion because it is fearless; it is like an elephant because it is powerful; it is like a white bull because it is considered highly auspicious; it is like Valāhaka the horse king because it leads to the land of safety. This giving is the path I have traveled; it is my lineage. While I was fulfilling the ten perfections, I performed many great sacrifices such as the Velāma Great Sacrifice, the Mahāgovinda Great Sacrifice, the Mahāsudassana Great Sacrifice, and the Vessantara Great Sacrifice. Even when I was a hare king, I won the heart of the seeker (Sakka) who arrived by sacrificing myself into the blazing fire. In the world, giving grants the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Māra, the prosperity of Brahmā, the prosperity of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), and it also grants the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (Sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa), the Knowledge of a Private Buddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), and the Knowledge of Supreme Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi-ñāṇa). Thus, the Buddha gave a discourse connected with the virtues of giving.

Because one who gives is able to undertake virtue, the Buddha taught the Discourse on Virtue (Sīlakathā) immediately after the Discourse on Giving. The Discourse on Virtue is as follows: Virtue is the support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, resort, and refuge. Virtue is my...
214:
...lineage. When I was the Nāga king Saṅkhapāla, the Nāga king Bhūridatta, the Nāga king Campeyya, King Sīlava, the elephant king who cared for his mother (Mātuposaka), and the elephant king Chaddanta, I fulfilled virtue throughout countless existences. For the prosperity of this world and the world beyond, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, resort, or refuge equal to virtue. There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no scent like the scent of virtue. Indeed, the world with its devas cannot tire of looking at a person adorned with the ornament of virtue and anointed with the scent of virtue. Thus, the Buddha gave a discourse connected with the virtues of virtue.

To show that this heaven can be obtained by relying on this virtue, he taught the Discourse on Heaven (Saggakathā) immediately after the Discourse on Virtue. The Discourse on Heaven is as follows: "This heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasant; here there is constant play, and prosperity is always obtained. The devas of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) enjoy divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsā devas enjoy it for thirty-six million years." Thus, he gave a discourse connected with the virtues of heaven. Even the mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the prosperity of heaven. It has also been said: "Monks, I could speak a discourse on heaven in many ways."

After enticing him with the discourse on heaven, just like decorating an elephant and then cutting off its trunk, he taught the danger, vileness, and corruption of sensual pleasures to show that "this heaven is also impermanent and unstable; one should not form strong passion for it," using methods such as: "Sensual pleasures provide little satisfaction, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is great." In this context, 'danger' (ādīnava) means fault. 'Vileness' (okāra) means a low state or the fact of being inferior. 'Corruption' (saṅkilesa) means the defilement of beings in Saṃsāra by those sensual pleasures. As it was said: "Alas, friends, beings are indeed corrupted."

Having thus threatened him with the danger of sensual pleasures, he revealed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). A 'ready mind' (kallacitta) means a mind free from the sickness of defilements. 'Exalted' (sāmukkaṃsikā) means the teaching of the Noble Truths which was extracted by himself, seen by his own self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), and not shared with others. Therefore, he taught: Suffering (dukkha), the Origin (samudaya), Cessation (nirodha), and the Path (magga). 'Stainless and pure' (virajaṃ vītamalaṃ) means free from dust and free from impurities due to the absence of the dust of passion and so forth. In the term 'Dhamma-eye' (dhamma-cakkhu), the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) is intended. To show the manner in which that Path of Stream-entry arises, he taught: "Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation." Indeed, that knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry arises by taking Nibbāna—the cessation of suffering—as its object, while penetrating all conditioned things by way of its function. That General Sīha became one who had seen the Noble Truths.
215: Because one is free from impurities such as lust and so on, one is called 'vītamala' (one who is stainless). 'Dhammacakkhu' (the Dhamma-eye) in this context refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). To show the manner in which that Path of Stream-entry arises, it is said: 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' This is because that Path-knowledge arises by taking Nibbāna—the cessation of suffering—as its object, and by penetrating all conditioned things (saṅkhata) through its function in this way. Because the truth of the Noble Truths has been seen by this Path-knowledge, one is called 'diṭṭhadhamma' (one who has seen the Dhamma). The same method applies to the remaining terms. Because one has crossed over doubt by this Path-knowledge, one is called 'tiṇṇavicikiccha' (one who has crossed over doubt). Because indecision or wavering such as 'is it this or that?' has been removed from that person, one is called 'vigatakathaṅkatha' (one who is free from indecision). Because one has attained fearlessness, one is called 'vesārajjappatta' (one who has attained fearlessness). In what place is one fearless? It is in the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Teacher. Because that person no longer needs to rely on others and does not exist in this Dispensation by believing others, one is called 'aparappaccaya' (one who is independent of others). 'Pavattamaṃsa' means to search in the market for allowable meat that is being sold normally by paying its price. 'Sambahulā nigaṇṭhā' refers to about five hundred Nigaṇṭhas. 'Thūlaṃ pasuṃ' refers to a large-bodied four-legged animal such as a deer, a buffalo, or a pig. 'Uddissakata' means meat from an animal specifically killed for oneself. 'Paṭiccakamma' means that the person, on account of that meat, comes into contact with the unwholesome kamma of killing a living being. It is the view of those Nigaṇṭhas that the unwholesome kamma of killing belongs half to the donor and half to the recipient. Another way: 'Paṭiccakamma' means what is done on account of oneself. Or, 'paṭiccakamma' is a designation for an action caused by a reason, and because that action exists in this meat, the meat is also called 'paṭiccakamma'. 'Upakaṇṇake' means at the base of the ear (whispering into the ear). 'Alaṃ' is a word of prohibition, meaning 'what is the use of this?'. It means that although those venerable ones, desiring to speak dispraise for a long time, speak dispraise and make accusations, they cannot reach an end (cannot exhaust it). Or, the word 'jiridanti' should be understood in the sense of being ashamed, meaning they are not ashamed. ## ၃။ အဿာဇာနီယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ In the third sutta, 'aṅgehi' means by the factors of quality. 'Tassaṃ disāyaṃ jāto hoti' means being born in that region on the banks of the Sindhu River. Other noble thoroughbred horses are also born in that very place. 'Allaṃ vā sukkhaṃ vā' means wet grass or dry grass. 'Nāññe asse ubbejetā' means not frightening other horses, not kicking, not biting, and not causing a quarrel. 'Sāṭheyya' means deceitfulness, 'kūṭeyya' means fraudulence, 'jimheyya' means crookedness, and 'vaṅkeyya' means tortuousness. Thus, by these four terms, only the untrained (uncultured) nature of that horse is meant.
216:
It is taught. 'Vāhī' means one who has the nature of carrying, one who follows the given advice. 'Yāva jīvitamaraṇapariyādānā' means until life is ended by death. 'Sakkaccaṃ paribhuñjati' means consuming after reflecting as if it were the Deathless. In the words 'purisathamena' and so on, the power of wisdom and so forth are taught. 'Saṇṭhānaṃ' means receding, subsiding.

## 4. Assakhaḷuṅkasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'Pehi' is said, meaning 'Go!' 'Piṭṭhito rathaṃ pavatteti' means he drives the chariot from behind, pressing the yoke with the shoulder bone and turning the chariot with the rear part while receding. 'Pacchā laṅghati, kubbaraṃ hanati' means lifting the two hind legs and kicking with them, destroying the chariot's wheel-rim. 'Tidaṇḑaṃ bhañjati' means breaking the three poles at the front of the chariot. 'Rathīsāya satthiṃ ussajjitvā' means bending the head, letting the yoke fall to the ground, and then kicking the chariot axle with the thigh. 'Ajjhomaddati' means standing while trampling the chariot axle with the two front legs. 'Ubbaṭumaṃ rathaṃ karoti' means driving the chariot onto high ground or thorny places. 'Anādiyitvā' means staying without paying attention, without counting. 'Mukhādhānaṃ' means the iron ring (bit) given to be placed in the mouth. 'Khīlaṭṭhāyī' means standing still like a post, keeping the four legs motionless like pillars. In this sutta, only the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) is taught.

## 5. Malasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'Asajjhāyamalā' means non-recitation of the learned mantras is a stain. 'Anuṭṭhānamalā gharā' means lack of exertion is the stain of houses. 'Vaṇṇassa' means of the physical complexion. 'Rakkhato' means of one who protects any of one's own property. 'Avijjā paramaṃ malaṃ' means ignorance, which is the lack of knowledge regarding the eight instances, called the root of the round of suffering, and which is like a thick mass of darkness, is the supreme stain among the remaining stains of unwholesome states. There is indeed no stain greater than that ignorance. In this sutta also, only the round of suffering is taught.

## 6. Dūteyyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'Dūteyyaṃ' means the work of a messenger. 'Gantumarahati' means being worthy of carrying the message called messengership. 'Sotā' means one who listens to the message given by that person.
217:
He gives (the message); he is a listener to those words. 'Sāvetā' means one who, having grasped that message, repeats it, saying, "You have said such a thing." 'Uggahitā' means one who learns it well. 'Dhāretā' means one who (having listened) bears it well in mind. 'Viññātā' means one who personally understands the meaning of that speech (whether it is beneficial or not). 'Viññāpetā' means one who makes others understand. 'Sahitā sahitassa' means one who is skilled in what is consistent and what is inconsistent, thinking, "This message is consistent, this message is inconsistent"; being skilled in what leads to welfare and what does not, when making the message known, he notes the meaning connected with welfare and speaks it. 'Na vyathati' means he does not tremble or have his hair stand on end. 'Asandiddhaṃ' means being without doubt, having doubt removed. 'Puccito' means being able to answer when asked for the sake of a problem.
