17-18. In the seventh sutta, 'ruṇṇena' means by crying. 'Ākappena' means by the arrangement of dress, such as wearing and cloaking. 'Vanabhaṅgena' means by gifts such as flowers and fruits brought from the forest by breaking them off. In the eighth sutta, the method is the same.

## 9. Pahārādasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, 'Pahārādo' is the name of an Asura. 'Asurindo' means the chief of the Asuras. Among the Asuras, these three—Vepacitti, Rāhu, and Pahārāda—are the chiefs. "Approached where the Blessed One was" means that from the day the Ten-Powered Blessed One attained Enlightenment, he thought, "I will go today, I will go tomorrow," and thus eleven years passed. In the twelfth year, while the Teacher was residing in Verañjā, he gave rise to the thought, "I will go to the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One." Thinking, "Twelve years have passed while I was imagining 'today' and 'tomorrow'; now I shall go indeed," at that very moment, surrounded by a host of Asuras, he departed from the Asura abode and approached the Blessed One during the day, and stood at one side. It is said that he came with the intention, "I will listen to the Dhamma only after asking the Tathāgata a question." However, from the moment he saw the Tathāgata, out of reverence for the Buddha, he was unable to ask and, having paid homage to the Teacher, stood at one side. Then the Teacher thought: "This Pahārāda will not be able to speak first if I do not speak. I will ask him a single question in the area where he is experienced and proficient, in order to initiate the conversation."
218:
Then, to initiate the conversation, He said, "Api pana Pahārāda," and so on, asking him a question. In that text, "abhiramanti" means "do they find delight?" or "do they live without weariness?" That Pahārāda Asura, being pleased with the thought, "The Blessed One asks me only about things in which I am experienced," replied, "Venerable Sir, they do delight."

"Anupubbaninno" and all subsequent terms are synonyms for the state of sloping down gradually. "Na āyatakeneva papāto" means it is not a sudden precipice from the very beginning like a deep pit with a broken bank. It shows that the ocean, starting from the shore, becomes gradually deeper by an inch, two inches, a span, a cubit, a fathom, an usabha, a gāvuta, a yojana, and so on, until it reaches a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas at the foot of Mount Sineru.

"Ṭhitadhammo" means having a stable nature. "Kuṇapena" means with the carcass of any animal such as an elephant or a horse. "Thalaṃ ussāreti" means it casts it onto the dry land by the striking of waves alone, as if picking it up with a hand.

In this passage "Gaṅgā Yamunā," it is appropriate to pause here and tell the story of the origin of these rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. First, this Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent. Within this Jambudīpa, the region of four thousand yojanas covered by water is known as the Great Ocean. Humans live in a region of three thousand yojanas. In the remaining three thousand yojanas, the Himavā (Himalaya) is situated. It is five hundred yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and is picturesque with five hundred rivers flowing in all directions. In that Himavā, there are seven great lakes: Anotatta, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Chaddanta, Kuṇāla, Mandākinī, and Sīhappapāta, each being fifty yojanas in length, breadth, and depth, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.

Among those seven great lakes, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by five mountains: Sudassana, Cittakūṭa, Kāḷakူṭa, Gandhamādana, and Kelāsa. Among those five mountains, Mount Sudassana is made of gold, two hundred yojanas in height, and stands covering that very lake, curved inward like a crow's beak. Mount Cittakūṭa is made of all kinds of jewels. Mount Kāḷakūṭa is made of collyrium (black stone). Mount Gandhamādana is made of plateaus, is the color of mung beans inside, and possesses the scent of roots, the scent of heartwood, the scent of softwood, the scent of bark, the scent of shoots, the scent of sap, the scent of leaves, the scent of flowers...
219:
(Mount Gandhamādana), suffused with these ten kinds of scents such as the scent of fruits and the scent of perfumes, and covered with various kinds of medicinal plants, stands shining like a glowing ember on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight. The peak of Mount Kelāsa is made of silver. All those mountain peaks have the same height and shape as Mount Sudassana and stand covering that very Lake Anotatta. On all those mountains, it rains through the power of the devas and the power of the nāgas, and rivers flow on those mountains. All that water enters only into Lake Anotatta. When the moon and the sun travel by the southern or northern course, they cast light into Lake Anotatta through the gaps between the mountains; however, when they travel directly overhead, they do not cast light. For that reason, the name 'Anotatta' (not heated) became well-known for that lake.

In that Lake Anotatta, there are delightful stone slabs; bathing places are well-prepared with clear water like crystal, free from fish and tortoises. In those bathing places, the Buddhas, the Arahants (those whose taints are destroyed), the Paccekabuddhas, and powerful hermits (isis) bathe; devas, yakkhas, and others play in the water.

On the four sides of that Lake Anotatta, there are four outlets: the lion face, the elephant face, the horse face, and the bull face, through which four rivers flow. On the banks of the river issuing from the lion face, lions are very numerous; on the banks of the rivers issuing from the elephant face and others, elephants, horses, and bulls are numerous. The river issuing from the eastern direction circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without approaching the other three rivers, flows through the Eastern Himavanta by a path not frequented by humans and enters the Great Ocean. The rivers issuing from the western and northern directions likewise circle Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and flow through the Western Himavanta and Northern Himavanta respectively by paths not frequented by humans and enter the Great Ocean.

The river issuing from the southern face, however, circles that Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and flows straight towards the north over a stone surface for sixty yojanas. Then, striking a mountain and rising up, it becomes a water current three gāvutas in circumference and travels through the air for sixty yojanas, falling onto a stone slab named Tiyaggala. That stone slab was broken by the force of the water current. There, a great lotus pond named Tiyaggala, fifty yojanas in size, was formed. Breaking the bank of that pond, the water enters into the stone and travels for sixty yojanas. From there, breaking through the solid earth and traveling through a tunnel for sixty yojanas, it strikes the long mountain named Gijjha and flows out as five currents resembling the five fingers on the palm of a hand.
220:
That water current is called Āvaṭṭagaṅgā at the place where it goes circling Lake Anotatta three times. It is called Kaṇhagaṅgā at the place where it goes straight over the stone surface for sixty yojanas. It is called Ākāsagaṅgā at the place where it goes through the air for sixty yojanas. The water current staying on the Tiyaggala stone slab for fifty yojanas is called Tiyaggalapokkharaṇī. It is called Bahalagaṅgā at the place where it breaks the bank, enters the stone, and travels for sixty yojanas. It is called Ummaṅgagaṅgā at the place where it travels through a tunnel for sixty yojanas. At the place where it strikes the long mountain named Gijjha and flows as five currents like the five fingers on a palm, it is known by five names: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus, it should be understood that these five great rivers flow from the Himavanta mountains.

'Savantiyo' refers to any great or small rivers that flow. 'Appenti' means they cling or flow into. 'Dhārā' refers to currents of rainwater. 'Pūrattaṃ' means the state of being full. Indeed, the fact that the ocean's fullness or depletion is not apparent despite the rivers is the nature (dhammatā) of the Great Ocean. It is not possible to say, "Now the rain is scarce, let us take nets and catch fish and tortoises," or "Now the rain is heavy, shall we get a chance to stretch our backs?" In fact, since the beginning of the aeon, the water that stands touching the girdle of Mount Sineru does not sink down even by a finger's breadth, nor does it rise up. 'Ekarasa' means having an unmixed flavor.

'Muttā' refers to various kinds of pearls: small, large, round, long, etc. 'Maṇi' refers to various kinds of gems: red, blue, etc. 'Veḷuriya' refers to various kinds of beryl: the color of bamboo shoots, the color of sirīsa flowers, etc. 'Saṅkha' refers to various kinds of conch shells: those that spiral to the right, those with red interiors, those used for blowing, etc. 'Silā' refers to various kinds of crystals: white, black, the color of kidney beans, etc. 'Pavāḷa' refers to various kinds of coral: small, large, red, deep red, etc. 'Masāragalla' refers to variegated gems. 'Nāga' refers to both the nāgas living on the surface of the waves and the nāgas residing in celestial mansions.

Regarding the words "Aṭṭha Pahārādā" and so on, the Teacher is capable of teaching eight dhammas, or sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, or even thousands. However, because the Asura Pahārāda spoke of the eight (wonders of the ocean), the Buddha thought, "I too will teach by making dhammas similar to those wonders," and thus spoke in this way. In the words "Anupubbasikkhā" (gradual training) and so on: by 'gradual training', the three trainings are taken. By 'gradual action', the thirteen dhutaṅga practices are taken. By 'gradual practice', the seven contemplations (anupassanā), the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā), the thirty-eight classifications of meditation objects, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) are taken. "Not from the very beginning" means that there is no such thing as penetrating the fruit of Arahantship without first fulfilling virtue and so on from the beginning, like a frog jumping. Indeed, one can reach the fruit of Arahantship only by gradually fulfilling virtue, concentration, and wisdom. This is the meaning. 'Ārakā' means it occurs only in a distant place. "Neither depletion nor fullness" means that even if not a single being attains Parinibbāna during the times when no Buddha arises for incalculable aeons, it cannot be said that the Nibbāna element (nibbānadhātu) decreases. When a Buddha arises, even in a single assembly, incalculable beings reach the deathless Nibbāna; even then, it cannot be said that the Nibbāna element becomes full.
221:
Regarding the Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma (factors of enlightenment), the phrase "it is not only from the beginning that one penetrates the fruit of Arahatship" means that there is no such thing as penetrating the fruit of Arahatship without first fulfilling virtue (sīla) and so forth, like a frog jumping. Indeed, it means that one can only reach Arahatship after fulfilling virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) in due order. "Ārakā" means only in a distant place. "Because beings cannot enter Nibbāna, there is no decrease or fullness in the Nibbāna element" means that even during incalculable aeons (kappas) when no Buddha arises and not even a single being can attain Parinibbāna, it cannot be said at that time that "the Nibbāna element is depleted." Conversely, when a Buddha arises and incalculable beings attain the Deathless (Nibbāna) in a single assembly, it cannot be said at that time that "the Nibbāna element is full."

## 10. Uposatha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth discourse, "nisinno hoti" (he was sitting) refers to the Buddha staying in the jeweled palace of the lay devotee Visākhā for the purpose of performing the Uposatha. After sitting, while observing the minds of the monks, he saw an immoral person and thought, "If I were to recite the Pātimokkha while this person is sitting here, his head would split into seven pieces." Out of compassion for that person, he remained silent. "Abhikkantā" means passed or exhausted. "Uddhaste aruṇe" refers to the time when the dawn rises. "Nandimukhiyā" refers to the time of having a joyful face. "Apari-suddhā, Ānanda, parisā" means that instead of saying directly, "Such and such a person is impure," he said, "Ānanda, the assembly is impure." The remaining words are clear in all places.

## Mahāvagga, the Second.

## 3. Gahapati Vagga

## 1. Paṭhama Ugga Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first discourse of the third vagga, regarding the phrase "he sits on the prepared seat," the decision should be understood. In the house of Ugga the householder, five hundred seats were always prepared for five hundred monks; he sat on one of those seats. "Taṃ suṇāhi" means "listen to those eight wonderful things" or "listen to that wonderful thing which has eight aspects." "Cittaṃ pasīdi" means that even the thought "Is he the Buddha or not?" did not arise; rather, the clear and undisturbed thought "This is indeed the Buddha" arose. "Sakāni vā ñātikulāni" means just enough for one's own sustenance...
222:
...taking just enough wealth for his own sustenance, let them go to the houses of their relatives. "To whom among you shall I give?" means "To which man among you shall I give? Tell me your desire." One who gives rise to the thought, "I will give this much, I will not give this much; I will give this, I will not give this," is called a "discriminator" (paṭivibhatta). But for me, there is no such mind. Indeed, it is shared with those of virtue, just like the property of the Saṅgha or the property of a group. "I will attend with respect" means "I will serve with my own hands; I will approach with respect."

"Venerable Sir, it is not wonderful that deities approach me and speak thus. But that I do not recognize any elevation of mind (māna) because of those deities' words, that alone is wonderful," he says. "Sādhu, sādhu, bhikkhū"—here, although he addresses the monks, it should be understood that this "Sādhu" is to express delight in the householder Ugga's explanation.

## 2. Dutiya Ugga Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "Nāgavane" refers to the garden named Nāgavana belonging to that wealthy merchant. That merchant, having had perfumes, garlands, and so on taken to that garden in the morning, went there wishing to enjoy the garden, and while enjoying himself, he saw the Blessed One. Immediately upon seeing him, his mind became clear as in the previous method, and the intoxication caused by drinking liquor vanished at that very moment. Referring to that, he spoke thus. "Oṇojesiṃ" means he donated by pouring water on the hands. "Asuka" means a person with such a name. "I give with an even mind" shows that he gives by making the gift equal, without making a distinction in mind such as "a little to this person, a lot to that person." "Ārocenti" means they speak while standing in the sky. By the words "That fetter (saṃyojana) does not exist," the lay follower declares his own fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmī-phala).

## 3. Paṭhama Hatthaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "Hatthako Āဠဝကော" refers to the prince who received the name "Hatthaka" because he was received by the hands of the Blessed One from the hands of the demon Āḷavaka. He is called "sīlavā" (virtuous) because he is endowed with the five precepts and the ten precepts. He is called "cāgavā" (generous) because he is endowed with generosity. "Venerable Sir, how is it in this explanation of the Blessed One?" is the meaning of "Kaccittha, bhante." He is called "appiccho" (of few wishes) because of his fewness of wishes regarding his attainments.
223:
## 4. Dutiya Hatthaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth discourse, "with about five hundred lay devotees" means being surrounded by five hundred noble disciple lay devotees who were Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) or Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī). After having breakfast, he took perfumes, flowers, scents, and powders and approached the Blessed One. Sangaha-vatthu (bases of sympathy) are the causes for supporting others. "Tehāhaṃ" means "I, by means of those four bases of sympathy." "I support that person with giving (dāna)" means supporting by giving plows, oxen, food, seeds, etc., as well as perfumes, flowers, capital, and so forth. "By endearing speech (peyyavajja)" means supporting by speaking pleasant, gentle, and endearing words such as "mother," "father," "brother," or "sister." "By beneficial conduct (atthacariyā)" means knowing that "this person does not need support through giving or endearing speech, but is one who should be supported through beneficial conduct," and thus supporting them by performing beneficial acts to complete a task that has arisen. "By impartiality (samānattatā)" means knowing that "this person does not need support through giving, etc., but should be supported through impartiality," and thus supporting them by treating them as an equal to oneself through eating, drinking, and sitting together. "But they do not think that the words of a poor man should be listened to in that way" means that they do not consider the words of a poor person, who is unable to give or do anything, as something to be listened to. However, they do consider my words as something to be listened to; they abide by the advice given and do not think my instruction should be transgressed. "Yoni kho tyāyaṃ" means "this support through these four bases of sympathy is indeed your means (upāya)." It should be understood that in these two discourses, the Teacher taught virtue (sīla), generosity (cāga), and wisdom (paññā) in combination.

## 5-6. Mahānāma Sutta etc. Vaṇṇanā

25-26. In the fifth discourse, "atthūpaparikkhitā hoti" means one who investigates what is beneficial and what is not, and what is a cause and what is not. In the sixth discourse, faith (saddhā), virtue (sīla), and generosity (cāga) are taught in combination.

## 7. Paṭhama Bala Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh discourse, "ujjhatti-balā" means having the power of fault-finding. For fools, fault-finding is their only power, thinking, "This person said such and such; he said it to me, not to anyone else." "Nijjhatti-balā" means the power of conviction, seeing whether a meaning is beneficial or not, thinking, "This meaning is not like this, it is like that." "Paṭisaṅkhāna-balā" means the power of reflection. "Khanti-balā" means the power of patience (endurance).
224:
## 8. Dutiya-bala-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "powers" (balāni) refer to the powers of knowledge (ñāṇa-balāni). "Claims the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayaṃ paṭijānāti) means he claims Arahantship. "As impermanent" (aniccato) means in the manner of non-existence after having come to be. "As it really is" (yathābhūtaṃ) means according to its true nature. "With right wisdom" (sammapaññāya) means with the path-wisdom (magga-paññā) together with insight (vipassanā). "Like a pit of glowing coals" (aṅgārakāsūpamā) means these sensual pleasures are compared to a pit of glowing coals in the sense of causing burning torment.

"Inclined toward seclusion" (vivekaninnaṃ) means inclined toward Nibbāna through the power of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Established in seclusion" (vivekaṭṭhaṃ) means secluded or far removed from defilements. "Delighting in renunciation" (nekkhammābhirataṃ) means delighting in monkhood. "Byantibhūtaṃ" means having reached an end, not clinging even in part, detached, and unmixed. "By things that are the basis for taints" (āsavaṭṭhāniyehi) means by defilements that are the cause of taints through association. Alternatively, "byantibhūtaṃ" means having reached the state of being free from craving. Why? Because it is detached from all things of the three planes of existence that are the basis for taints. In this sutta, the Noble Path is taught as a mixture of the mundane and supramundane.

## 9. Akkhana-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, one is called "khaṇakicco" because he performs duties when the opportunity arises; it means he performs duties only after obtaining the opportunity. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Peaceful" (opasamiko) means bringing about the subsiding of defilements. "Leading to Nibbāna" (parinibbāyiko) means causing the total extinction of defilements. He is called "sambodhagāmī" because he reaches enlightenment (sambodhi), which is the knowledge of the four paths. "The long-lived assembly of gods" is said with reference to the assembly of non-percipient (asaññasatta) gods.

"Among those who do not understand" (aviññātāresu) means among those who are extremely ignorant. "Well-proclaimed" (suppavedite) means well-spoken. "Obstacle-causing" (antarāyikā) means those that create obstacles. "Let not the moment pass" (khaṇo ve mā upaccagā) means let not this obtained moment pass by. "If one misses it in this teaching" means if some negligent person, even after obtaining this moment in this teaching, misses the Noble Path, which is the fixed law of the True Dhamma, and does not accomplish it. "One whose benefit has passed" (atītattho) means one whose welfare has declined. "Will regret for a long time" (cirattaṃ anutapiဿati) means he will sorrow for a long night. For example, a merchant hears that "goods have appeared in such a place" but does not go, while others go and take them, and for them, those goods yield eightfold or tenfold profit. Then the other merchant regrets, thinking, "My benefit has passed." Similarly, one who obtains the moment in this teaching but does not practice and misses the Noble Path, which is the fixed law of the True Dhamma, will be just like this merchant (regretting).
225:
One who has lost their benefit will regret and grieve for a long time. The phrase "enveloped by ignorance" is likewise the same. "Paccavidu" means they have penetrated and realized. "Saṃvarā" refers to the restraints of virtue (sīla-saṃvara). "Māradheyyaparānuge" refers to those who follow the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), which is known as the realm of Māra. "Pāraṅgatā" refers to those who have reached Nibbāna. "Ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ" refers to those who have attained the fruit of Arahatship. Thus, in these verses, the Buddha taught the round of existence (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa).

## 10. Commentary on the Anuruddhamahāvitakka Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "Cetīsu" refers to the country named Ceti, so called because it was the dwelling place of kings named Ceti. "Pācīnavaṃsadāya" refers to the bamboo grove situated to the east of the Buddha's dwelling place, a forest densely covered with dark green bamboo. "Thus a reflection arose in his mind" means that the Elder Anuruddha, having ordained and become an attainer of meditative attainments within his first rainy season retreat, had developed the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) capable of seeing a thousandfold world system.

That Elder Anuruddha went to the Elder Sāriputta and said: "Friend Sāriputta, here with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I behold a thousandfold world. My energy is aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness is established and unconfused; my body is tranquil and unperturbed; my mind is concentrated and one-pointed. Yet, my mind is not yet liberated from the taints through non-clinging."

Then the Elder Sāriputta said to him: "Friend Anuruddha, that thought of yours, 'I behold with the divine eye... etc.,' is your conceit (māna). That thought of yours, 'My energy is aroused... one-pointed,' is your restlessness (uddhacca). That thought of yours, 'Yet, my mind is not yet liberated from the taints,' is your remorse (kukkucca). It would be well if the venerable Anuruddha, having abandoned these three states and not attending to them, would direct his mind toward the deathless element (amata-dhātu)." In this way, the Elder taught him the subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna).

Having taken the meditation subject and taken leave of the Teacher, Elder Anuruddha went to the Ceti country. While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, he spent eight months in walking meditation. Because he was oppressed by the intensity of his exertion, his body became weary, and he sat down under a bamboo thicket. Then, this reflection arose in his mind. The meaning is: "This thought of a Great Man has arisen."
226:
Regarding "one of few wishes" (appiccha), there are four kinds: fewness of wishes regarding requisites, fewness of wishes regarding attainments, fewness of wishes regarding learning, and fewness of wishes regarding ascetic practices. Among them, one of few wishes regarding requisites takes only a little when much is given, takes even less when a little is given, and does not habitually take everything without remainder. One of few wishes regarding attainments, like the Elder Majjhantika, does not allow others to know of his own special attainments. One of few wishes regarding learning, even if he is a master of the Tipitaka, has no desire to let others know of his great learning, like the Elder Sāketatissa. One of few wishes regarding ascetic practices does not allow others to know of his practice of dhutaṅga, like the elder brother of the two brother elders. This story is told in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, by concealing evident virtues and by knowing moderation in receiving, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is fulfilled for a person of few wishes, but not for one of great wishes. This should be applied to all sentences.

"One who is contented" (santuṭṭha) means one who is contented with the four requisites through the three types of contentment. "One who is secluded" (pavivitta) means one who is secluded through physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka). Among them, physical seclusion is living alone by means of the object of exertion, having dispelled the entanglement of the group. Thinking that the work of a monk is not finished merely by living alone, one performs the preliminary work for kasina and produces the eight attainments; this is called mental seclusion. Thinking that the work of a monk is not finished merely by the attainments, one uses jhāna as a basis, contemplates conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), and reaches the fruit of Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); this is called seclusion from the substrata in every aspect. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Physical seclusion is for those with secluded bodies who delight in renunciation; mental seclusion is for those of purified minds who have reached supreme purity; and seclusion from substrata is for those free from substrata who have reached the unconditioned."

"One who delights in company" (saṅgaṇikārāma) refers to one who delights in the company of a group and the company of defilements. "One of aroused energy" (āraddhavīriya) refers to one who exerts effort by way of physical and mental energy. "One of established mindfulness" (upaṭṭhitassati) refers to one who has mindfulness closely established by way of the four foundations of mindfulness. "One who is concentrated" (samāhita) refers to one who has a one-pointed mind. "One who is wise" (paññavato) refers to one who possesses the wisdom of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-paññā).

The Blessed One said, "Sādhu, Sādhu," encouraging the Elder's reflection, and spoke thus. "This eighth thought" is spoken as if giving an eighth treasure pot to a man who has already obtained seven treasure pots; or as if giving an eighth jewel to a man who has obtained seven gems, seven elephant-treasures, and seven horse-treasures. It was spoken thus because He wished to make known the eighth thought to the Elder who remained having reflected on the seven thoughts of a Great Man (mahāpurisavitakka).
227:
"Nippapañcārāmassa" refers to a person who greatly delights in Nibbāna, which is called "nippapañca" because it is free from the proliferations (papañca) of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi). The remaining term "papañcārāmassa" is also a synonym of that same "nippapañcārāmassa". "Papañcārāmassa" refers to a person who greatly delights in the aforementioned proliferations. The other term is also a synonym of that "papañcārāmassa".

"Yato" means when; "tato" means then. "Nānārattānaṃ" refers to [clothes] dyed with various colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white. "Paṃsukūlaṃ" is a rag-robe obtained from twenty-three places. "Khāyissati" means that just as when that monk wears a robe he desires in the morning etc., that robe appears to him like a delightful casket of clothes; in the same way, for you who live delighting in the noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa) of contentment with robes, the rag-robe will appear [as such] and will be of service. "Ratiyā" means for the sake of delight. "Aparitassanāyā" means for the sake of non-distress caused by the attachments of craving and views. "Phāsuvihārāya" means for the sake of living comfortably. "Okkamanāya nibbānassa" means for the sake of entering the deathless Nibbāna.

"Piṇḍiyālopa-bhojanaṃ" is almsfood consisting of morsels obtained by wandering from house to house in villages, towns, and royal cities, relying on the strength of one's legs. "Khāyissati" means it will appear like the various choice flavors of a householder's food. "Santuṭṭhassa viharato" refers to a monk who lives contentedly with the noble lineage of contentment with almsfood. "Rukkhamūla-senāsanaṃ khāyissati" means the foot of a tree will appear like a gabled chamber scented with perfumes and flowers in a three-storied palace of a householder. "Santuṭṭhassa" refers to a person who is content with the noble lineage of contentment with lodging. "Tiṇasanthārako" is a spread laid out on any of these: grass, leaves, the ground, or a wooden board or stone slab. "Pūtimuttaṃ" is any kind of urine. Because of its foul smell, even if taken at that moment [fresh], it is called putrid urine. "Santuṭṭhassa viharato" refers to a monk who lives contentedly with the medicinal requisites for the sick.

In this way, the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject by incorporating the fruit of Arahantship in four places, reflected, "In what kind of lodging would the meditation subject be suitable for Anuruddha?" Realizing that it would be suitable for Anuruddha while staying in that very Pācīnavaṃsa forest, He said, "Tena hi tvaṃ, Anuruddha," and so on. "Pavivittassa viharato" refers to a person who lives secluded with the three types of seclusion. "Uyyojanika-paṭisaṃyuttaṃ" refers to the matters of serving and going of the audience such as kings, which are connected with words of urging and dismissal. "Papañca-nirodhe" means...
228:
In the state of Nibbāna, ("pakkhandati" means) one plunges into it by way of making it an object. In words such as "pasīdati," clarity, steadying, and leaning [towards the object] should also be understood as occurring by way of the object. In this way, the Blessed One, having taught the eight thoughts of a great man to the venerable Anuruddha in the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park in the Ceti country, later taught them in detail to the Saṅgha of monks while staying at the Bhesakaḷāvana Monastery.

"Manomaya" refers to a body produced by the mind, and also to a body that goes by the mind; here, it is said with reference to the body that goes by the mind. "Yathā me ahu saṅkappo" means "just as my thought was"; wishing to show the eighth thought of a great man, He taught further than that. All the remaining words are clear in meaning.

## The Third Householder Chapter (Gahapati-vagga).

## 4. The Chapter on Giving (Dāna-vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Giving (Paṭhama-dāna-sutta)

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, "āsajja dānaṃ deti" means giving a gift upon encountering recipients who have arrived. Seeing an arrived recipient, one makes them sit at that very moment, honors them, and gives the gift; one does not weary the recipient by saying, "I will give later." "Bhayā" means either out of fear of being blamed as "this person does not give, does not do good," or out of fear of the lower realms. "Adāsi me" means giving with the thought, "This person has given me such a thing in the past." "Dassati me" means giving with the thought, "This person will give me such a thing in the future." "Sāhu dānaṃ" means giving with the thought that giving is good and excellent, praised by the wise such as the Buddha. "Cittālaṅkāra-cittaparikkhāratthaṃ dānaṃ deti" means giving for the purpose of adorning and equipping the mind of serenity and insight. Giving indeed softens the mind. The one who receives thinks, "I have received," and has a soft mind. The one who gives also thinks, "I have given," and has a soft mind. In this way, giving softens the minds of both. Therefore, it is called "the taming of the untamed." As it was said:
229:
“Giving tames the untamed; not giving ruins the tamed. Through giving and pleasant speech, [beings] are uplifted and inclined.”

Among these eight types of giving, giving for the purpose of adorning the mind (cittālaṅkāradāna) is the most excellent.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Dāna Sutta
In the second sutta, ‘saddhā’ refers to the faith with which one gives a gift. ‘Hiri’ refers to the shame (of wrongdoing) with which one gives a gift; that is what is intended. ‘Kusalanca dānaṃ’ means a blameless gift (volition). ‘Diviyaṃ’ means going to heaven (diviṅgama).

## 3. Commentary on the Dānavatthu Sutta
In the third sutta, ‘dānavatthūni’ means the causes for giving. ‘Chandā dānaṃ deti’ means one gives a gift out of affection. ‘Dosā’ means one gives out of anger, being provoked and quickly taking whatever is available to give. ‘Mohā’ means one gives out of delusion. ‘Bhayā’ means one gives out of fear of blame, or fear of the lower realms, or fear of various other dangers. ‘Kulavaṃsaṃ’ means the family tradition (lineage).

## 4. Commentary on the Khetta Sutta
In the fourth sutta, ‘na mahapphalaṃ hoti’ means not being of great benefit in terms of the grain produced. ‘Na mahassādaṃ’ means the fruit of that crop is not very pleasant (tasty); it has little pleasure and is not sweet. ‘Na phātiseyyaṃ’ means there is no growth of that crop; it means the crop does not stand well. ‘Unnāmaninnāmi’ means having an uneven surface due to high and low spots. In such ground, water does not stay on the high parts and stays in excess in the hollows. ‘Pāsāṇasakkharikaṃ’ means being filled with spreading rock slabs, small stones, and gravel. ‘Ūsaraṃ’ means saline soil. ‘Na ca gambhīrasitaṃ’ means because the ground is hard, it is not possible to plough deep furrows; it results only in shallow furrows. ‘Na āyasampannaṃ’ means lacking a proper water inlet. ‘Na apāyasampannaṃ’ means subsequently lacking a proper water outlet. ‘Na mātikāsampannaṃ’ means lacking small and large water channels.
230:
is. “Na mariyādasampannaṃ” means not being endowed with field boundaries and dykes. All terms such as “na mahapphalaṃ” should be understood only in terms of the result, which is the grain.

“Sampannaṃ” means complete or endowed with success. “Bījasampadā” means the planting of perfect seeds. “Deve sampādayante” means when the rain falls properly. “Anītisampadā hoti” means the absence of calamities such as pests, which is one kind of perfection. “Virūḷhi” means growth, which is the second perfection. “Vepullaṃ” means abundance, which is the third perfection. “Phalaṃ” means the complete fruit, which is the fourth perfection.

“Sampannasīlesu” means among those with perfected virtue. “Bhojanasampadā” means a variety of excellent food. “Sampadānaṃ” means the three types of wholesome perfection. “Upaneti” means that the perfection of food leads [to it]. Why does it lead? Because that merit performed by that person is complete. Because that action performed by him is complete and perfect, it is called “sampanna” (perfected). “Sampannatthu idha” means “the matter is successful in this Dispensation.” “Vijjācaraṇasampanno” means being endowed with the three knowledges and the fifteen types of conduct. “Laddhā” means such a person, having obtained the perfection of mind, which is the state of being complete and without deficiency, “karoti kammasampadaṃ” means he performs perfected action, and “labhati ca atthasampadaṃ” means he also obtains the complete benefit. “Diṭṭhisampadါ” refers to the view of insight (vipassanā-diṭṭhi). “Maggasampadါ” refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). “Yāti sampannamānaso” means having a perfected mind, he reaches the fruit of Arahantship. “Sā hoti sabbasampadါ” means that liberation from all suffering is called the total perfection.

## 5. Commentary on the Dānūpapatti Sutta
In the fifth sutta, “dānūpapattiyo” means rebirths that have giving as their cause. “Dahati” means he places or sets. “Adhiṭṭhāti” is simply a synonym (pariyāya) for “dahati.” “Bhāveti” means he develops. “Hīne vimuttaṃ” means inclined towards the low five cords of sensual pleasure. “Uttari abhāvitaṃ” means not developed for the sake of the path and fruit which are superior to those low sensual pleasures. “Tatrūpapattiyā saṃvattati” means it leads to being reborn in whatever place one has performed merit and aspired to. “Vītarāgassa” refers to a person whose lust has been completely cut off by the Path, or whose lust has been suppressed by meditative attainment. Indeed, it is not possible to be reborn in the Brahma world through giving alone; however, giving is an adornment and an accompaniment for the mind of concentration and insight. For that reason, a person who has a softened mind through giving develops the Brahma-vihāras and is reborn in the Brahma world. Therefore, it is said, “It is for one free from lust, not for one possessed of lust.”
231:
## 6. Puññakiriyavatthusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth discourse, they are called 'grounds for making merit' (puññakiriyavatthu) because they are the causes for various benefits. Indeed, establishing their minds in the characteristics of giving and so forth, beings perform merits, thinking, 'We should give such a gift, we should observe virtue, we should develop meditation.' Giving itself is 'consisting of giving' (dānamaya). Alternatively, among the initial, middle, and final volitions of giving, the decisive volition arising from the initial ones is 'consisting of giving.' This is like figures made of flour or figures made of stone. The same method applies to the remaining two: 'consisting of virtue' (sīlamaya) and 'consisting of meditation' (bhāvanāmaya).

'Parittaṃ kataṃ hoti' means it is done only to a small or slight extent. 'Nābhisambhoti' means it does not succeed or come to fruition. 'Akataṃ hoti' means there is no effort at all in meditation. 'Manussadobhagyaṃ' refers to being born into a low family of five kinds, devoid of prosperity among humans. 'Upapajjati' means arriving by way of rebirth, meaning being born in that place. 'Mattaso kataṃ' means a gift given in measure, being only a little and not much. 'Manussasobhagyaṃ' means the state of being fortunate among humans, the prosperity of a three-fold family. 'Adhimattaṃ' means an excessive measure or a powerful gift. 'Adhigaṇhanti' means they take over by surpassing; it means they become especially noble and superior.

## 7. Sappurisadānasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh discourse, 'suciṃ' means giving an object that is pure and of beautiful appearance. 'Paṇītaṃ' means an object endowed with flavor. 'Kālena' means at the proper and suitable time. 'Kappiyaṃ' means giving what is allowable. 'Viceyya deti' means giving after choosing the gift, either by seeking a recipient, thinking, 'Giving to this person will be of great fruit, giving to that person will not be of great fruit,' or by way of making a resolution (aspiration).

## 8. Sappurisasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth discourse, 'atthāya' means for the sake of benefit. 'Hitāya sukhāya' means for the sake of welfare and happiness. 'Pubbapetānaṃ' means for the sake of relatives who have passed on to the next world. In this discourse, during times when a Buddha has not arisen, wheel-turning monarchs, Bodhisattas, and Paccekabuddhas can be found; during the time of a Buddha, the Buddha and the Buddha's disciples are found. Indeed, they lead to the benefit, welfare, and happiness of those mentioned, such as parents. 'Bahunnaṃ vata atthāya, sappañño gharamāvasanti' means a wise person living in a house truly exists for the benefit of many. 'Pubbe' means from the very beginning.
232:
Recalling the past favors done by parents, they are said to 'recollect what was done in the past' (pubbekatamanussaranti). Honoring with requisites along with the reason is called 'righteously' (sahadhammena). Showing respect to those living the holy life (brahmacārī) and assuming a humble posture toward them is called 'respecting those living the holy life' (apace brahmacārayo). 'Pesalo' refers to a person of lovable virtue.

## 9. Commentary on the Abhisanda Sutta

In the ninth discourse, 'dānāni' refers to the gifts of volition. The meaning of terms such as 'aggaññāni' has already been stated below in the commentary on the Catukka Nipāta.

## 10. Commentary on the Duccaritavipāka Sutta

In the tenth discourse, 'pāṇātipāto' refers to the volition of taking life. 'Sabbalahuso' refers to the result that is the lightest among all acts of taking life. 'Appāyukasaṃvattaniko' means having a short life due to even a slight consequence of that act of taking life. One may pass away (the life-force is destroyed) just as the rebirth-consciousness arises or just as one emerges from the mother's womb. Such shortness of life is not the result of any other karma but is the path taken by the act of taking life itself. 'Bhogabyasanasaṃvattaniko' means causing the destruction of wealth in such a way that even a small amount like a kākaṇika coin does not remain in one's hand. 'Sapattaverasaṃvattaniko hoti' means it leads to enmity along with rivals. For such a person, rivals are many. Whoever sees him develops only enmity and is not appeased. Such abundance of enemies is the result of having offended against the property guarded and protected by others.

'Abhūtabbhakkhānasaṃvattaniko hoti' means it leads to being accused with what is untrue. Even an act committed by someone else falls upon him. 'Mittehi bhedanasaṃvattaniko' means it leads to division from friends. With whatever friend he associates, he is bound to be divided from that friend. 'Amanāpasaddasaṃvattaniko' means it leads to unpleasant sounds. One hears in every place one goes the kind of speech that is like a thorn, harsh, bitter, offensive, and heart-cutting. One does not get to hear pleasant sounds. Such a result is the path taken by harsh speech (pharusavācā). 'Anādeyyavācāsaṃvattaniko' means leading to being one whose words are not accepted by others. One comes to the state of being told, 'Why do you speak? Who will listen to your words?' This is the path taken by frivolous talk (samphappalāpa). 'Ummatta-ka-saṃvattaniko hoti' means it leads to madness.
233:
(Drinking alcohol) leads to madness. Because of that drinking, a person becomes mad, or mentally deranged, or one with a dribbling mouth (dull-witted). This is the consequence (nissanda) of drinking alcohol. In this sutta, only the round of suffering (vatta) is taught.

## Dānavagga, the Fourth.

## 5. Uposathavagga

## 4. Vāseṭṭhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta of the fifth vagga (Vāseṭṭhasutta), with the words "Vāseṭṭha, if even these great sāla trees," the Buddha spoke an imagined analogy, pointing to two great sāla trees standing in front. This is the meaning: These great sāla trees are insentient. If even these trees were sentient and observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, that observance of Uposatha would be for their welfare and happiness for a long time. What need is there to mention sentient beings (humans)? (It would certainly be so), this is the meaning.

## 6. Anuruddhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, regarding the phrase "yena āyasmā anuruddho": It is said that those deities, looking at their own prosperity and reflecting, "Depending on what did we obtain this prosperity?", saw the Elder Anuruddha and thought, "In the past, when our lord (Anuruddha) was a Cakkavatti king, we were his attendants. By following the advice given by him, we obtained this prosperity. Let us go, invite the Elder, and enjoy this prosperity." Thus, during the day, they approached where the Venerable Anuruddha was.

"Tīsu ṭhānesu" means in three causes. "Ṭhānaso paṭilabhāma" means we obtain it instantly. "Sara" refers to the sound of speech, song, or ornaments. ## 1. Commentary on the Gotamĩ Sutta
In the first sutta of the sixth chapter, the phrase "dwells among the Sakyans" (Sakkesu viharati) means that he arrived and was staying there during his first visit. The name "Mahāpajāpati" was given to her because she was the great mistress of a large retinue of sons and daughters. The phrase "approached where the Blessed One was" (yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami) refers to the time when the Buddha went to the city of Kapilavatthu; he first ordained Prince Nanda, and on the seventh day, he ordained Prince Rāhula.

Due to the quarrel over the water-distributing coil (the Rohiṇī river dispute), when the citizens of the two kingdoms (Kapilavatthu and Koliya) came out to wage war, the Buddha went there, explained the situation to the kings to make them understand, and preached the Attadaṇḁa Sutta. The kings, being inspired with faith, each offered two hundred and fifty princes, and those five hundred princes were ordained in the presence of the Buddha. At that time, their former wives sent messages, causing spiritual discontent (anabhirati) to arise in them.

Knowing that discontent had arisen in those monks, the Buddha took those five hundred young monks to Lake Kuṇāla. Sitting on the stone slab where he used to stay when he was the Kuṇāla cuckoo, he preached the Kuṇāla Jātaka, thereby dispelling their discontent and establishing them all in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Later, he brought them back to the Great Wood (Mahāvana) and established them in the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala).

To know their state of mind, the former wives sent messages again, to which the monks replied, "We are no longer fit for the household life." Those women then consulted among themselves, saying, "It is no longer proper for us to return home. Let us go to the Great Mother Mahāpajāpati Gotamĩ, ask for permission to ordain, and then become monastics." Thus, the five hundred women approached Mahāpajāpati and said, "Noble Lady, please obtain permission for our ordination." Mahāpajāpati took those women and approached the Buddha. Some also say that this approach occurred after King Suddhodana had passed away (attained Parinibbāna) under the white parasol.

"Enough, Gotamĩ, let it not please you..." Why did he refuse? Do not all Buddhas have the fourfold assembly? Indeed, they do. However, he refused initially because he wished to grant the ordination with gravity, thinking, "Having obtained it with difficulty after repeated requests, they will guard it well." The word "pakkāmi" (he departed) means he entered the city of Kapilavatthu again.
236:
"Having stayed as long as he wished" means he stayed for as long as he desired while observing the decisive support (upanissaya) of beings who were capable of being enlightened. "He set out on a wandering" means that while benefiting the masses, he departed on a journey at an unhurried pace, endowed with supreme Buddha-glory and incomparable Buddha-grace.

"Together with many Sakyan women" means that within the palace itself, they took up the appearance of renunciants for the sake of the Buddha. Having caused the five hundred Sakyan women to also take up the renunciant appearance, she went together with all those many Sakyan women. "He set out on a wandering" refers to the commencement of the journey. At the time of departure, the Sakyan and Koliyan kings, thinking that those delicate royal women would not be able to travel on foot, prepared golden palanquins. However, those women considered, "Traveling by vehicle would be a sign of disrespect toward the Teacher," and thus they traveled the fifty-one league journey only on foot. The kings also arranged for guards in front and behind, and sent men with carts filled with rice, ghee, oil, and other provisions, instructing them, "Prepare food at every place they reach."

"With swollen feet" means that because those women were very delicate, blisters arose and burst on their soles. Both feet became swollen as if covered with katakaṭṭhi seeds. Therefore, it is said, "with swollen feet." "Outside the gateway" means outside the main entrance. Why were they standing there? It is said that Mother Gotamĩ had this thought: "I have taken the renunciant appearance on my own without the Buddha's permission, and this act of mine has become known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. If the Buddha permits the ordination, it will be well. But if he does not, it will be a great disgrace." Thus, unable to enter the monastery, she stood there weeping.

"Gotamĩ, why is this?" means "Has some calamity befallen the royal families? For what reason have you come to such a discolored state and are standing with swollen feet?" "By another means" means for another reason. Having spoken of her virtues, starting with "Venerable Sir, the Mother is of great service," Ānanda requested the ordination again. The Buddha, considering that "Women are of limited wisdom; if permitted to ordain with just one request, they will not take up my Dispensation with gravity," refused three times. Now, wishing them to accept it with gravity, he said, "Ānanda, if Mahāpajāpati..."

Gotamī accepts the eight heavy rules (garudhammas); the Buddha said, "Let that acceptance itself be her higher ordination (upasampadā)," and so forth. In this context, "sāvassā" means let the acknowledgement of those heavy rules be both her going forth (pabbajjā) and her higher ordination. "Tadahūpasampannassa" refers to one who was ordained on that very day. "Salutation, rising to greet, making the anjali gesture, and proper respect should be performed" means that without being humble or proud, one should salute with the five points (prostration), rise from one's seat to welcome, join the ten fingernails in anjali, and perform proper respect such as preparing a seat or fanning. "A residence where there is no monk" refers to a residence where there is no teacher (ācariya) who can give exhortation when a bhikkhunī approaches for it without danger. In such a residence, the rains retreat (vassa) should not be spent. "Anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ" means every half-month (on Uposatha days). "Ovādūpasaṅkamanaṃ" means approaching for the sake of exhortation. "Diṭṭhena" means by seeing with the eye; "sutena" means by hearing with the ear; "parisaṅkāya" means by suspicion based on seeing or hearing. "Garudhammaṃ" refers to the heavy offense of Saṅghādisesa. "Pakkhamānattaṃ" means the mānatta penance to be practiced for a full fifteen days. "In the six rules" refers to the six training rules, including the rule against eating at the wrong time. "One who has trained in the training rules" refers to one who has fulfilled the training without breaking even a single rule. "Should not be reviled or scolded" means one should not be reviled with any of the ten grounds for reviling, nor should one be scolded in any way by threatening danger. "The path of speech for bhikkhunīs towards bhikkhus is closed" means the path of speech consisting of exhortation, instruction, and Dhamma talk is closed for bhikkhunīs; no bhikkhunī should exhort or prohibit any bhikkhu. However, it is proper to speak in terms of lineage, such as, "Venerable sir, the elder monks of old used to fulfill this practice regarding robes." "The path of speech for bhikkhus towards bhikkhunīs is not closed" means the path of speech for bhikkhus towards bhikkhunīs is not prohibited; they may exhort, instruct, or give Dhamma talks as they wish. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation of the heavy rules should be understood as stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary.

Upon hearing these eight heavy rules learned from the Teacher and being told to her by the Elder Ānanda, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī's great distress was instantly calmed. Just as if a hundred jars of cool water brought from Lake Anotatta were poured over her head, she became free from fever and full of joy. Wishing to manifest the rapture (pīti) born from accepting the heavy rules, she uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) beginning with, "Venerable sir, just as..."

"Kumbhatthenakehi" refers to thieves who light a lamp in a pot and, by that light, search for and steal goods in others' houses. The disease called "setaṭṭhikā" (mildew/white-rot) is when a type of insect bores into the core within the stalk, and because of that bored stalk, the emerging head of rice cannot hold its milky sap. The disease called "mañjiṭṭhikā" (red-rust) is the redness inside the sugarcane.

"Just as one would build an embankment for a great reservoir in advance," by this statement, this meaning is shown: Just as some water remains even if the embankment of a great reservoir is not yet built, but if it is built beforehand, the water that would not have remained due to the lack of an embankment will remain; even so, these heavy rules were prescribed in advance to prevent transgression before any incident occurred. If these heavy rules had not been prescribed, the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) would have lasted only five hundred years because of women going forth. But because they were prescribed in advance, it will last another five hundred years; thus, it will last for the one thousand years originally mentioned. "One thousand years" is said in terms of Arahants who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Beyond that, it will last one thousand years in terms of dry-insight Arahants (sukkhavipassaka), one thousand years in terms of Non-returners (anāgāmī), one thousand years in terms of Once-returners (sakadāgāmī), and one thousand years in terms of Stream-enterers (sotāpanna). Thus, the True Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-saddhamma) will last for five thousand years. The Dhamma of learning (pariyatti-dhamma) will also last that long. For there is no realization when learning is absent, nor is there a lack of realization when learning is present. However, the outward appearance (liṅga) of a monk will continue for a long time even after the learning has disappeared.

## 3. Saṅkhitta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

## 1. Commentary on the Icchā Sutta

## 2. Commentary on the Alaṃ Sutta

In the second sutta, alaṃ attano alaṃ paresaṃ means one who is capable, competent, and suitable in practicing for the benefit of oneself and others. Khippanisantī means one reflects quickly; it means that when the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so on are being taught, one understands those dhammas quickly. In this sutta, serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are taught. This teaching is delivered starting from the top and descending to the bottom, according to the inclination of the individual and the elegance of the instruction.

## 3. Commentary on the Saṅkhitta Sutta

In the third sutta, evameva means simply without cause, or just as this monk requests. Moghapurisā means foolish persons, persons empty of merit. Ajjhesantī means they request. Anubandhitabbaṃ means one should be followed by following the postures; they think, "I should not be abandoned." To make him understand, the Buddha spoke thus by way of rebuke. This monk, even when given advice, only practices negligence; having heard the Dhamma, he remains just there and does not wish to practice the monk's duties (samaṇadhamma). Therefore, the Blessed One, after rebuking him, spoke the words beginning with "Therefore, monk, you should train thus," because He wished to discipline him as he was endowed with the strong support (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship. In those words, by the passage, "My mind will be steady internally, well-settled, and arisen evil unwholesome states will not remain overwhelming the mind," the Buddha first taught the monk the basic concentration (mūlasamadhi), which is merely one-pointedness of mind by the power of the Dhamma within his own continuity. After that, to show that "one should not be satisfied with just this much concentration, but should develop that concentration in this way," He said, "Monk, when your mind is well-settled internally... and arisen evil unwholesome states do not remain overwhelming the mind, then, monk, you should train thus: 'My deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) will be developed... well-undertaken.'" Thus, He made the monk develop the meditation by the power of loving-kindness. Again, He spoke the words beginning with, "Monk, when this concentration of yours is thus developed and practiced frequently, then you, monk, should develop this concentration with applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra)." Regarding the Pali beginning with "Yato kho"...

That monk is endowed with the strong support (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship; therefore, wishing to discipline him, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with, "Therefore, monk, you should train thus." In those words, by this instruction, "My mind will be steady internally, well-settled, and arisen evil unwholesome states will not remain overwhelming the mind," He first taught the monk the basic concentration (mūlasamadhi), which is merely one-pointedness of mind by the power of the Dhamma within his own continuity.

After that, to show that "one should not be satisfied with just this much concentration, but should develop that concentration in this way," He said, "Monk, when your mind is well-settled internally, and arisen evil unwholesome states do not remain overwhelming the mind, then you should train thus: 'My deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) will be developed... well-undertaken,'" thus causing the monk to develop the meditation by the power of loving-kindness. Again, He spoke the words beginning with, "Monk, when this concentration of yours is thus developed and practiced frequently, then you should develop this concentration with applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra)." The meaning of those words is: Monk, when this basic concentration of yours is thus developed by the power of loving-kindness, then, without being satisfied with just that much development of loving-kindness, you should develop this basic concentration in other objects as well, reaching the fourth and fifth jhanas, by the method of "with applied thought and sustained thought."

Having spoken thus, wishing to show that one should also practice the development of the fourth and fifth jhanas in other objects, preceded by the remaining divine abodes (brahmavihāra), He spoke the words beginning with, "Monk, when this concentration of yours is thus well-developed, then, monk, you should train thus: 'My deliverance of mind through compassion (karuṇā-cetovimutti)...'" Having thus shown the development of the fourth and fifth jhanas preceded by loving-kindness, He again spoke the words beginning with, "Monk, when this concentration of yours is thus well-developed, then you [should train thus]: 'Contemplating the body in the body...'" to show the meditation preceded by the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) and so on.

"Monk, when this concentration of yours is thus well-developed, then, wherever you go, you will go [in comfort]." He spoke the words beginning with this. In those words, gagghesi means "you will go."
