## 4. Commentary on the Gayāsīsa Sutta
In the fourth sutta, the phrase "etadavoca" (he said this) refers to the Buddha speaking the words beginning with "Monks, formerly I..." in order to inform the Saṅgha of the thoughts (vitakka) that arose at his place of exertion (padhāna-bhūmi). "Obhāsa" (radiance) refers to the light associated with the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). "Ñāṇadassana" (knowledge and vision) is the vision consisting of knowledge that has become the divine eye. "Sannivutthapubba" means having lived together once before. In this sutta, these eight knowledges are directly mentioned in the Pali text: the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa), the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhi-vidha-ñāṇa), the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (ceto-pariya-ñāṇa), the knowledge of beings passing away according to their karma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the present (paccuppannaṃsa-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the past (atītaṃsa-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). Because this sutta is preached by combining these knowledges with the insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa), the four path knowledges (magga-ñāṇa), the four fruition knowledges (phala-ñāṇa), the four reviewing knowledges (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), and the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), it should be called a well-preached sutta.

## 5. Commentary on the Abhibhāyatana Sutta
In the fifth sutta, "abhibhāyatanāni" refers to the causes of overcoming (mastery). What do they overcome? They overcome both opposing states (paccanīka-dhamma) and objects (ārammaṇa). These mastery jhānas overcome opposing states because they are of an opposite nature, and they overcome objects because of the person's superior knowledge. In the phrases beginning with "ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī" (perceiving form internally), one is called "one who has the perception of form in oneself" by the power of performing preliminary work (parikamma) on the form within one's own body. One who performs the preliminary work on blue does so on the hair, bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on yellow does so on the fat, the skin, the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on red does so on the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on white does so on the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. However, that form within the body is not extremely blue, yellow, red, or white; it is merely impure (unclean).

"Eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati" (alone, he sees forms externally) means that for such a person, the preliminary work (parikamma) occurs within his own body, but the sign (nimitta) occurs externally. By the power of the internal preliminary work and the external absorption (appanā), he is said to be "perceiving form internally, he sees forms externally." "Parittāni" (limited) refers to objects that have not been expanded (small objects). "Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni" (beautiful or ugly) means that whether they are beautiful or ugly, this mastery base is preached solely by the power of the limited object. In the phrase "tāni abhibhuyya" (overcoming them), just as a person with good digestion, upon receiving only a spoonful of rice, thinks, "What is there to eat in this much rice?" and gathers it into a single mouthful to eat; in the same way, a person with superior and clear knowledge, regarding a limited object, thinks, "What is there to attain in this small object? This object is no burden for me," and thus overcomes those forms and enters attainment. He reaches absorption (appanā) as soon as the sign arises; this is the meaning. By the words "jānāmi passāmi" (I know, I see), the Buddha describes his attention (ābhoga). Such attention occurs to one who has emerged from attainment, not within the attainment itself. "Evaṃsaññī hoti" (he is thus perceiving) means he has such a perception through the perception of attention or the perception of jhāna. Indeed, his perception of overcoming exists even within the attainment, but the perception of attention belongs only to one who has emerged from attainment. "Appamāṇāni" (immeasurable) refers to large objects that have been expanded. In the phrase "abhibhuyya"...
244:
Just as a man with a strong digestive fire, upon receiving a spoonful of rice, thinks, "What is there to eat in this spoonful?" and gathers it into just one mouthful; in the same way, a person with superior and clear knowledge thinks, "What is there to be attained in this small object? This object is not a burden for me," and thus overcomes and masters those kasina forms and enters attainment. The meaning is that he reaches absorption (appanā) as soon as the sign (nimitta) arises. By the words "I know, I see," his attention (ābhoga) is described. That attention occurs only to one who has emerged from attainment, not within the attainment itself. "He is thus perceiving" means he has such a perception through the perception of attention or the perception of jhāna. His perception of overcoming exists even within the attainment, but the perception of attention belongs only to one who has emerged from attainment.

"Appamāṇāni" (immeasurable) means large objects that have been expanded. Regarding the word "abhibhuyya" (overcoming) here, for example, a man who eats a lot (a glutton), upon receiving a large serving of rice, thinks, "Let there be another serving, and another; what can this one serving do to me?" and does not see that serving as large. In the same way, a person with superior and clear knowledge thinks, "What is there to be attained in this immeasurable object? This is not immeasurable [for me]; there is no burden in making my mind one-pointed," and thus overcomes it and enters attainment. The meaning is that he reaches absorption as soon as the sign arises.

"Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī" (perceiving formlessness internally) means being devoid of the perception of preliminary work (parikamma-saññā) on the internal form, either because of not obtaining it or because of not desiring it.

"Alone, he sees forms externally" means that for a person whose preliminary work and sign both arise externally, he is said to be "perceiving formlessness internally, alone he sees forms externally" by the power of the external preliminary work and absorption. The remaining explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the fourth mastery base. Among these four mastery bases, the limited (paritta) object comes by way of the initial thought temperament (vitakka-carita), the immeasurable (appamāṇa) by way of the delusion temperament (moha-carita), the beautiful (suvaṇṇa) by way of the hatred temperament (dosa-carita), and the ugly (dubbaṇṇa) by way of the lust temperament (rāga-carita). These objects are suitable for those respective persons. Their suitability is described in the Visuddhimagga in the Description of Temperaments (Cariya-niddesa).

In the fifth mastery base and others, the word "nīlāni" (blue/dark) is used in a comprehensive sense. "Nīlavaṇṇāni" (blue-colored) is by way of color. "Nīlanidassanāni" (blue-manifesting) is by way of appearance. It means they appear as having no visible gaps, having unmixed color, and being a solid mass of blue.
245:
The phrase "nīlanibhāsāni" is spoken in terms of the radiance of color. It means having a blue color or being endowed with a blue radiance. By this term (nīlobhāsāni), the extreme purity of those objects is shown. Indeed, these bases of mastery (abhibhāyatanas) are taught solely by way of their pure appearance. "One who takes up the blue kasiṇa takes the sign in a blue object, or in a flower, or in a cloth, or in a color element," and so forth; all the details regarding the preparation of the kasiṇa, the preliminary work (parikamma), and the procedure for attainment (appanā) have already been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

## 6. Vimokkhasutta-vaṇṇanā

Why are they called liberations (vimokkhas)? They are called liberations in the sense of being released (from opposing states) and in the sense of being fully inclined (towards the object). What is this sense of being fully inclined (adhimuccana)? It is the sense of being well-released from opposing states, and being well-released by way of delighting in the object. It means occurring in the object without anxiety and without restraint, like the sleep of a young child who sleeps in his father's lap with his limbs relaxed. This sense (of being fully inclined) does not exist in the last liberation, but it exists in the preceding liberations.

In the phrase "rūpī rūpāni passati" (possessing form, one sees forms), the fine-material sphere jhāna produced by way of the blue kasiṇa etc. in one's own hair etc. is called "rūpa" (form); because one possesses that jhāna, one is called "rūpī" (possessing form). Externally also, one sees forms such as the blue kasiṇa with the eye of jhāna. By this statement, the four fine-material sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna in kasiṇas based on internal (ajjhatta) and external (bahiddhā) objects are shown. "Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī" means being without the perception of form internally; it refers to one who has not produced a fine-material sphere jhāna in one's own hair and so forth. By this statement, the fine-material sphere jhānas produced only externally by performing the preliminary work externally are shown.

By the phrase "one is fully inclined only to the beautiful," the jhānas occurring in the extremely pure color kasiṇas such as blue are shown. In that regard, although there is no such attention as "it is beautiful" within the appanā impulsion, because a person who dwells taking an extremely pure and beautiful kasiṇa as an object reaches a state that can be described as "being fully inclined to the beautiful," this teaching was given in this way.

However, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "How is there the liberation of being fully inclined only to the beautiful? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... Because loving-kindness has been developed, beings are not repulsive (not opposing). Compassion..."
246:
Appreciative joy. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity. Because equanimity has been developed, beings are free from repulsiveness (or) are not opposing. Thus, the inclination towards only "the beautiful" is called liberation, as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

What should be said regarding the terms beginning with "sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. This eighth liberation is called the eighth noble liberation because it is always released and freed from the four mental aggregates.

## 7-8. Anariyavohārasutta-vaṇṇanā

67-68. In the seventh discourse, "ignoble modes of speech" (anariyavohāra) refers to speech that is not the speech of the noble ones, but is faulty speech. It is the name for the volitions (cetanās) with which those modes of speech are spoken. In the eighth discourse, the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of the method already stated.

## 9. Parisāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth discourse, "assembly of nobles" (khattiyaparisā) refers to a gathering or meeting of the warrior-noble class. This method should be understood in all cases. "An assembly of nobles of many hundreds" refers to an assembly of nobles similar to the gathering of King Bimbisāra, the gathering of relatives, or the gathering of the Licchavīs. It is also found in other world-systems (cakkavāḷas). "Sallapitapubba" means having previously engaged in conversation and reciprocal talk. "Sākacchā" means having previously engaged in Dhamma discussion. "What was their appearance like?" means those kings were fair-skinned, dark-skinned, or had a complexion like a bedbug's back. The Blessed One, however, has a complexion like the color of gold. This statement is made with reference to the physical form. To those kings, only the physical form is apparent. Just as the Blessed One is not like a barbarian, nor is he one wearing ruby earrings; he sits only in the guise of a Buddha. Those kings also see only a form similar to their own.

"What was their voice like?" means although those kings might have broken voices, stammering voices, or voices like a crow, the Blessed One has a voice like that of the Great Brahmā. This statement is made with reference to various languages. Even if the Blessed One preaches while sitting on the king's throne, those kings think, "Today the King preaches with a sweet voice." When the Blessed One has finished preaching and departed, upon seeing the king who has arrived again, an inquiry arises: "Who was this person who just spoke with such a sweet voice and left?" In that inquiry, they investigate: "Who was this person who just now, in this very place, preached so sweetly in the Magadhan language or the Sinhalese language and then vanished? Was it a deity?" Yet they do not know. Thus the meaning should be understood. For what purpose this...
247:
"Or is he a human?"—this means that even though they investigate in this way, they do not know. For what purpose does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not know? It is for the purpose of establishing habitual tendencies (vāsanā). For Dhamma heard in this way becomes a supporting condition (for the Path and Fruition) in the future; thus, he teaches with the future benefit in mind. The origin of the words "many hundreds of the assembly of brahmins," etc., should be understood through the assembly of the brahmin Soṇaḍaṇḍa and others, as well as through other world systems.

## 10. Bhūmicālasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth (Bhūmicāla) Sutta, "nisīdanaṃ" refers here to a piece of skin (a sitting mat). "Udenaṃ cetiyaṃ" refers to a monastery built at the dwelling place of the yakkha Udena. The same method applies to Gotamaka Cetiya and others. "Bhāvitā" means developed. "Bahulīkatā" means practiced frequently. "Yānīkatā" means made like a well-hitched vehicle. "Vatthukatā" means made like a foundation in the sense of a basis. "Anuṭṭhitā" means well-established. "Paricitā" means well-developed from all sides. "Susamāraddhā" means well-undertaken.

Having taught in this general way without specification, he spoke the words "Tathāgatassa kho," etc., wishing to show it again with specification. Here, "kappaṃ" refers to the lifespan aeon (āyukappa). He could remain for the full duration of the human lifespan at that particular time. "Kappāvasesaṃ vā" means a period exceeding the one hundred years mentioned as "a little more or less." However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "There is no such thing as an empty boast for the Buddhas; by repeatedly entering fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti) and warding off the pains leading to death, he could remain for the entire Bhadda-kappa." Why did he not remain? Because the physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa) is oppressed by things such as the loss of teeth. Buddhas attain parinibbāna in the fifth portion of their lifespan, at a time when they are still dear and pleasing to many people. Furthermore, when the Great Disciples, the followers of the Buddha, have attained parinibbāna, he would have to remain alone like a tree stump or surrounded only by young monks and novices. At that time, it might lead to contempt, with people saying, "Oh, look at the Buddha's assembly!" Therefore, he did not remain. Even though this was said, the meaning defined in the Commentary is only "lifespan aeon" (āyukappa).

In the passage "yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto," the word "taṃ" is a mere particle. Just as any other worldling whose mind is overwhelmed and possessed by Māra would be unable to penetrate (the meaning), so too (Venerable Ānanda) was unable to penetrate it. Māra...
248:
Indeed, for one who has not abandoned all twelve perversions (vipallāsa), Māra can overwhelm their mind. Since the Elder Ānanda had not yet abandoned four perversions, Māra overwhelmed his mind. When Māra overwhelms the mind, what does he do? He either shows a terrifying visual object or makes one hear a terrifying sound. Then, beings, seeing or hearing that object, lose mindfulness and stand with their mouths open. Māra then thrusts his hand into their mouths and squeezes their hearts. Because of that squeezing, they remain unconscious. However, how could this Māra be able to thrust his hand into the mouth of the Great Elder? He could only show a terrifying object. Having seen that object, the Great Elder did not penetrate the hint (nimittobhāsa). Why did the Blessed One, though knowing, address him up to three times? It was for the purpose of reducing the Elder Ānanda's anxiety by placing the blame later when he would beg, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One remain," saying, "This is your own bad deed, this is your own fault."

## Māro pāpimāti ettha satte anatthe niyojento māretīti māro. Pāpimāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. So hi pāpadhammasamannāgatattā “pāpimā”ti vuccati. Kaṇho, antako, namuci, pamattabandhūtipi tasseva nāmāni.

He is called 'Māra' because he kills beings by engaging them in harm (destroying their virtues). 'Pāpimā' (the Evil One) is just a synonym for him. He is called 'Pāpimā' because he is possessed of evil qualities. Kaṇha, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu are also names for him.

## Bhāsitā kho panesāti ayañhi bhagavato sambodhipattiyā aṭṭhame sattāhe bodhimaṇ膽eyeva āgantvā “bhagavā yadatthaṃ tumhehi pāramiyo pūritā, so vo attho anuppatto, paṭividdhaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, kiṃ te lokavicāraṇenā”ti vatvā yathā ajja, evameva “parinibbātu dāni, bhante bhagavā”ti yāci. Bhagavā cassa “na tāvāha”ntiādīni vatvā paṭikkhipi. Taṃ sandhāya – “bhāsitā kho panesā, bhante”tiādimāha.

This Māra, in the eighth week after the Blessed One attained Enlightenment, came to the very site of the Bodhi tree and said, "Blessed One, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has been reached; you have penetrated the knowledge of omniscience. What is the use of your wandering in the world?" and just as he did today, he begged, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain parinibbāna." The Blessed One rejected him, saying, "I will not yet," and so on. Referring to that rejection, (Māra) said, "Venerable Sir, this word was spoken by you," and so forth.

In that passage, 'viyattā' means those who are skilled by way of the Path. Similarly, 'vinītā' means those who are disciplined. 'Visāradā' means those who are confident. 'Bahussutā' means those who have much learning by way of the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka). Because they bear that very Dhamma, they are 'dhammadharā'. Alternatively, they are those with much learning in both scriptural study (pariyatti) and realization (paṭivedha). Because they bear the Dhamma of scriptural study and realization, they are 'dhammadharā'; this is how the meaning should be understood here. 'Dhammānudhamma-paṭipannā' means those who practice the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā), which is the secondary Dhamma to the Noble Dhamma. 'Sāmīci-paṭipannā' means those who practice the appropriate way. 'Anudhamma-cārino' means those whose habit is to practice the secondary Dhamma. 'Sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ' means one's own teacher's doctrine. 'Ācikkhissanti' and all the following words are merely synonyms of one another. 'Sahadhammena' means with reasoned and causal speech. 'Sappāṭihāriyaṃ' means they will teach the Dhamma so as to make it leading to liberation (niyyānika).
249:
Brahmacariya refers to the entire holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings. Iddha means successful through the power of the enjoyment of jhāna. Phīta means reaching growth, like a tree in full bloom, through the power of the attainment of direct knowledge (abhiññā). Vitthārika means widespread by being established in various directions. Bāhujañña means known by many people through the power of the masses' penetration. Puthubhūta means having reached a state of vastness in every aspect. How? Up to being well-proclaimed to gods and humans. It means it is well-proclaimed by all wise gods and humans that exist. Appossukka means being unconcerned (nirālaya). "O Evil One, from the eighth week onwards, you have been wandering around crying out, 'Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna; let the Sugata attain Parinibbāna.' From today onwards, be one who is without effort; do not strive for the sake of my Parinibbāna," he said.

"Being mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra)" means making mindfulness well-established and, having delimited it with knowledge, he gave up or abandoned the life-force. In this regard, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-force like throwing a stone with his hand. Rather, he entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) for only three months and then produced the thought, "After this, I shall not enter it again." Referring to the arising of such a thought, it is said, "he relinquished (ossajji)." There is also a reading "ussajji." Mahābhūmicāla means a great earthquake. At that time, it is said that the ten-thousandfold world system shook. Bhiṃsanaka means causing terror. "The celestial drums sounded" means the sky thundered out of season, flashes of lightning appeared, and a momentary rain fell.

Why did he utter this inspired utterance (udāna)? Someone might say, "The Blessed One, being harassed by [Mara] following him constantly and saying 'Venerable Sir, attain Parinibbāna,' relinquished the life-force out of fear." To ensure there is no opportunity for such a person to say so (since there is no inspired utterance for one who is afraid), he uttered this inspired utterance released by the force of joy (pīti).

In that inspired utterance, it is called "tula" (measurable/comparable) because it is clearly delimited even to dogs and jackals and the like. What is that? It is kamma of the sensuous sphere (kāmāvacara). It is called "atula" (immeasurable/incomparable) because there is no other mundane kamma equal to it. What is that? It is sublime (mahaggata) kamma. Alternatively, kamma of the sensuous and fine-material spheres is called tula, and kamma of the immaterial sphere is called atula. Or, kamma with little fruit is called tula, and kamma with much fruit is called atula. Sambhava means being the cause of arising, making a heap, making a mass...
250:
...meaning that which produces a collection. Bhava-saṅkhāra is the kamma that conditions renewed existence. Avassaji means He relinquished. Muni refers to the Buddha-Sage. Ajjhattarato means delighting in the Dhamma that occurs within one's own internal being. Samāhito means being concentrated through the power of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Abhindi kavacaṃ iva means He broke it as if breaking a coat of mail (armor). Attasambhavaṃ refers to the defilements (kilesa) that have arisen within oneself. The meaning is this: He relinquished the mundane kamma known as "tula" and "atula," which is called "sambhava" because it is accompanied by results, and "bhava-saṅkhāra" because it conditions the cycle of existence. Just as a great warrior at the head of a battle breaks his armor, He, delighting in the internal Dhamma and being concentrated, broke the defilements that arose within Himself.

Alternatively, "tulaṃ" means weighing or investigating. "Atulañca sambhavaṃ" refers to Nibbāna and existence. "Bhava-saṅkhāra" is the kamma that leads to existence. Weighing in this manner: "The five aggregates are impermanent; Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the five aggregates, is permanent," the Buddha-Sage, seeing the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished that kamma—the bhava-saṅkhāra which is the root of the aggregates—through the Noble Path (ariya-magga) which is said to "lead to the exhaustion of kamma." How did He relinquish it? Delighting in the internal and being concentrated, He broke the defilements arisen within Himself like a coat of mail. That Blessed One, delighting in the internal through the power of insight (vipassanā) and being concentrated through the power of tranquility (samatha), thus from the preliminary stage onwards, by the power of tranquility and insight, broke the entire web of defilements known as "attasambhava" because they arise within oneself and stand wrapping around the individual existence (attabhāva) like a coat of mail. Because kamma performed in the absence of defilements does not cause rebirth, it is said to be "relinquished." Thus, by abandoning the defilements, He relinquished kamma. For one who has abandoned defilements, there is no such thing as fear; therefore, He relinquished the life-principle without any fear. It should be understood that He made the inspired utterance to make known His state of fearlessness.

'Yaṃ mahāvātā' means at which time the great winds blow. 'Vāyanti' means the winds called "upakkhepaka" (upheaving winds) arise. When those winds blow, they cut through the water-supporting wind which is 960,000 leagues thick. Because of that cutting, the water falls in space; when that water falls, the earth falls. Again, the wind, by its own power, binds and holds the water as if in a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa). Then the water rises; when that water rises, the earth rises. In this way, the water...
251:
It causes the trembling earth to shake. Such earth-shaking continues to occur even up to the present time. However, due to the vastness of the earth, the sinking and rising are not clearly apparent.

'Mahiddhikā mahānubhāvā' means: 'Mahiddhika' due to the greatness of the fulfillment of results, and 'Mahānubhāva' due to the greatness of the sovereignty to be experienced. 'Parittā' refers to those who are weak. 'Appamāṇā' refers to those who are powerful. 'He shakes this earth' means that a monk endowed with psychic power and direct knowledge causes the earth to shake, like the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna who, having exercised his psychic power, caused the King of Devas (Sakka), who was negligent in heavenly bliss, to be struck with a sense of urgency (saṃvega); or like the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Elder Mahānāga, who shook the earth while testing his own psychic power. 'Saṅkampeti' means to shake from all sides. The word 'sampakampeti' is a synonym for 'kampeti'.

Thus, among these eight types of earthquakes, the first is caused by the disturbance of elements; the second by the majesty of psychic power; the third and fourth by the power of merit; the fifth by the power of knowledge; the sixth by the influence of giving applause (sādhukāra); the seventh by the nature of compassion; and the eighth by lamentation.

When the Great Being (Bodhisatta) descended into his mother's womb and when he was born from it, the earth shook due to the power of his merit. At the time of his Enlightenment, it shook being struck by the power of the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. When the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion, it shook by way of giving applause, being established in the state of appreciation. When he relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), it shook because it could not endure the agitation of the mind, being established in the nature of compassion. At the time of his Parinibbāna, it shook being driven by the force of lamentation. This meaning of earth-shaking due to applause, etc., should be understood as being through the power of the earth-deity. For the physical earth, which is a great primary element, this does not occur because it is insentient. The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all places.

## The Seventh Chapter on Earthquakes (Bhūmicālavagga) is finished.

## 1-2. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Faith (Saddhāsutta)

71-72. In the first discourse of the eighth chapter, 'no ca sīlavā' means one who does not fulfill the practice of the precepts. 'Samantapāsādiko' means one who inspires confidence from all sides. 'Sabbākārapuripūro' means one who is complete in all the attributes and factors of a recluse's practice. In the second discourse, 'santā' means they are called 'peaceful' because of the subsiding of opposing defilements. 'Vimokkhā' means they are called 'liberations' because of being liberated from opposing states.
252:
## 3-9. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Mindfulness of Death, etc.

73-79. In the third discourse, 'bhāvetha no' means 'bhāvetha nu' (do you develop?). 'Sāsanaṃ' means the instruction. 'Āsavānaṃ khayāya' means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship.

In the fourth discourse, 'patihitāya' means when one has encountered (some danger). 'So mamassa antarāyo' means that such an earthquake, etc., would be a danger to my life; and if I were to die as a worldling, it would be a danger to heaven and a danger to the Path. 'Satthakā vā me vātā' means winds called 'satthaka' because they cut through the limbs and body like weapons.

The fifth discourse and others follow the same method already mentioned.

In the ninth discourse, 'saṃsaggārāmatā' means delighting in the five kinds of social association.

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on Grounds for Laziness and Effort

In the tenth discourse, 'kusītavatthūni' means the bases or foundations for a lazy person, meaning the causes of indolence. 'Kammaṃ kattabbaṃ hoti' means there is work to be done, such as preparing robes and so on. 'Na vīriyaṃ ārabhati' means not exerting even the two kinds of effort. 'Appattassa' means for the attainment of the states of Jhana, Insight (Vipassanā), the Path, and the Fruit which have not yet been reached. 'Anadhigatassa' means for the realization of those very states which have not yet been realized. 'Asacchikatassa' means for the sake of witnessing those very states which have not yet been witnessed. 'Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ' means this sinking down in the form of 'Now I shall lie down' is the first ground for laziness (kusītavatthu). In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sentences. In the phrase 'māsācitakaṃ maññe', 'māsācita' refers to wet beans. Just as wet beans are heavy, the meaning is that it is similarly heavy. 'Gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti' means one who has recovered after being ill. 'Ārambhavatthūni' means the grounds for effort. Their meaning should also be understood in this very same manner. The remaining words are clear in all places.

## The Eighth Chapter of Pairs (Yamakavagga) is finished.

## (9) 4. The Chapter on Mindfulness (Sativagga)

## 1-2. Commentary on the Discourses on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension

81-82. The first discourse of the ninth chapter follows the same method already mentioned below. In the second discourse, 'saddho' means one who is endowed with the two kinds of faith. 'No cupasaṅkamitā' means one who does not approach or attend upon (others).
253:
He is one who does not habitually inquire about what is beneficial or not, or what is a cause or not. 'Samannāgato' (endowed with) is meant in the sense of the possessive case (sāmi-attha) as 'samannāgatassa' (of one who is endowed), though expressed in the nominative case (paccatta-vibhatti). 'Ekantapaṭibhānā tathāgataṃ dhammadesanā hoti' means that the Buddha's teaching of the Dhamma is a teaching that is absolutely manifest; it means it is only and definitely manifest and clear.

## 3. Mūlaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'sabbe dhammā' (all things) refers to the five aggregates (khandhas). 'Chandamūlakā' (rooted in desire) is said because the desire of intention (ajjhāsayachanda) and the desire to act (kattukamyatāchanda) are the roots of those five aggregates. 'Manasikārasambhavā' (originating from attention) is said because they arise due to attention. 'Phassasamudayā' (arising from contact) is said because they arise in heaps due to contact. 'Vedanāsamosaraṇā' (converging in feeling) is said because they converge in feeling. 'Samādhippamukhā' (headed by concentration) is said because concentration is the head of those five aggregates. 'Satādhipateyyā' is said because mindfulness is the governor in the sense of being the chief; it means having mindfulness as the chief. 'Paññuttarā' (transcended by wisdom) is said because wisdom is superior to those five aggregates. 'Vimuttisārā' (having liberation as the essence) is said because liberation, which is the fruit of Arahantship, is the only essence of those five aggregates. Among these eight things, the first four starting from 'rooted in desire' are taught as mundane (lokiya) states, while the remaining four are taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane (lokuttara) states.

## 4. Cora Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'mahācoro' (great thief) refers to a great thief who is capable of committing offenses within a kingdom. 'Pariyāpajjati' means he reaches exhaustion. 'Na ciraṭṭhitiko hoti' means he is unable to endure for a long time. 'Appaharantassa paharati' means he strikes and oppresses those who are not his enemies, those who do not strike him, those endowed with virtues who should not be struck, the elderly, and young children. 'Anavasesaṃ ādiyati' means he takes everything without leaving any remainder. The conduct of a clever thief is as follows: if another person has two garments, only one should be taken; if there is only one, the poor quality one should be left and the durable one should be taken. In the case of packets of cooked rice, raw rice, etc., one portion should be left and only one portion should be taken—such is their conduct. 'Accāsanne kammaṃ karoti' means he commits theft in the vicinity of villages, market towns, and royal capitals. 'Na ca nidhānakusalo hoti' means he is not skillful in storing the wealth he has obtained with those worthy of offerings; he does not clear the path for the future life.
254:
## 5. Samaṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "yaṃ samaṇena" refers to the collection of virtues that should be attained by a recluse. "Vusīmatā" refers to a person who has completed the practice by living the holy life (brahmacariya). "Mutto mocemi bandhanā" means, "I, having been freed from all bonds, also free the multitude of people from the bonds of lust (rāga) and so forth." "Paramadanto" (the supremely tamed) is so called because he has realized through self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) without being taught or urged by others, and is tamed by the supreme discipline. "Parinibbuto" means one who is cooled by the extinguishing of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna).

## 6. Yasa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "mā ca mayā yaso" means, "let fame not follow along with me." "Akasiralābhī" means one who obtains abundant gains. "Sīlapaññāṇaṃ" refers to virtue (sīla) and wisdom (paññā). "Saṅgamma" means having assembled. "Samāgamma" means having come together. "Saṅgaṇikavihāraṃ" refers to living in association with a group. "Na hi nūnameti" should be resolved as "na hi nūna ime." "Tathā hi panameti" should be resolved as "tathā hi pana ime." "Aṅgulipatodakehi" means by poking and prodding with fingers. "Sañjagghante" refers to laughing loudly. "Saṅkīḷante" refers to playing or jesting.

## 7. Pattanikujjana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "nikkujjeyya" (should overturn) means one should overturn [the bowl] by the formal act of overturning the bowl (pattanikkujjana-kammavācā) for the purpose of not accepting the offerings given by that person; it does not mean placing it face down. "Alābhāya" means for the purpose of not receiving the four requisites. "Anatthāya" means for the purpose of misfortune and lack of growth. "Ukkujjeyya" (should set upright) means one should set the bowl upright by the formal act of setting the bowl upright (ukkujjana-kammavācā).

## 8. Appasādapavedanīya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "appasādaṃ pavedeyyuṃ" means they should make known their lack of confidence/dissatisfaction. As for what should be done by one who makes known dissatisfaction: one should not rise from one's seat, should not pay homage, should not go out to welcome, and should not give offerings. "Agocare" refers to the five kinds of improper resorts (agocara).
255:
## 9. Paṭisāraṇīya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "dhammikañca gihipaṭissavaṃ" refers to giving a promise when told, "You must stay right here for these three months of the rains retreat," by saying, "Very well," and so on. "Na saccāpeti" means not making it true as said, or breaking the promise.

## 10. Sammāvattana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "paccekaṭṭhāne" means in a position of authority or seniority. One is not allowed to perform any formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) by making that monk (who is subjected to the Tassapāpiyasika-kamma) the senior. "Na ca tena mūlena vuṭṭhāpetabbo" means one is not allowed to perform the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna-kamma) based on that monk. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

Following this, in the sections starting with "Atha kho bojjhā upāsikā," the practice of the eight-fold Uposatha is described for all these female lay disciples: Bojjhā the lay follower, Sirimā the lay follower, Padumā the lay follower, Sutanā the lay follower, Manujā the lay follower, Uttarā the lay follower, Muttā the lay follower, Khemā the lay follower, Rucī the lay follower, Princess Cundī, Bimbī the lay follower, Princess Sumanā, Queen Mallikā, Tissā the lay follower, the mother of Tissā the lay follower, Soṇā the lay follower, the mother of Soṇā the lay follower, Kāṇā the lay follower, the mother of Kāṇā the lay follower, Uttarā the mother of Nanda, Visākhā the mother of Migāra, Khujjuttarā the lay follower, Sāmāvatī the lay follower, Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter, Suppiyā the lay follower, and Nakulamātā the housewife.
