257:
## Aṅguttara Nikāya
## Navakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka
## 1. Sambodhisutta-vaṇṇanā
## 1. Sambodhivagga
In the first sutta of the Book of the Nines, 'sambodhipakkhikānaṃ' means the factors that belong to or are helpful to 'sambodhi', which is the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths known as the four paths. He asks this with reference to the nine things mentioned in the Pāḷi text. 'Kā upanisā' means what is the primary cause (upanissaya-paccaya)? They are called 'abhisallekhikā' because they lead to the extreme attenuation of defilements. They are called 'cetovivaraṇasappāyā' because they are suitable and helpful for the opening (development) of the mind in serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Talk that proceeds based on fewness of wishes (appicchata) is called 'appicchakathā'. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

'Foulness (asubha) should be developed for the abandoning of lust (rāga)'—this meaning should be illustrated by the simile of the man reaping hill-rice. Indeed, a man takes a sickle and starts reaping the hill-rice in a field from the edge. While he is reaping, cows break through the fence and enter. He puts down the sickle, takes a stick, drives the cows out by the same path they entered, repairs the fence to its original state, and then takes the sickle again to continue reaping the rice.

In this simile, the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana) should be understood as the rice field. The meditator (yogāvacara) should be understood as the man reaping the rice. Wisdom (paññā) should be understood as the sickle. The time of performing the work of insight (vipassanā) should be understood as the time of reaping. The foulness meditation (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) should be understood as the stick. Restraint (saṃvara) should be understood as the fence. The arising of lust due to heedlessness and lack of reflection, like cows breaking the fence and entering, should be understood. The time of suppressing lust with the foulness meditation and resuming the work of insight—like putting down the sickle, taking the stick, driving out the cows by the way they entered, repairing the fence, and starting to reap again from the edge—should be understood. With reference to this meaning, it was said: "Foulness should be developed for the abandoning of lust."

In that phrase (beginning with 'asubha bhāvetabbā'), 'rāgassa' refers to lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Mettā' refers to the meditation on loving-kindness. In the phrase 'byāpādassa pahānāya', it is for the abandoning of arising anger, according to the method already mentioned. 'Ānāpānassati' is mindfulness of breathing in sixteen aspects. In the phrase 'vitakkupacchedāya', it is for the cutting off of arising thoughts, according to the method already mentioned. 'Asmimānasamugghātāya' is for the uprooting of the conceit that arises as "I am". 'Anattasaññā saṇṭhāti' means that if one sees the mark of impermanence (anicca), one also sees the mark of non-self (anatta). Indeed, among these three marks, if one sees one mark, one also sees the other two. Therefore, He said: "Bhikkhus, for one who perceives impermanence, the perception of non-self becomes established." 'Diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānaṃ' means reaching Nibbāna without conditions (apaccaya-parinibbāna) in this very life. Thus, in this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

2. In the second sutta, 'nissayasampanno' refers to one who is endowed with faith, which is the support.
258:
Among those phrases (beginning with 'asubha bhāvetabbā'), 'rāgassa' refers to lust that arises in the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Mettā' is the meditation on loving-kindness. 'Byāpādassa pahānāya' is for the purpose of abandoning arising anger by the method already mentioned. 'Ānāpānassati' is mindfulness that takes the sixteen aspects of the breath as its object. 'Vitakkupacchedāya' is for the purpose of cutting off arising thoughts by the method already mentioned. 'Asmimānasamugghātāya' is for the purpose of uprooting the conceit that arises as "I am". 'Anattasaññā saṇṭhāti' means that when the mark of impermanence is seen, the mark of non-self is already seen. This is because among these three marks, if one sees any one, the other two are also already seen. Therefore, He said: "Bhikkhus, for one who has the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self is established." 'Diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānaṃ' means reaching Nibbāna, the state where conditions cease, in this very life. Thus, in this sutta, the round of suffering and the cessation of the round are taught.

## 2. Nissayasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'nissayasampanno' means being endowed with a support (foundation). 'Saddhā' refers to faith of conviction (okappana-saddhā). 'Vīriya' refers to bodily effort and mental effort. 'Yaṃsā' should be resolved as "yaṃ assa". 'Ariyāya paññāya' refers to path-wisdom together with insight. 'Saṅkhāya' means having known (having reflected). 'Ekaṃ paṭisevati' means using the four requisites that are suitable to be used. 'Adhivāseti' means enduring heat, cold, and so on, which are suitable to be endured. 'Parivajjeti' means avoiding elephants, horses, and so on, which are suitable to be avoided. 'Vinodeti' means dispelling sensual thoughts and so on, which are suitable to be dispelled. Thus, a monk who, through the power of learning and inquiry, and through the power of defining the Dhamma, has well-penetrated and clearly realized what should be used and so forth, and who then uses, endures, avoids, and dispels, is called a monk endowed with support.

## 3. Meghiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'cālikāyaṃ' means in the city of that name. It is said that because that city was built depending on a moving path (calamagga), it appeared to onlookers as if it were moving; therefore, it acquired the name Cālikā. 'Cāliyapabbate' means that mountain also, because it was entirely white, appeared to onlookers as if it were moving on the new moon Uposatha day; therefore, it was called Mount Cāliya. A great monastery was built on that mountain. Thus, the Blessed One, depending on that city, dwelt at the Cāliyapabbata Mahāvihāra. 'Jantugāmaṃ' refers to another village of this name, which was the alms-resort village for that monastery.
259:
The word 'Jattugāma' is also read as such. 'Padhānatthikassa' means for one who has the task of striving in meditation. 'Padhānāya' means for the purpose of performing the practice of meditation, which is the Dhamma of a recluse. The Blessed One, after hearing the words of Elder Meghiya and investigating, knew that the Elder's knowledge was not yet mature; wishing to restrain him, He spoke the words 'Āgamehi tāva' (Wait a while). As for the words 'Ekakamhi tāva' (For a while alone), He spoke them to generate gentleness of mind, thinking: "Even if this Elder goes and his task is not accomplished, he will return again out of affection, free from hesitation."

'Natthi kiñci uttari karaṇီyaṃ' means that because the four tasks regarding the Four Noble Truths have been completed, there is no other further task to be done. There is also no 'paṭicayo' (repetition) for the Path already attained. Indeed, a Path already developed is not developed again, and defilements already abandoned are not to be abandoned again. The Buddha said, "Meghiya, what else shall we say to you who are saying, 'I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse'?"

'Divāvihāraṃ nisīdi' means he sat for the purpose of the day's rest. While sitting, Elder Meghiya sat on that very auspicious stone slab where, in five hundred previous lives, he had sat as a king, surrounded by three types of dancers while enjoying himself in the park. Then, from the time he sat down, it was as if he had abandoned his state as a recluse; he took on the appearance of a king, surrounded by a group of excellent dancers, as if sitting on a costly throne under a royal white umbrella. Then, while enjoying that prosperity, sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) arose in that Elder. At that very moment, he seemed to see two thieves brought before him, captured by generals. Among those thieves, a thought of ill-will (byāpādavitakka) arose with the desire to order the execution of one, and a thought of cruelty (vihiṃsāvitakka) arose with the desire to order the binding of the other. Thus, that Elder was surrounded by unwholesome thoughts, like a tree entwined by a web of creepers, or like a honey-gatherer surrounded by bees. With reference to that, it was said: 'Atha kho āyasmato Meghiyassa...' and so on. 'Anvāsattā' means followed or surrounded. 'Yena Bhagavā tenupasaṅkami' means that, being overwhelmed by such evil thoughts and unable to practice meditation properly, he reflected, "The Buddha, who sees far, surely forbade me seeing this reason," and thinking, "I will report this matter to the Buddha," he rose from his seat and approached where the Buddha was.
260:
## 4. Nandakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'upaṭṭhānassālāyaṃ' means in the refectory. The Blessed One heard the sound of the Dhamma being preached with a sweet voice by the Elder Nandaka and asked, "Ananda, who is this preaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice in the refectory?" When he heard, "Venerable Sir, today is the turn of the Dhamma-preacher Elder Nandaka," He said, "Ananda, this monk is preaching the Dhamma very sweetly; let us also go and listen," and He approached the refectory. Standing at the doorway, He stood in an unrecognized form, concealing the six-colored rays within His robes. Awaiting the end of the discourse, which is marked by the words 'Idamavoca' (This he said), He remained standing while listening to the Dhamma talk. Then, when the first watch of the night had passed, the Venerable Ananda gave a sign to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the first watch has passed; please rest for a while." The Blessed One remained standing right there. When the middle watch had also passed, the Venerable Ananda spoke again: "Venerable Sir, you are delicate by nature as a Khattiya, and you are also delicate as a Buddha, thus you are supremely delicate. The middle watch has also passed; please rest for a moment." The Blessed One continued to stand right there.

While He was standing thus, the dawn appeared. The rising of the dawn, the Elder reaching the end of his discourse, and the Blessed One releasing the six-colored rays from His body occurred simultaneously. 'Aggaḷaṃ ākoṭesi' means he knocked on the door panel with the tip of his fingernail. 'Sārajjamānarūpo' means being bashful or apprehensive, but it was not the kind of fear caused by mental distress for that Elder. 'Ettakampi no nappaṭibhāseyyā' is intended to show that although there is no lack of inspiration for one who has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), it was as if he could no longer preach even this much Dhamma. The Buddha said, "Sādhu, sādhu," gladdening the Elder's Dhamma teaching. Its meaning is: "Your Dhamma teaching was well-grasped and well-preached."

'Kulaputtānaṃ' refers to sons of good family by conduct and sons of good family by birth. The phrase 'ariyo ca tuṇhībhāvo' (noble silence) was said with reference to the attainment of the second jhāna. 'Adhipaññādhammavipassanāya' refers to the insight knowledge that comprehends formations (saṅkhāra). 'Catuppādako' refers to four-footed animals such as horses, cattle, and donkeys. 'Idaṃ vatvā' means after preaching this Dhamma endowed with these four factors. 'Vihāraṃ pāvisi' means He entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi).

'Kālena dhammassavane' means listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. 'Dhammasākacchāya' means discussion by way of questions and answers. 'Gambhīraṃ atthapadaṃ' means a profound, hidden, and secret meaning.
261:
"By wisdom" means by path-wisdom (magga-paññā) along with insight (vipassanā). Contemplative wisdom (sammasana-paññā), penetrative wisdom (paṭivedha-paññā), and wisdom derived from learning and inquiry (uggaha-paripucchā-paññā) are also appropriate. "Whether one has reached or will reach" means having reached Arahantship or being about to reach it; this is stated as praise for his virtues. "Those with unreached minds" (appattamānasā) refers to those who have not yet attained Arahantship, or it is said of them because their minds have not yet reached Arahantship. In the phrase "living happily in the present life" (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra), this happiness can be either mundane (lokiya) or supramundane (lokuttara).

## 5. Bala Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, the powers of wisdom and so forth (paññā-bala etc.) should be understood as being unshakable in the face of unwholesome states such as ignorance (avijjā), laziness (kosajja), blamefulness (sāvajja), and lack of faith (assaddhiya). "Called unwholesome" refers to those states known as unwholesome. This method should be applied everywhere. "Those unworthy of being Noble Ones" (nālamariyā) means those incapable of becoming Noble Ones, or those unsuitable for Noble Ones. "Vodiṭṭha" refers to things that are well-seen. "Vocarita" refers to things that have reached the state of frequent occurrence (practice) in the mind-door. "To one who desires" means to one who desires the teaching of the Dhamma. "Fear for livelihood" (ājīvika-bhaya) is the fear concerning one's means of living. "Fear of ill-repute" (asiloka-bhaya) is the fear of being blamed. "Fear of embarrassment in an assembly" (parisāsārajja-bhaya) is the fear of being overcome by stage fright upon entering an assembly. In this sutta, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 6. Sevanā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "requisites of life" (jīvitaparikkhāra) are the supports for life. "Should be sought" (samudānetabbā) means should be well-collected. "Obtained with difficulty" (kasirena samudāgacchanti) means they arise with hardship and toil. In the phrase "whether during the night or during the day," if one realizes (the fault) at night, one should depart even at night. If there are dangers such as fierce wild animals at night, one should wait for dawn. If one realizes it during the day, one should depart even during the day. If there are dangers during the day, one should wait for sunset. "Even after reflecting" (saṅkhāpi) means after knowing that one has reached the fulfillment of meditation practice, which is the benefit of monkhood. The phrase "that person" (so puggalo) should be connected with "should not be followed" (nānubandhitabbā). "Without asking" (anāpucchā) here means one should depart without asking permission from that person. "Even if expelled" (api panujjamānena) means even if being dragged out. For if such a person imposes a penalty of a hundred bundles of wood, a hundred pots of water, or a hundred pots of sand, or expels one saying, "Do not live here," one should apologize to him and follow him for the rest of one's life; he should not be abandoned.
262:
## 7. Sutavā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "pañca ṭṭhānāni ajjācarituṃ" means to transgress five things. "Life" (pāṇaṃ) refers to even an ant or a small insect. "Not given" (adinnaṃ) refers to even a blade of grass belonging to another. "Known as theft" (theyyasaṅkhātaṃ) means with the intention to steal. "To consume stored-up sensual pleasures" (sannidhikārakaṃ kāme paribhuñjituṃ) means being incapable of storing and using sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and defilements (kilesa-kāma). This is said with reference to improper sensual pleasures. "To renounce the Buddha" (buddhaṃ paccakkhātuṃ) means to reject him by saying, "This is not the Buddha." The same method applies to the Dhamma and so forth. This is how it appears in the Commentary. In the Pali text, however, this sutta teaches the taking of wrong courses (agati).

## 8-10. Sajjha Sutta etc. Vaṇṇanā
8-10. In the eighth sutta, the renouncing of the Buddha and so forth is taught. In the ninth sutta, "worthy of offerings" (āhuneyya) is mentioned because it is taken together with worldlings (puthujjana). In the tenth sutta, the Gotrabhū person is one endowed with powerful insight (vipassanā) that has reached its peak and acts as the immediate condition (anantara-paccaya) for the path of stream-entry. The remaining words are clear in meaning everywhere.

## The First Chapter: Sambodha Vagga.

## 2. Sīhanāda Vagga

## 1. Sīhanāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, regarding the phrase "approached where the Blessed One was": Thinking, "If the Teacher wishes to go on a walking tour, he will go at this time; I will ask the Teacher for permission to go on a walking tour," he approached surrounded by the community of monks. Regarding the phrase "Venerable sir, to me": It is said that the monk, seeing the Elder (Sāriputta) departing with a large retinue of monks, became angry at an inappropriate thing, thinking, "These monks have abandoned the Tathāgata and are departing surrounding Sāriputta; I will cause an obstruction to his journey," and spoke thus. Therein, "assajja" means having struck or offended. "Appaṭinissajja" means without asking for forgiveness or without confessing the fault. For what reason did he bear a grudge? It is said that as the Elder was leaving after bowing to the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha), the corner of his robe touched the monk's body; some also say the wind blew it against him. Bearing a grudge for just this much, and seeing the Elder departing with a large retinue, he became envious and thought, "I will cause an obstruction to his journey," and spoke thus. The phrase "Come, monk"...
263:
The Teacher, hearing the monk's words, asked, "Monk, did Sāriputta strike you and then leave?" Knowing that the monk might think, "Venerable Sir, you are taking the side of your own chief disciple and not mine," and thus harbor ill-will toward the Buddha and be reborn in a state of misery, the Teacher thought, "I will summon Sāriputta and ask about this matter." He then called a monk and said, "Monk, go," and so on. 'Avāpuraṇaṃ ādāya' means taking the key (or bolt). 'Sīhanādaṃ' means a noble sound, a foremost sound, a sound that others cannot turn back. The Saṅgha of monks, urged by the two Great Elders (Venerable Moggallāna and Venerable Assaji), left their places of night and day rest and came to the Teacher. 'Khīyanadhammaṃ' means words of reproach.

'Gūthagataṃ' means having reached excrement. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Pathavīsamena' means being like the earth in the sense of not getting angry. Just as the earth does not feel joy when people throw clean things on it, nor does it feel displeasure when they throw unclean things, this shows that "My mind is of such a nature." 'Vipulena' means in the sense of being non-narrow (vast). 'Mahaggatena' means in the sense of having reached greatness (exalted). 'Appamāṇena' means in the sense of having a developed measure (immeasurable). 'Averaṇa' means in the sense of being free from the enmity of unwholesome states or persons. 'Abyāpajjhena' means in the sense of being free from suffering and displeasure. 'So idha' means only such a monk who possesses mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) that does not cling to objects would act in such a way (offending others); "How could one like me do such a thing, Venerable Sir?" Thus he first uttered a bold sound like a lion's roar. This application should be understood in all places.

'Rajoharaṇaṃ' means a cloth for wiping away dust; 'pādapuñchanaṃ' (foot-wiper) is also a name for that same rajoharaṇa. 'Kaḷopihattho' means holding a basket or holding a rice pot in the hand. 'Nantakavāsī' means one who wears old rags with torn edges. 'Surato' means one who has pure virtue and is endowed with gentleness (soracca). 'Sudanto' means one who has reached the state of being well-tamed. 'Suvinīto' means one who is well-trained. 'Na kañci hiṃsati' refers to an ox that does not harm anyone even when someone grasps its horns or strokes its back. 'Usabhachinnavisāṇasamena' means being like the mind of a bull with broken horns.

'Aṭṭīyeyya' means one would be oppressed or troubled. 'Harāyeyya' means one would be ashamed. 'Jiguccheyya' means one would reach a state of loathing. 'Medakathālikā' refers to a pot in which butchers have made holes here and there for the grease (juice) to flow out. 'Parihareyya' means one would carry it filled with meat. 'Chiddavanti' refers to a pot full of small and large holes. The grease flowing from the holes mentioned above as openings... 'Parimaṃ' means the openings situated below...
264:
...having filled it and lifting it (with hands), one would go. 'Chiddāvachiddaṃ' means being full of small and large holes. 'Uggharantan' means the grease (liquid) oozing from the holes on the upper surface. 'Paggharantan' means the grease dripping from the holes on the lower surface. In this way, the person's entire body would be smeared and stained with grease. 'Chiddāvachiddaṃ' means having small and large holes through the nine wounds (orifices). Thus, in this sutta, through the eighth and ninth factors, the Elder spoke of the state of being free from desire and lust (nicchandarāgata) regarding his own body.

'Atha kho so bhikkhu' means after the Elder had uttered the bold words like a lion's roar through the nine reasons, then that monk (confessed his fault). 'Accayo' means a fault (aparādha). 'Maṃ accagamā' means it has overcome and transcended me. 'Paṭiggaṇhatu' means please forgive. 'Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya' means for the sake of restraint in the future and so that such a fault is not committed again. 'Taggha' means certainly. 'Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi' means you act according to the nature of the Dhamma, meaning you confess and ask for forgiveness. 'Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma' means we forgive that fault of yours. 'Vuddhihesā bhikkhu ariyassa vinaye' means, "Monk, this (seeing a fault and confessing it) is called growth in the Discipline of the Noble One." How? It is seeing a fault as a fault, atoning for it according to the Dhamma, and achieving restraint in the future. Because he wished to give the teaching in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), he said, "Whoever sees a fault as a fault, atones for it according to the Dhamma, and achieves restraint in the future." 'Phalati' means if the Elder had not forgiven, that monk's head would have split into seven pieces right there. Therefore, the Buddha spoke in this way. 'Sace maṃ so' means if this monk says, "Forgive me." 'Khamatu ca me so' means "May this venerable one also forgive me." Thus, the Elder accepted the monk's fault and himself made the monk be forgiven in the presence of the Teacher.

## ၂။ သဥပါဒိသေသသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the second sutta, 'Saupādisesaṃ' means having remaining clinging (upādāna). 'Anupādisesaṃ' means being free from remaining clinging. 'Mattaso kārī' means one who acts to a certain measure and is not one who fulfills the practice completely. In the phrase, "Sāriputta, this Dhamma-exposition is not yet clear to you," it does not mean that knowledge is not clear to the Buddha; it means "I have not yet preached this Dhamma-exposition to that extent." "Do not become negligent after hearing this Dhamma teaching" means so that they do not remain without making effort for the higher paths and fruits (Arahantship), thinking, "We are already free from the four states of misery." 'Pañhādhippāyena bhāsito' means it is preached according to the intention of the question you asked. To show this meaning, for the sake of the nine types of persons to naturally abandon lust, and based on their liberation from the states of misery, he preached this sutta: "Monks, just as even a small amount of excrement has a foul smell, so I do not praise even a finger-snap's duration of existence." Of the nine types of persons...
265:
It is shown that it is spoken according to its nature. For the purpose of dispelling lust for existences in these nine types of persons, based on this very matter, the Buddha spoke this sutta: “Monks, just as even a small amount of excrement has a foul smell, even so, monks, I do not praise even a small amount of existence, even for as long as a finger-snap.” (AN 1.321). It is not only these nine persons whose destiny is fixed; those families who possess constant merits such as the three refuges, the five precepts, a single ticket-food, a single fortnightly food, a single rains-residence robe, a single pond, and a single dwelling—their destiny is also fixed. These families are just like stream-enterers (sotāpannas).

## 3. Koṭṭhikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'diṭṭhadhammavedanīya' refers to kamma that ripens in this very life. 'Samparāyavedanīya' refers to kamma that ripens in the second existence. 'Sukhavedanīya' refers to kamma that produces pleasant feeling. 'Dukkhavedanīya' refers to kamma that produces painful feeling. 'Paripakkavedanīya' refers to kamma whose turn to ripen has arrived. 'Aparipakkavedanīya' refers to kamma whose turn to ripen has not yet arrived. 'Bahuvedanīya' refers to kamma that gives much result. 'Appavedanīya' refers to kamma that does not give much result. 'Avedanīya' refers to kamma that does not give the feeling of result. In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 4. Samiddhisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'Samiddhi' is the name of an elder who was a co-resident (saddhivihārika) of the Elder, so named because of the perfection (samiddhatā) of his physical form. 'What is their cause?' means 'By what reason do they arise?' 'Thoughts that are intentions' means thoughts having the nature of intention. 'Having name-and-form as their object' means having name-and-form as their cause. By this term 'name-and-form', it is shown that the four mental aggregates and the primary and derived matter are the causes of thoughts. 'Where do they reach diversity?' means 'In what place do they reach various natures or differences?' 'In the elements' means in the form-element (rūpadhātu) and so on. Thought of form is one thing; thoughts of sound and so on are each distinct. 'Arising from contact' means having the associated contact as their cause. 'Having feelings as their meeting place' means the three feelings are their meeting place. With these words, thoughts mixed with wholesome and unwholesome are taught. The words 'having concentration as their head' and so on should be understood as belonging to the side of the destruction of defilements (apacayapakkhika). In that context, they are called 'samādhippamukha' (headed by concentration) because concentration is the head, either in the sense of being a precursor or being the chief. They are called 'satādhipateyya' (governed by mindfulness) because mindfulness is the governor in the sense of exercising lordship. They are called 'paññuttara' (surpassed by wisdom) because the wisdom of the path is supreme. They are called 'vimuttisāra' (having liberation as their essence) because they reach the essence by attaining liberation, which is the fruit. By the power of the object, towards the deathless Nibbāna...
266:
Because they plunge into Nibbāna and remain there, they are called 'plunging into the deathless' (amatogadha). 'And do not think [highly] of yourself because of that' means: do not be proud or arrogant because of being able to answer, thinking, 'I have answered the questions asked by the Chief Disciple.'

## 5-6. Gaṇḍa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

15-16. In the fifth (Gaṇḍa) sutta, 'having many years' (anekavassagaṇika) means having many years such as three or four years. 'May they be for him' (tassassū) means they may arise in that house which is the body. 'Openings of the boil' (abhedanamukhāni) are the openings of wounds that are not made by anyone cutting them, but arise solely due to kamma. 'Only loathsome' (jegucchiyaṃyeva) means it is purely disgusting and repulsive.

'Consisting of the four great elements' (cātumahābhūtika) means made of the four great elements. 'Accumulated from rice and gruel' (odanakummāsūpacaya) means grown and nourished by rice and barley gruel. 'Having the nature of impermanence, anointing, massaging, breaking, and disintegration' (aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammassa) means: having the nature of impermanence because it ceases to exist after having arisen; having the nature of anointing (ucchādana) with perfumes to dispel foul odors; having the nature of massaging (parimaddana) by minor rubbing to dispel the ailments of the limbs; or the nature of massaging by pulling and pressing to properly shape the limbs that were poorly formed due to the stay in the womb while being made to sleep on the thighs in infancy; and even when thus cared for, having the nature of breaking and disintegration, which is the nature of breaking apart and scattering. Here, by the word 'impermanence' (anicca) and the words 'breaking and disintegration' (bhedanaviddhaṃsana), the cessation (atthaṅgama) of the body is stated, while by the remaining words, its arising (samudaya) is stated. 'Be weary' (nibbindatha) means it is shown that one should be weary of and abandon this body. Thus, in this sutta, strong insight (balavavipassanā) is discussed. The sixth sutta follows the same method already mentioned. However, in this sutta, insight-knowledge (ñāṇa) is discussed by taking 'perception' (saññā) as the head.

## 7-8. Kula Sutta Vaṇṇanā

17-18. In the seventh (Kula) sutta, 'they do not rise up pleasantly' (na manāpena paccuṭṭhenti) means they do not rise from their seats to welcome [monks] with a mind-brightening or mind-attaching manner. 'They do not greet pleasantly' (na manāpena abhivādenti) means they do not pay homage with the five-point prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita). 'They give without respect' (asakkaccaṃ denti) means they give without showing honor. 'Not with respect' (no sakkaccaṃ) means they do not give with their own hands. 'They do not sit near to hear the Dhamma' (na upanisīdanti dhammasavanāya) means they do not sit nearby saying, 'We will listen to the Dhamma.' 'They do not listen' (na sussūsanti) means [the Dhamma] rolls away like water poured on the back of a pot. In the eighth sutta, by the power of the inclination of those to be led (veneyya), loving-kindness meditation (mettā bhāvanā) is included, and it is said to be endowed with nine factors.
267:
## 9. Devatāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth (Devatā) Sutta: 'Vippaṭisārino' means they arrived at a state of remorse (mental unease). In the phrase 'hīnaṃ kāyaṃ' (inferior body/realm), the lower celestial realm is called 'inferior' (hīna) when compared to the upper celestial realms. 'They did not distribute according to their ability and strength' means they did not eat after having shared with the virtuous in accordance with their own capability and power.

## 10. Velāmasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the tenth (Velāma) Sutta: 'Householder, are alms given in your house?'—the Blessed One does not ask this regarding the alms given to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Indeed, it is not that the Teacher does not know that excellent alms are constantly given to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha in the merchant's house; he certainly knows. However, there is an alms-giving for the ordinary people of the world which is coarse and does not satisfy the merchant's heart. He asks referring to that alms-giving. 'Kaṇājaka' refers to broken rice cooked with bran; it is rice cooked only with bran and small broken grains. 'Bilaṅgadutiya' means having sour gruel as the second (companion); that is, eaten together with sour gruel. 'Giving disrespectfully' (asakkaccaṃ deti) means giving without showing respect. 'Without making it a matter of mind' (acittīkatvā) means giving with a lack of reverence toward the recipient. 'Not giving with one's own hand' (asahatthā deti) means giving through the hands of others instead of one's own; it means merely giving the order. 'Giving as if throwing away' (apaviddhaṃ deti) means not giving regularly, like the annual offerings of drunkards (soṇḍabali). 'Giving with the view that there is no coming [of results]' (anāgamanadiṭṭhiko deti) means giving without faith in kamma and its fruit.

'In whichever [place]' (yattha yattha) means in whichever family among the three types of family prosperity. In the phrases such as 'the mind does not incline toward enjoying grand food,' even when fragrant Sāli rice of various flavors is served, the mind does not incline toward it. Saying, 'Take this away, it increases disease,' he eats broken rice with whatever boiled leaves are available, enjoying it as if it were ambrosia. When excellent garments such as those from Kāsi are offered, he says, 'Take these away; they cannot even cover the wearer properly, nor do they stay firm on the limbs.' Instead, he takes pleasure in wearing coarse cloths similar to coconut fiber or bark, saying, 'Wearing these, one knows one is clothed, and they cover what should be covered.' When elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariots, or golden palanquins are offered, he says, 'Take these away; they are too shaky, one cannot sit here.' But when an old, rickety chariot is brought, he accepts it, saying, 'This is steady; it is comfortable to sit here.' 'The mind does not incline toward the five grand cords of sensual pleasure' means that upon seeing beautiful, well-adorned women, he says, 'These women are just ogresses; they want to eat me. What is the use of these women?' and spends his time with whatever sensual pleasures are available. 'They do not wish to listen' means having no desire to hear, a lack of faith. 'They do not lend an ear' means not applying the sense of hearing (sotapasāda) to listen to the spoken word. Other things to be known should be understood in another way. 'Velāma' is so named because he was endowed with noble qualities that surpassed the boundaries (vela) of birth, lineage, appearance, wealth, faith, and wisdom.
268:
Upon seeing women, he thought, "They must be ogresses; they want to eat me. What benefit is there in them?" and thus spent his time as comfortably as possible. "Na sussūsanti" means they do not wish to listen, meaning they do not believe. "Na sotaṃ odahanti" means they do not lend the ear-sensitivity (do not pay attention) to listen to the spoken words. The words "sakkaccaṃ" and so on should be understood as the opposite of what was just said.

## Velāma

Velāma is so named because he was endowed with lofty qualities that surpassed the boundaries (velā) of birth, lineage, appearance, wealth, faith, wisdom, and so on. He gave such a great gift (mahādāna). Here is the sequential account—In the past, he took conception in the house of the chaplain (purohita) in the city of Bārāṇasī and was named Velāma Kumāra. At the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā with the prince of Bārāṇasī to study the arts. Both of them began learning the arts from a world-renowned teacher (disāpāmokkha). Just like them, eighty-four thousand other princes in Jambudīpa were also learning the arts. The Bodhisatta became an assistant teacher in the subjects he had already mastered and taught the eighty-four thousand princes. He himself mastered in three years the arts that usually took sixteen years to learn. The teacher, knowing that "Young Velāma is proficient in the arts," said, "Dear sons, Velāma knows everything I know. All of you, in harmony, learn the arts from him," and handed over the eighty-four thousand princes to the Bodhisatta.

The Bodhisatta paid homage to the teacher and departed, surrounded by the eighty-four thousand princes. Reaching a nearby city, he taught the prince who was the lord of that city, and once he became proficient, he left him there. In this manner, he went to eighty-four thousand cities, made the eighty-four thousand princes proficient in the arts, left each of them in their respective cities, and returned to Bārāṇasī with the prince of Bārāṇasī. The people consecrated the prince, who was fully trained in the arts, as king and gave Velāma the position of chaplain. Those eighty-four thousand princes also attained kingship in their respective countries and came annually to pay homage to the King of Bārāṇasī. After seeing the King of Bārāṇasī, those kings would go to Velāma and say, "Teacher, we are established in kingship; please tell us whatever you need," and then depart. When those kings traveled, they seized carts, palanquins, cows, bulls, chickens, pigs, and so on, causing the countryside (janapada) to be greatly oppressed and weary. The people gathered and lamented in the palace courtyard. The King summoned Velāma and said, "Teacher, the countryside is being oppressed. The kings cause great destruction when they travel, and the people cannot live. Please do something to end this oppression." Velāma replied, "Very well, Great King, I shall do so. Your Majesty, divide and take as much of the countryside as you desire." He then arranged the territories of the eighty-four thousand kings, placing the territory of the King of Bārāṇasī in the center, like the hub of a wheel. From then on, those kings traveled only by their own routes, and thus they no longer plundered, destroyed, or oppressed the territory of the King of Bārāṇasī. The country-folk lived happily, free from noise and lamentation.
269:
During their travels to and fro, they would seize carts, palanquins, cows, bulls, chickens, pigs, and so on, causing the countryside (janapada) to be greatly oppressed and exhausted. The people gathered and lamented in the royal courtyard.

The King summoned the brahmin Velāma and said, "Teacher, the countryside is being oppressed. When the kings travel, they cause great destruction, and the people cannot endure it. Please find a way to appease this oppression of the countryside." He replied, "Very well, Great King, I shall find a way. However much of the countryside Your Majesty desires, please demarcate and take it." The King did as suggested. The brahmin Velāma arranged the territories of the eighty-four thousand kings, placing the King of Bārāṇasī's territory in the center, like the hub of a wheel with spokes.

From then on, whether those kings were coming or going, they traveled only by their own routes. Thinking, "This is our own territory," they did not plunder. Out of respect for the King, they also did not oppress the King of Bārāṇasī's territory. The country-folk lived in peace, silent and free from lamentation. All the kings were delighted and invited him, saying, "Teacher, whatever you desire, please tell us."

The brahmin Velāma, having bathed his head, opened the doors of the chambers filled with the seven kinds of jewels within his house. Looking at the wealth accumulated through seven generations and considering the income and expenditure, he thought, "It is fitting for me to give an alms-giving that will stir the whole of Jambudīpa." He then informed the King. He had rows of hearths twelve leagues long constructed on the banks of the Ganges and established large granaries in various places to store ghee, honey, molasses, oil, sesame, rice, and so forth. He instructed the people, "In each place, let this many people make arrangements. Whatever things are to be obtained by people are available; if even one thing is lacking, inform me." He then had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing, "From such-and-such a day, come and partake of the brahmin Velāma's alms." When those engaged in the alms-giving reported, "The alms-hall is completed," he put on a garment worth a thousand pieces and placed another worth five hundred pieces over one shoulder. Adorned with all ornaments, he filled a golden pitcher with water as clear as crystal to test the alms-giving. He made an act of truth (saccakiriya): "If there are worthy recipients (dakkhiṇeyya) in this world fit to receive this gift, may this water flow out and touch the earth. If there are none, let it remain as it is." He then turned the pitcher upside down. The water remained as if held by a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa). The Bodhisatta, without becoming disheartened, thought, "Alas, Jambudīpa is indeed empty! There is not even a single person fit to receive the gift." He thought, "If..."
270:
He thought, 'If this gift is to be purified through the power of the donor, may the water flow out and take hold of the earth.' Water, resembling the color of crystal, flowed out and took hold of the earth. Thinking, 'Now I shall give the gift,' he went to the alms-hall, inspected the offerings, and at the time for gruel, he had gruel given; at the time for snacks, snacks; and at the time for meals, meals. In this manner, the gift was given day after day.

In that alms-hall, it was so complete that there was no occasion to say, 'Such a thing exists, such a thing does not exist.' Thinking, 'Now this gift is not yet finished with only this much,' he had red gold brought out and made into golden bowls. Then, for the sake of the eighty-four thousand golden bowls and other items, he sent word to eighty-four thousand kings. The kings, saying, 'It has been a long time indeed since we were favored by our teacher,' provided everything and sent it. While the gift was being given, seven years and seven months passed. Thereafter, the Brahmin thought, 'I shall give the gift by distributing gold, silver, and jewels,' and he had the gift prepared in a vast area. After preparing it, he gave, starting from the eighty-four thousand golden bowls and beginning from the periphery.

In that gift, 'rūpiyapūrāni' means bowls filled with silver plates, silver coins, and silver pieces. Those bowls should not be considered small; they were so large that only four bowls could be placed in an area of land about one karīsa in size. The height of the bowl was nine cubits, and from the rim, it was eight cubits. A chariot drawn by six thoroughbred horses could circle around the rim of the bowl. When giving, he placed the recipients in groups around the outer edge of the bowl, and first gave the gift-objects placed inside the bowl, and later, separating them from the joints, he gave the bowl itself. In this way, he gave eighty-four thousand golden bowls. The same method applies to the silver bowls and others. Here also, 'suvaṇṇapūrāni' means bowls filled with golden plates, golden coins, and golden pieces. 'Hiraññapūrāni' means bowls filled with the seven kinds of gems. 'Sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni' means golden ornaments. 'Kaṃsūpadhāraṇāni' means silver milk-pails. The horns of those cows were covered with golden sheaths. Noble flower garlands were adorned on their necks. Anklets were placed on their four feet, noble silk cloths were draped over their backs, and golden bells were tied to their necks. In the phrase 'vatthakoṭisahassāni,' according to worldly usage, twenty pairs of garments are called one roll.
271:
A 'koṭi' (in this context) is said to mean ten garments. In the phrase 'khomasukhumānaṃ' and so on, whatever was fine among the linen from the Khoma country and other fabrics, that alone he gave. Even those things regarded as 'non-gifts,' such as the gift of women, the gift of bulls, the gift of intoxicants, and the gift of entertainment, he gave as an accompaniment to cut off the path of speech that 'such a thing does not exist in Velāma’s gift-offering.' The alms-water flowed like rivers.

The Teacher, having spoken of Velāma’s gift, said: 'Householder, no one else gave that great gift; I myself gave it. Yet, even while giving such a gift, I did not find a person worthy of receiving it. Why do you, while giving a gift when a Buddha like me is seen in the world, think [it is small]?' Thus, wishing to expand the discourse to the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, He said, 'It might be, however, [Ananda]...' and so on. Indeed, have not the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that existed when he was Velāma ceased? Why then did He say, 'I was Velāma the Brahmin at that time'? He said so because the continuity of the aggregates is uninterrupted. Although those forms and so on cease, they cease having given the condition for the present aggregates. Taking the uninterrupted continuity from one stage to another, He spoke thus. 'No one could purify that gift' means there was no ascetic, brahmin, deva, or Mara who could rise and be said to purify that offering. The person who could purify that offering would be, at the upper limit, a Buddha, and at the lower limit, a disciple like the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta.

'Diṭṭhisampanna' means a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer) who is endowed with vision. 'This gift is more fruitful than that' means this gift given to a Sotāpanna is more fruitful than the gift given by the worldly multitude who sacrificed such gold and silver for seven years and seven months.

In the phrase 'than a hundred Sotāpannas,' one should understand the number of Sotāpannas by making it one hundred and one through the power of one Sakadāgāmi (Once-returner). By this method, in all instances, one should understand the number of persons by making it a hundredfold more than the person mentioned immediately below.

In the phrase 'headed by the Buddha,' the Saṅgha sitting with the Fully Enlightened Buddha as the presiding Elder of the Saṅgha is to be understood as 'the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.' In the phrase 'dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters,' a monastery dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters is a place where a stupa is established, where the Dhamma is heard, and where monks coming from the four directions and the intermediate directions can, without even asking permission, wash their feet, open the door with a key, and stay or move about comfortably. Even if that monastery is a leaf-hut only four cubits in size, it is still called 'a monastery dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.'
272:
(The monks) having maintained and lived there, depart at their convenience. Even if that dwelling is at minimum a leaf-roofed hut of four cubits, it is simply called a monastery built dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.

In the phrase "saraṇaṃ gaccheyya" (should go for refuge), the irreversible going for refuge attained through the Path is intended. Other teachers, however, say that the undertaking of the going for refuge is superior and more fruitful than that (the gift of a monastery) because it is given by dedicating oneself. "Sikkhāpadāni samādiyeyya" means one should undertake the five precepts. Regarding virtue (sīla), only the irreversible virtue attained through the Path is spoken of. Other teachers, however, say that virtue is superior and more fruitful than that (the going for refuge) because it is the giving of freedom from fear to all beings.

"Gandhohanamatta" means the duration of a whiff of fragrance, or the duration of smelling a lump of perfume held with two fingers. Other teachers, however, stating the Pali as "gaddohanamatta," say the meaning is the duration of milking a cow once. "Mettacitta" is a mind pervaded with the welfare of all beings. That mind of loving-kindness should be understood only by way of absorption (appanā). "Aniccasañña" (perception of impermanence) refers to powerful insight (vipassanā) that has reached its peak as the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) for the Path.

By way of illustration, these meritorious deeds such as giving should be understood thus: If one were to make the island of Jambudīpa as level as the surface of a drum and, starting from the edge, arrange seats and invite noble persons (ariyas) to sit there. Among those seated, there might be 10 rows of Stream-enterers, 5 rows of Once-returners, 2 and a half rows of Non-returners, 1 and a half rows of Arahants, and 1 row of Paccekabuddhas. The Perfectly Enlightened Buddha would be alone. A gift given to the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is far superior and more fruitful than a gift given to all these many persons.

As for other gifts:
The gift of a monastery, paying respect,
The precepts, and the development of loving-kindness,
Are not worth even a sixteenth part
Of one who contemplates (impermanence).

Therefore, the Blessed One, at the time of his Parinibbāna, said: "Practice in accordance with the Dhamma is the highest worship." The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all places.

## The Second Chapter: The Lion's Roar (Sīhanāda-vagga).
273:
## 3. The Chapter on the Abodes of Beings (Satta-āvāsa-vagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Tiṭṭhāna Sutta
In the first sutta of the third chapter, the Satta-āvāsa-vagga, "Uttarakurukā" refers to the inhabitants of Uttarakuru. "Adhiggaṇhanti" means they surpass, excel, are superior, or are the foremost. "Amamā" means those who have no craving for perceptions, clothing, homes, or possessions. In the Commentary, however, it is said they are "niddukkhā" (free from suffering). "Apariggahā" means those free from the acquisition of "this is mine." "Niyatāyukā" means the lifespan of those in Uttarakuru is fixed at exactly one thousand years; their destination (gati) is also fixed, for after passing away from there, they are reborn only in the heavenly realms. "Satimanto" (possessing mindfulness) is said because, for the deities, mindfulness is not firm due to their absolute happiness; nor is it firm for the hell-beings due to their absolute suffering. For these inhabitants of Jambudīpa, however, mindfulness is firm because of the mixture of happiness and suffering. "Idha brahmacariyavāso" (here is the living of the holy life) means that because Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas arise in Jambudīpa, the living of the holy life of the Eightfold Path also occurs only here.

## 2. Commentary on the Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta
In the second sutta, "javasampanno" means endowed with speed of foot. "Na vaṇṇasampanno" means not endowed with beauty of body. Among "stallion-like men" (purisakhaḷuṅka), "javasampanno" means endowed with speed of wisdom. "Na vaṇṇasampanno" means not endowed with the beauty of virtue. The rest should be understood according to the method of the Pali text. Whatever should be said here has already been stated in the commentary on the Tika Nipāta.

## 3. Commentary on the Taṇhāmūlaka Sutta
In the third sutta, regarding the phrase "taṇhaṃ paṭicca" (dependent on craving), there are two kinds of craving: "esana-taṇhā" (craving for seeking) and "esita-taṇhā" (craving for what has been sought). The craving by which one seeks and searches for wealth by traveling on goat-paths, spike-paths, etc., is called "esana-taṇhā." The craving for those riches once they have been sought and obtained is called "esita-taṇhā." In this context, "esana-taṇhā" should be understood. "Pariyesanā" means the search for sense objects such as forms. That search occurs when there is "esana-taṇhā." "Lābho" means the acquisition of sense objects such as forms. That acquisition occurs when there is a search.

The decision (vinicchaya) is fourfold by way of wisdom, craving, views, and thought. Among those four, "One should know the decision of happiness; having known the decision of happiness, one should pursue internal happiness" (M. Ni. 3.323)—this...
274:
Decision by knowledge (ñāṇa-vinicchaya). As stated in the Mahāniddesa, "Decisions are of two kinds: decision through craving (taṇhā-vinicchaya) and decision through views (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya)"; the one hundred and eight modes of craving-conduct (taṇhā-vicarita) are called craving-decision. The sixty-two types of views are called view-decision. However, in this sutta, as it is said, "Sakka, Lord of Devas, desire (chanda) has thought (vitakka) as its source," the term 'decision' (vinicchaya) mentioned here refers specifically to thought (vitakka). Indeed, when people obtain gain, they decide through thought alone whether it is desirable or undesirable, good or bad. They decide: "This much of my wealth will be for the sake of visual objects, this much for the sake of sounds, this much will be for me, this much for others, this much I will use, and this much I will store." Therefore, it is said, "Dependent on gain, decision (vinicchaya) arises."

Regarding 'desire and lust' (chanda-rāga): weak lust and strong lust arise toward an object that has been thought about with such unwholesome thoughts. In this sutta, 'desire' (chanda) is a designation for weak lust. 'Clinging' (ajjhosāna) is the strong determination and attachment as "I" and "mine." 'Possession' (pariggaha) is the act of taking possession through the power of craving and views. 'Stinginess' (macchariya) is the inability to endure sharing with others. For this reason, ancient teachers gave the etymological definition of macchariya as: "Because it occurs as 'May this wonderful thing be mine alone, let it not be a wonder for another,' it is called macchariya."

'Guarding' (ārakkha) is protecting well by means of closing doors, securing boxes, and so forth. Because it acts excessively, it is called 'adhikaraṇa' (cause/reason); this is a name for the cause. 'Ārakkhādhikaraṇa' is a word in the neuter form (bhāvana-pumsaka), meaning "because of the cause of guarding" (ārakkhā-hetu). In the phrase 'taking up a stick' (daṇḍādāna) and so forth, taking up a stick or staff to ward off others is called daṇḍādāna. Taking up a weapon such as a one-edged blade is called 'taking up a weapon' (satthādāna). 'Quarrel' (kalaha) refers to both physical and verbal quarreling. The initial strife is called 'viggaha', and the subsequent dispute is called 'vivāda'. 'Tuvaṃtuvaṃ' (thouing) is saying "you, you" in a disrespectful manner.

## 4. Sattāvāsa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the fourth sutta, 'sattāvāsa' means the dwelling places or abodes of beings. Among those nine abodes of beings, the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) are also indeed abodes of beings, but they are not included here because they do not exist at all times. Indeed, the Pure Abodes are like the encampments of the Buddhas; during the incalculable aeons (asaṅkheyya-kappa) when no Buddhas arise, those places remain empty. Thus, they are not included because they do not exist at all times. The rest of the content here should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Stations of Consciousness (viññāṇatthiti).

## 5. Paññā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the fifth sutta, "yato" means at which time. "Suparicitaṃ hoti" means it is well accumulated and well developed. "Kallaṃ vacanāya" means fit for speaking. "Vītarāgaṃ" means free from lust. "Asarāgadhammaṃ" means not having the nature of attachment. "Anāvattidhammaṃ" means not having the nature of returning, not liable to be reborn; it means having the nature of ceasing specifically because of the state of non-rebirth. In this sutta, only the Arahant (khīṇāsava) is spoken of.

## 6. Silāyūpa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, "Candikāputta" refers to the Elder who was the son of Candikā, known by his mother's name. "Cetasa citaṃ hoti" means the mental continuum is accumulated and developed through cycles of thought-processes. "Cetasa cittaṃ suparicitaṃ" means it is well accumulated and well developed successively through cycles of thought-processes. "Neva-ssa cittaṃ pariyādiyanti" means those sense objects are unable to take hold of and exhaust the Arahant's thought-arising. "Amissīkataṃ" means not mixed with those objects because there is no attachment to them. "Āneñjappattaṃ" means having reached the state of imperturbability or motionlessness.

"Silāyūpa" means a stone pillar. "Soḷasakkukkuko" means sixteen cubits in length. "Heṭṭhānemangamā" means reaching the bottom of the pit (established at the base). "Upari nemassa" means standing above the pit. "Sunikhātattā" means being well planted by repeatedly pounding and ramming with pestles (musala). In the phrase "evameva kho," the Arahant should be understood as being like the stone pillar, and the defilements arising at the six doors should be understood as being like great winds. Just as winds coming from the four directions are unable to move the stone pillar, it should be understood that the defilements arising at the six doors are unable to move the mind of the Arahant. In this sutta as well, only the Arahant is spoken of.

27-28. In the commentary on the seventh sutta, "bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati" means obtaining the fear of mental alarm and the enmity of persons. "Cetasikaṃ" means dependent on the mind (arising in the mind). "Dukkha" is the suffering that has the physical sensitivity (kāya-pasāda) as its basis.

Domanassa (mental distress) is suffering (dukkha) associated with aversion (dosa). In this sutta, the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is taught. The eighth sutta was taught to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; however, it is said that in this sutta, only the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is spoken of.

## 9. Āghātavatthusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'grounds for resentment' (āghātavatthu) means the causes of resentment. 'Āghātaṃ bandhati' means one binds or gives rise to anger.

## 10-11. Āghātapaṭivinayasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
30-31. In the tenth sutta, 'removal of resentment' (āghātapaṭivinaya) means the causes for removing resentment. 'Taṃ kutettha labbhā' means: 'How can it be obtained in this person?' or 'By what reason can it be obtained?' thinking, 'May that harmful conduct not happen.' One removes resentment by reflecting, 'Another person, according to their own or another's mental inclination, performs what is harmful.' Alternatively, it means: 'If I were to become angry, how could that anger be obtained in this person? By what reason should it be obtained?' There is also a variant reading 'kuto lābhā'. It means: 'If I were to become angry with this person, what benefits would there be for me in that anger? What would those benefits be?' In this context, the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle (nipāta). In the eleventh sutta, 'successive cessation' (anupubbanirodha) means cessation in successive order. The remaining words in all places have meanings that are quite clear.

## 1-2. Anupubbavihārasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
32-33. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'successive abidings' (anupubbavihāra) means the abidings (states of dwelling) to be attained in successive order. In the first jhāna, sensual pleasures cease. 'Te ca' means those persons who attain the first jhāna; they are said to dwell having repeatedly caused sensual pleasures to cease. 'Pañjaliko' means having raised the hands in salutation (añjali). 'Payirupāseyya' means one should attend upon or serve. In this way, the meaning in all sentences should be understood.

## 3. Nibbānasukhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'Udāyī' refers to the Elder Lāḷudāyī. 'Etadeva khvettha' is just the phrase 'Etadeva kho ettha'. 'Kāmasahagatā' means associated with sensual pleasures. 'Samudācaranti' means they frequent the mind-door. 'Ābādhāya' is due to the sense of affliction or oppression. 'Pariyāyena' means by way of a reason. Thus, the meaning in all sections should be understood. In this sutta, what is called 'happiness not felt' (avedayitasukha) is taught.

## 4. Gāvīupamāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'pabbateyyā' refers to a cow that frequents the mountains. 'Na suppatiṭṭhitaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā' means without having made it well-established. 'Taṃ nimittaṃ' refers to that sign known as the first jhāna. 'Na svādhiṭṭhitaṃ adhiṭṭhāti' means one does not well-resolve or well-establish. 'Anabhihiṃsamāno' means without striking or harming. 'Mudu cittaṃ hoti kammaññaṃ' means just as the insight mind is supple and wieldy at the moment of the supramundane path, so too the fourth jhāna mind, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), is supple and wieldy for that yogi. 'Appamāṇo thamādhi' (immeasurable concentration) refers to concentration associated with the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra) as well as concentration associated with the paths and fruits. In this context, however, concentration that is well-practiced by way of 'having an immeasurable object' should be understood as immeasurable concentration. In this place, 'so appamāṇena samādhinā subhāvitena', this bhikkhu, having developed insight, reaches the fruit of Arahantship. Now, wishing to show the sequence of direct knowledges of an Arahant, he spoke the words beginning with 'yassa yassa ca'.

## 5. Jhānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khayaṃ) refers to the fruit of Arahantship. 'Yadeva tattha hoti rūpagataṃ' refers to the form (rūpa) that arises at the moment of the first jhāna, either by way of the physical base (vatthu) or by way of mind-produced matter, etc. 'Vedanāgatā' and so forth should be understood by way of the associated feeling and so forth.
278:
They should be known. "Te dhamme" refers to those five aggregates of phenomena, such as form and so on. In the terms beginning with "aniccato," they should be known as: impermanent (aniccato) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be; suffering (dukkhato) in the sense of oppression; a disease (rogato) in the sense of aching; a boil (gaṇḍato) because of internal corruption; a dart (sallato) because of entering and piercing sequentially; a calamity (aghato) because of being painful; an affliction (ābādhato) because of being oppressive; alien (parato) because of not being one's own; disintegrating (palokato) because of destruction; empty (suññato) because of the absence of an owner; and non-self (anattato) because of not following one's will. "Samanupassati" means seeing with strong insight-wisdom.

"Tehi dhammehi" means withdrawing the mind from those five aggregates. "Paṭivāpeti" means turning away from them by means of Nibbāna. "Amatāya dhātuyā" refers to the element of Nibbāna. "Cittaṃ upasaṃharati" means making the mind enter after seeing the benefits through wisdom. "Santaṃ" means peaceful due to the calming of opposing states. "Paṇītaṃ" means sublime because of the absence of distress. "Staying there, he reaches the destruction of the taints" means that while staying in that first jhāna, he develops that strong insight and reaches the fruit of Arahantship.

Another method: "So tehi dhammehi"—among the terms beginning with "aniccato," the mark of impermanence is shown by the two terms "aniccato" and "palokato." The mark of suffering is shown by the six terms beginning with "dukkhato." The mark of non-self is shown by the three terms "parato," "suññato," and "anattato." Therefore, having attributed the three marks in this way, he withdraws, releases, and removes the mind from the five aggregates within the attainment that he has seen. "Upasaṃharati" means that he first directs the insight-mind towards the unconditioned deathless element, thinking "Nibbāna is peaceful," through hearing, praise, scripture, and designation. The path-mind does not verbally say "This Nibbāna is peaceful, this Nibbāna is sublime" merely by the power of taking Nibbāna as an object. However, it means that by penetrating Nibbāna in this manner, he directs the mind towards it.

"So tattha ṭhito" means staying in that insight which takes the three marks as its object. "Reaches the destruction of the taints" means reaching the fruit of Arahantship by developing the four paths in succession. "Teneva dhammarāgena" means by the desire and lust occurring in the states of serenity and insight. "Dhammanandi" is just a synonym for that lust for the Dhamma. Indeed, one who can completely exhaust desire and lust in serenity and insight reaches Arahantship. One who is unable to do so becomes a Non-returner.
279:
In a straw figure or in a doll made of straw. He is called "dūrepātī" because he makes the arrow fall at a distance. He is called "akkhaṇavedhī" because he shoots without missing. In the phrase "whatever state there is connected to feeling in that attainment," form (rūpa) is not taken. Why? Because it has been transcended. Indeed, this yogi, having previously attained the fine-material jhānas and transcended form, has now attained the formless attainments; thus, form has been transcended by him through the power of serenity. Having previously comprehended form and transcended it, he now comprehends the formless; thus, form has been transcended by him through the power of insight. Furthermore, since form is entirely absent in the formless realm, form is not taken with reference to that formless realm. Moreover, why is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception not taken? Because it is subtle. In that base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the four mental aggregates are so subtle that they are not suitable for comprehension by insight. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Thus, bhikkhus, as far as there is the attainment of perception, so far there is the penetration of final knowledge."

The meaning is this: as far as there is what is called an attainment with mind, for one comprehending gross states, there is the penetration of final knowledge; he reaches Arahantship. But the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not called an "attainment of perception" because it is extremely subtle. "Jhāyīhete" refers to these attainments possessed by meditators who delight in jhāna. "Vuṭṭhahitvā" means having emerged from that attainment. "Samakkhātabbāni" means they are states that should be well-declared, merely spoken of, praised, and extolled as "peaceful and sublime."

## 6. Ānanda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "sambādhe" means in the confinement of the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Okāsādhigamo" means the obtaining of an opening. "Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā" means for the purpose of the purification of beings. "Samatikkamāya" means for the purpose of overcoming. "Atthaṅgamāya" means for the purpose of passing away. "Ñāyassa adhigamāya" means for the purpose of attaining the path that occurs together with insight. "Nibbānဿ sacchikiriyāya" means for the purpose of realizing the unconditioned Nibbāna. "That very eye will exist" means that very sensitive eye will exist without being destroyed. "Te rūpā" means those very form-objects will come into the range of the eye. "He will not experience that base" means he will not know that form-base. In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

"Udāyī" refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. "Saññīmeva nu kho" means "Is it not indeed one who is percipient (with mind)?" The letter "ma" is merely a euphonic conjunction. "Kiṃsaññī" means being percipient of what perception?
280:
Why is this phrase “sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ” (with the complete surpassing of perceptions of form) taken? Does one endowed with the first jhāna, etc., not experience forms and so on? It is not that they do not; they do. However, as long as the kasina-form remains the object, one is not said to have well-surpassed form. Because it is not yet well-surpassed, [Arahantship] wisdom is not able to arise. Only after it is well-surpassed does that perception of form no longer exist; and to show that because of its non-existence, it can no longer serve as a condition, this phrase “sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ” alone is taken.

“Jaṭilavāsikā” means an inhabitant of the city of Jaṭila. In the phrases beginning with “na cābhinato,” it means not inclined through the power of lust, and not disinclined through the power of hatred. One who stands having suppressed and prevented defilements with effort (saṅkhāra) is meant, but since this person arises after having utterly cut off defilements, they are no longer “sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato” (one who has reached restraint through effortful suppression). Because of being liberated from defilements, they are stable. Because of being stable, they have become content. Because of being content, they do not tremble with fear. By the words, “Venerable Ānanda, what is the fruit of this concentration?”, this female elder (therī) asks about the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship, just as if one were holding a palm fruit and asking, “What fruit is this fruit named?” In the phrase “aññāphalo vutto,” “aññā” refers to Arahantship. The meaning is that the Blessed One described this concentration as the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. “Evaṃsaññīpi” means that even though one has such perception of the fruition of Arahantship, one does not experience that base (āyatana). Thus, in this sutta, the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship is discussed.

## ၇။ လောကာယတိကသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the seventh sutta, “Lokāyatikā” refers to those who recite and speak the Lokāyata texts. “Satataṃ” means at all times; “samitaṃ” means continuously. “Tiṭṭhatetaṃ” means “let this matter stand (stop here)”; do not speak this; what benefit is there for you in this? “Brahmins, I will teach you the Dhamma” means I will teach you the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

“Daḷhadhammo” refers to one who stands holding a firm bow. “Dhanuggaho” is an archer. A “daḷhadhanu” (strong bow) refers to a bow with the strength of two thousand men. A bow of two thousand-man strength refers to a type of bow where, when weights such as bronze or lead are hung on the bow-frame and it is drawn to the full length of an arrow, the bowstring is lifted off the ground. “Sikkhito” means one who has studied the art under a teacher for ten or twelve years. “Katahattho” means that while some may only learn the art without practical skill, this person is practically skilled and has attained mastery through practice. “Katūpāsano” means one who has already demonstrated their skill in royal courts and such. “Lahukena အသနေန” means with a very light arrow that has been made hollow inside and filled with cotton or similar materials, prepared for target practice. If made this way, one who can shoot the distance of one usabha can reach...
281:
...one who can shoot the distance of eight usabhas can shoot as far as sixteen usabhas. This refers to one who holds a bow that has been strung and drawn to the length of an arrow, lifted from the ground, with the strength of two thousand men. “Sikkhito” means one who has learned the art in a teacher’s family for ten or twelve years. “Katahattho” means one who does not merely learn the art but is dexterous, having attained mastery through practice. “Katūpāsano” means one who has demonstrated the art in royal courts and so on. “Lahukena asanena” means with a very light arrow, made hollow inside and filled with cotton, etc., and prepared for target practice. If so prepared, one who shoots one usabha can reach two usabhas... one who shoots eight usabhas can reach sixteen usabhas. “Appakasirena” means without any pain or difficulty. “Atipāteyya” means he would surpass or overtake. The meaning is this: just as that archer can quickly surpass a shadow that is a span and four finger-breadths long, so too, one endowed with such speed is capable of very quickly traversing the entire universe. “Sandhāvanikāya” means running by foot. “Evamāhaṃsu” means they spoke thus.

## ၈။ ဒေဝါသုရသင်္ဂါမသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the eighth sutta, “samupabyūဠှော အဟောသိ” means it was arrayed (the battle was imminent). “Saṅgāmeyyāma” means let us do battle, let us fight. “Apayiṃsuyeva” means they simply fled. “Uttarenābhimukhā” means facing the north. “Abhiyante vā” means continuously pursuing and attacking. “Bhīruttānagatena” means having reached a place of refuge that wards off fear. “Akaraṇīyā” means nothing at all should be done by means of fighting.

Why did the battle between those Devas and Asuras occur? The Asuras were formerly inhabitants of Tāvatiṃsa. When the Cittapāṭali trees bloom, they remember the divine Parichattaka flowers in the celestial realm. Then, arising in anger, they say, “Seize the Devas!” and climb Mount Sineru from various directions. The Devas also come out. The battle between those Devas and Asuras is like cowherd boys hitting each other with sticks. Sakka, the king of Devas, placed guards in five places below, and surrounding the celestial city above, he had statues of himself made, holding the vajra weapon. Although the Asuras climbed up, bypassing the five guard posts below, when they saw the statues of Indra, they were frightened and returned to the city of Asuras.

“Dakkhiṇenābhimukhā” means facing the south. “Apadaṃ vadhitvā” means destroying without any remainder. “Adassanaṃ gato” means Māra also, having made the basis of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), cannot know the mind of a person who has attained the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and thus that very rūpāvacara jhāna [is used as a basis for] insight (vipassanā)...
282:
Māra knows the mind of a person who has attained the fourth fine-material sphere absorption (rūpāvacara catutthajjhāna); he also knows the mind of a person who has attained that same fourth fine-material sphere absorption by making it the basis for insight (vipassanā). However, whether the formless attainment (arūpāvacara samāpatti) is the basis for the round of rebirth or the basis for insight, Māra cannot know the mind of the person who has attained that formless attainment. Therefore, it is said: "He has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One."

## 9. Nāgasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth, the Nāga Sutta: 'Āraññakassa' means for one who habitually dwells in the forest. 'Gocara-pasutassa' means for one who goes for the purpose of taking food (grazing). 'Hatthi-kalabhā' are very large bull elephants. 'Hatthi-chāpā' are very young elephant calves. 'Obhagga-obhaggaṃ' refers to places where branches have been repeatedly bent down. 'Ogāhaṃ otiṇṇassa' means for one who has descended into a watering place, which is called 'ogāha' because it is a place to be entered. 'Ogāhaā uttiṇṇassa' means for one who has emerged from the watering place. 'Vūpakaṭṭho' means being secluded (withdrawn). Now, although the Buddha has no need for bull elephants, this matter is brought forward to show a person in the Dispensation (sāsana) who is similar to that bull elephant; therefore, wishing to show that person, he said the words beginning with 'Evameva kho' (Even so).

## 10. Tapussasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the tenth, the Tapussa Sutta: 'Mallesu' means in the Malla country. Regarding the words "Ānanda, you stay here for a while," the Blessed One said this knowing, "The householder Tapussa will have a conversation with Ānanda who is staying here; based on that conversation, I will preach a great discourse on the Dhamma (dhamma-pariyāya)." 'Upasaṅkami' means that the householder Tapussa, after having his breakfast, set out thinking, "I will go to wait upon the Buddha," and seeing the Elder from afar, he approached the Venerable Ānanda. "This renunciation (nekkhamma), known as the going forth (pabbajjā), appears to us like a great precipice" means that leaving the world of people appears to us as if descending into a great abyss. 'Nekkhamme cittaṃ pakkhandati' means the mind rushes into the state of monkhood by way of its object; it becomes clear and confident by taking that state of monkhood as its object; it stands firm in that state of monkhood and is liberated from opposing states. "For the monks who see 'This renunciation is peaceful'" means for those monks who see renunciation as peaceful, free from distress and fever. 'Bahunā janena visabhāgo' means this state of monkhood is different from, or unlike, the majority of people.

'Kathā-pābhataṃ' is the source (reason) of the conversation. "Ānanda, even for me who was thinking thus, my mind did not enter into renunciation" means that even while thinking in that way, my mind did not enter into the state of monkhood.
283:
"For one who sees 'This renunciation is peaceful'" means for one who sees "This renunciation is peaceful" by way of reflecting "Renunciation is good." 'Anāsevito' means not practiced, not touched, not realized. 'Adhigamma' means having reached, having attained, having realized. 'Tamāseveyyaṃ' means one should practice, one should associate with that benefit of monkhood. 'Yaṃ me' means for which reason to me. 'Adhigammā' means for one who has reached. "To me who was such, there was oppression" means the arising of perceptions and mental applications associated with sensuality is called oppression for me because of its nature of being oppressive. 'The mind without thought does not rush in' means the mind does not rush into the second absorption (dutiyajjhāna), which is without thought and examination (vitakka-vicāra), by way of its object. 'In thoughts' means in thought and examination (vitakka-vicāra). The remaining words in all places have clear meanings.

## 5. Sāmaññavagga

## 1. Sambhādhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, 'Udāyī' refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī. 'Avidvā' means one who does not know individually. 'Bhūrimedhaso' means one with great wisdom. 'He who has understood the absorption' means he who has known the absorption. 'The bull-like one who dwells in seclusion' means one who is secluded by way of being alone and is called 'bull-like' (nisabha) because of his excellence. 'Muni' refers to the Buddha-muni (the Sage). 'By a figure of speech' (pariyāyena) means by one reason. The first absorption is called the 'attainment of an opening' (okāsādhigama) merely by the absence of the confinement of sensual pleasures; it is not an opening in every way and in its entirety. "In that first absorption, there is still confinement" means in that first absorption, there is indeed the oppression of confinement. There is also a variant reading 'Tatrāpitthi'. "What is the confinement in that absorption?" means what is called oppression in that absorption. "This is the confinement here" means the state where thought and examination (vitakka-vicāra) have not yet ceased is called confinement (sampīḷā). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sections. 'Directly' (nippariyāyena) means not just by one reason; rather, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya) is called the 'attainment of an opening' in every way because all confinements have been abandoned.

## 2. Kāyasakkhisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, the phrase "in whatever way that base is" means by whatever cause and in whatever manner that base, known as the first jhāna, exists. "He dwells having touched it with the body" means that by those causes and in those manners, he dwells having touched that attainment with the co-nascent mental body (nāmakāya); the meaning is that he enters into the attainment. "The Blessed One called him a body-witness (kāyasakkhī) in a figurative sense (pariyāyena)" means that because he has realized the first jhāna with that mental body, he is therefore called a body-witness in this figurative sense. "In a non-figurative sense (nippariyāyena)" means that because he has completed everything that is to be realized with the mental body, this person is called a body-witness in an absolute sense.

## 3. Paññāvimuttasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "he understands it with wisdom" means he understands that first jhāna with the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā). In this sutta also, the figurative and non-figurative senses should be understood in the same way as the previous method. As in this sutta, so should it be understood in the suttas following this.

## 4. Ubhatobhāgavimuttasutta-vaṇṇanā

The fourth sutta should be understood by both ways. Herein, "both-ways-liberated" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) refers to one who is liberated from the defilements opposing serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) through both parts. Ultimately, however, one who is liberated from the material body (rūpakāya) by means of attainment and from the mental body (nāmakāya) by means of the noble path (ariyamagga) should be understood as both-ways-liberated.

## 5-10. Sandiṭṭhikadhammasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā

46-51. In the fifth sutta and others, "visible" (sandiṭṭhika) means that which is to be seen by oneself. "Nibbāna" refers to the extinguishing of defilements. "Nibbāna in the present life" (diṭṭhadhammanibbāna) means extinguishing in this very existence. The remaining terms in all places have clear meanings.
