## 1. Commentary on the Kimatthiya Sutta

In the first sutta of the Book of the Tens, "wholesome virtues" (kusalāni sīlāni) refers to faultless virtues. They are called "having non-remorse as their purpose" (avippaṭisāratthāni) because they lead to the benefit of the state of non-remorse (avippaṭisāra). Since that non-remorse is the benefit of those virtues, they are called "having non-remorse as their benefit" (avippaṭisārānisaṃsāni). In the phrases beginning with "for the purpose of knowledge and vision of things as they are" (yathābhūtañāṇadassanattha), "knowledge and vision of things as they are" refers to tender insight (taruṇavipassanā). "Disenchantment" (nibbidā) refers to strong insight (balavavipassanā). "Dispassion" (virāga) refers to the path (magga). "Liberation" (vimutti) refers to the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala). "Knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). "They proceed to the peak" (aggāya parenti) means they go (occur) for the sake of the fruit of arahantship.

## 2. Commentary on the Cetanākaraṇīya Sutta

In the second sutta, "not to be done by volition" (na cetanāya karaṇီyaṃ) means it is not something to be done by inciting, planning, or detailed thinking. "This is the nature of things" (dhammatā esā) means this is the nature of the Dhamma, the fixed law of causes. "They flow forth" (abhisandenti) means they proceed. "They fulfill" (paripūrenti) means they make complete. "For going from the near shore to the far shore" (apārā pāraṃ gamanāya) means for the purpose of going from the cycle of the three realms, which is like the near shore, to the far shore of Nibbāna.

## 3-5. Commentary on the Three Upanisa Suttas

3-5. In the third sutta, "one whose proximate cause is destroyed" (hatūpaniso) means one who has a ruined cause. In the fourth and fifth suttas, the only distinction is the fact that they were spoken by the two elders (Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Ānanda).

## 6. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "he would not be percipient of earth in earth" (neva paṭhaviyaṃ paṭhavīsaññī assa) means that by taking the earth element as an object, he would not be one who has a perception arisen in the manner of "earth." The same method applies to the water element and so on.
288:
The same method applies (to the other elements). "Not in this world" (na idhaloke) means he would not be percipient with the fourth or fifth jhāna perceptions that arise in this world. "Not in the next world" (na paraloke) means he would not be percipient with the fourth or fifth jhāna perceptions that arise in the next world. "Yet he would be percipient" (saññီ ca pana assa) means that for him, that attainment would indeed be an attainment accompanied by thought (savitakka-samāpatti). "This is peaceful, this is sublime" (etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇီtaṃ) means that for one who sits having attained with the thought "peaceful, peaceful," the mental process occurs as "peaceful, peaceful" even for the whole day. For one who sits having attained with the thought "sublime, sublime," the mental process occurs as "sublime, sublime" even for the whole day. "Namely, the stilling of all formations" (yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho) means that for one who sits having attained with the thought "Nibbāna, Nibbāna," the mental process occurs as "Nibbāna, Nibbāna" even for the whole day. All this is stated with reference to the concentration of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti-samādhi).

## 7. Sāriputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "Friend, at that time I was percipient" means "Friend, at that time I was percipient with this perception of the attainment of fruition: 'The cessation of existence is Nibbāna.'" "That attainment of mine was with mind" is a statement regarding reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā).

## 8. Jhānasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "serene in every way" (samantapāsādika) means being serene from all around due to the presence of bodily actions and so on that bring about confidence. "Complete in every aspect" (sabbākāraparipūra) means being full of all causes.

## 9. Santavimokkhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "peaceful" (santā) means peaceful both because of the peacefulness of the object and the peacefulness of the factors. "Liberations" (vimokkhā) are so named because they are liberated from opposing states and because they are well-liberated from doubt regarding the object. "Transcending forms" (atikkamma rūpe) means occurring after having transcended the fine-material jhānas (rūpajjhāna). The remaining terms in all places have very clear meanings.

## 2. Nāthavagga
## 1. Senāsanasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'pañcaṅgasamannāgato' means being endowed with five qualities. Regarding the phrase 'nātidūraṃ hoti nāccāsannaṃ' (it is neither too far nor too near), if a monastery is in a very distant place, a monk returning to that monastery after wandering for alms may experience physical and mental fatigue. Due to such fatigue, he is unable to attain concentration that has not yet arisen, or to stabilize concentration that has already arisen. If it is too near, it tends to be crowded with many people. Living in a place at a distance of about forty usabhas is called a monastery that is free from the two faults of being too far or too near, and is well-suited for coming and going. 'Divāappākiṇṇaṃ' means not being crowded with people during the daytime.

## 2. Pañcaṅgasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'kevalī' means being endowed with all qualities. 'Vusitavā' means one who has the habit of practicing the noble life, which is the Path. 'Asekhena' means (being endowed) with the supramundane Dhamma that is included in the teachings for those beyond training (asekha). 'Sīlakkhandhena' means the aggregate of virtue. In this context of 'vimuttikkhandhena', excluding the three starting with virtue, the remaining fruition states (phala-dhamma) are called 'vimutti' (liberation). 'Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ' refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), and that knowledge is purely mundane.

## 3-4. Saṃyojanasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
13-14. In the third sutta, 'orambhāgiyāni' refers to states that lead to the lower realm of the sense sphere. 'Uddhambhāgiyāni' refers to states that lead to the higher realms of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. In this sutta, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is taught. In the fourth sutta, 'khilavinibandhā' (mental spikes and shackles) has already been explained in detail in the Book of Fives. 'Ārohapariṇāhena' means by the extent of length and breadth.

## 5. Appamādasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'evameva kho' means that just as the Buddha is the most supreme among all beings, so too should heedfulness (appamāda), which causes all wholesome states to be performed, be understood as the most supreme. Here, one might ask: "This heedfulness is only mundane, whereas wholesome states can also be supramundane; this heedfulness belongs only to the sense sphere, whereas wholesome states exist in all four planes; why then is heedfulness said to be the most supreme among those states?" (The answer is:) It is the most supreme because it is the means of attainment (paṭilābhakatthena). Since those wholesome states can only be obtained through heedfulness, heedfulness is superior to those states. That is why it is taught: "All those states have heedfulness as their foundation."

5. In the fifth sutta: Just as the Buddha is supreme among all groups of beings, so too should heedfulness (appamāda), which causes all wholesome states to be performed, be understood as supreme among all wholesome states. If it is objected: "This heedfulness is only mundane while wholesome states are also supramundane, and this heedfulness is only of the sense sphere while wholesome states occur in the four planes, how then is heedfulness supreme over those states?", it is said to be supreme because it is the means of attainment for those states. This is because those states can be obtained through heedfulness; therefore, heedfulness is supreme over those states. For this reason, He taught: "All those states have heedfulness as their foundation."

'Jaṅgalānaṃ' refers to beings that usually walk on the surface of the earth. 'Pāṇānaṃ' refers to beings with feet. 'Padajātāni' means footprints. 'Samodhānaṃ gacchanti' means they come to be included (contained) within. 'Aggamakkhāyati' means it is declared the best. 'Yadidaṃ mahantattena' means it is declared the best because of its greatness (size); it does not mean it is the best in terms of quality. 'Vassikaṃ' refers to the jasmine flower. It is said that after hearing this sutta, King Bhātiya, wishing to test it, decorated a room with four kinds of perfumes, had fragrant flowers brought in, placed a handful of jasmine flowers in the center of a casket, and placed the remaining flowers in bunches around that handful of jasmine. He then closed the door and went outside. After staying outside for a moment, he opened the door and entered; the scent of the jasmine flowers was the first to strike his nose before all other flowers. Right there on the palace floor, facing the Mahācetiya, he prostrated and worshipped the stupa, saying, "The Fully Enlightened One spoke well when He said, 'The jasmine is the best among them.'" 'Khuddarājāno' means minor kings. There is also a variant reading 'kūṭarājāno'.

## 6. Āhuneyyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'gotrabhū' refers to a person endowed with change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), which is insight that has reached its peak and has Nibbāna as its object.

## 7. Paṭhamanāthasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'sanāthā' means "live having protectors" or "having many relatives." They are called 'nāthakaraṇa' because they act as a refuge. It means acting as one's own protector or acting as a foundation. In the terms such as 'kalyāṇamitto', one who has good friends endowed with qualities such as virtue is called a 'kalyāṇamitta'. Those same good friends are called 'kalyāṇasahāya' because they are together in activities such as standing and sitting. One who is inclined toward good friends with both mind and body is called 'kalyāṇasampavaṅka'. 'Suvaco hoti' means being one who is easy to speak to and easy to admonish. 'Khamo' means being patient and not getting angry even when spoken to with harsh, rough, or coarse words. 'Padakkhiṇaggāhီ anusāsaniṃ' means that when being admonished, instead of taking it wrongly, or rebelling, or going away as if not hearing, one listens well, saying, "Venerable sirs, please admonish me; if you do not admonish me, who else will admonish me well?"

"Venerable sirs, please advise me, please instruct me; if you do not advise me, who else will?" Thus he respectfully accepts.

'Uccāvacāni' means large and small matters. 'Kiṃkaraṇīyāni' means tasks to be done, saying, "What shall I do?" Among those matters, large tasks (uccakamma) include sewing and dyeing robes, plastering a stupa, and tasks to be performed in the Uposatha hall, stupa-house, and Bodhi-tree house, etc. Small tasks (avacakamma) include minor duties such as washing feet and applying oil, etc. 'Tatrūpāyāya' means the means of approaching those tasks to complete them. 'Alaṃ kātuṃ' means being capable of doing. 'Alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ' means being capable of arranging.

Because of the desire and affection for the Dhamma, one is called 'dhammakāmo'. It means one loves the Buddha's word, the Tipiṭaka. 'Piyasamudāhāro' means listening respectfully when others speak and desiring to teach others oneself. In the phrase 'abhidhamme abhivinaye', the four—dhamma, abhidhamma, vinaya, and abhivinaya—should be understood. Among these four, 'dhamma' refers to the Suttanta Piṭaka, 'abhidhamma' refers to the seven books of Abhidhamma, 'vinaya' refers to the two-fold Vibhaṅga (ubhatovibhaṅga), and 'abhivinaya' refers to the Khandhakas and Parivāra. Alternatively, both the Suttanta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka are called 'dhamma', while the paths and fruits (magga-phala) are called 'abhidhamma'. The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is called 'vinaya', and the Dhamma that leads to the subsiding of defilements is called 'abhivinaya'. Thus, it means there is great joy in all these: dhamma, abhidhamma, vinaya, and abhivinaya. In the phrase 'kusalesu dhammesu', the locative case is used in the sense of cause. It means being one who has not laid down the burden (anikkhittadhura) for the sake of attaining wholesome states belonging to the four planes.

## 8. Dutiyanāthasuttavaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'therānukampitassa' refers to one who is compassionately assisted by the elders through their advice and instruction, which encourages and spreads benefit.

## 9. Paṭhamaariyāvāsasuttavaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'ariyāvāsa' means the dwelling of the noble ones; the noble ones have lived, are living, and will live there; therefore, they are called 'ariyāvāsa'. 'Yadariyā' means the noble ones' dwelling in those places.

## 10. Dutiyaariyāvāsasuttavaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, the monks of the Kuru country possess deep wisdom and make great effort in the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Therefore, just as the Mahānidāna Sutta and others were taught to them in the Dīgha Nikāya, etc., this sutta, which is deep, subtle, and marked with the three characteristics, was also taught in that same Kuru country. In that sutta, 'pañcaṅgavippahīno' means that an Arahant, being free from the five factors, has lived, is living, and will live. Therefore, this abandoning of the five factors is called 'ariyāvāsa' (dwelling of the noble ones). This method should be understood in all instances. "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with six factors" means being endowed with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). What are the states of six-factored equanimity? They are knowledge (ñāṇa), etc. When "knowledge" is mentioned, four consciousnesses associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta) are obtained from the eight great functional consciousnesses (mahakiriya). When "constant dwelling" (satatavihāra) is mentioned, all eight great functional consciousnesses are obtained. When "no lust or hatred" is mentioned, ten consciousnesses are obtained. Joy (somanassa) is obtained by way of habitual practice. In the phrase "with a mind guarded by mindfulness," mindfulness performs the task of guarding at the three doors at all times for an Arahant. For that reason, it is said that for that Arahant, whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, the vision of knowledge is constantly and continuously present.

'Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ' means of many ascetics and brahmins. Here, 'samaṇa' refers to those who have gone forth, and 'brahmins' refers to those who are accustomed to saying "Bho, bho." 'Puthupacceka-saccāni' means many individual truths. It means many truths individually grasped in this way: "Only this view of mine is true, only this is true." 'Nuṇṇāni' means removed. 'Panuṇṇāni' means well removed. 'Cattāni' means relinquished. 'Vantāni' means vomited out. 'Muttāni' means having the bonds severed. 'Pahīnāni' means abandoned. 'Paṭinissaṭṭhāni' means relinquished so that they do not arise in the mind again. All these words are synonyms expressing the state of having relinquished the views that were grasped.

In the term 'samavayasaṭṭhesano', 'avayā' means not deficient, and 'saṭṭhā' means relinquished. One is called 'samavayasaṭṭhesano' because one has searches (esanā) that are well and non-deficiently relinquished. It means one who has well relinquished all searches. By the words "the mind is liberated from lust," etc., the completion of the task of the Path (magga) is stated. By the words "lust has been abandoned by me," etc., the fruit of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) is stated. The rest of the words have clear meanings in all places.

## 3. Mahāvagga
## 1. Sīhanādasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta, the first sutta of the third vagga, the term 'visamagato' means going to haunts in uneven or rugged places. 'Saṅghātaṃ āpādesiṃ' means causing destruction or harm. Indeed, because that lion king possesses intense majesty, he tends to have compassion for small creatures. Therefore, thinking, 'Let those enemies who cannot stand in opposition, and those weak creatures who wish to flee, let them flee,' he roars the lion's roar and only then sets out for his hunting ground.

'Tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ' means—if a lion is so called because of its endurance (sahanatā) and its ability to destroy (hananatā), the Blessed One also endures all agreeable and disagreeable objects, and he destroys the doctrines of all those with other views by crushing their arguments. 'Idamassa sīhanādasmiṃ' means that the preaching of the Dhamma in this assembly is the very sound of the Blessed One's lion's roar.

'Tathāgatabalāni' refers to the powers that belong uniquely to the Tathāgata, not shared with others. Alternatively, it means the powers that have arisen just as the powers of previous Buddhas arose through the perfection of merit. Among those powers, the Tathāgata's power is twofold: physical power (kāyabala) and knowledge power (ñāṇabala). Among these, physical power should be understood according to the sequence of the ten lineages of elephants. The ancients said: 'There are ten lineages of elephants: Kālāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala, Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta.'

These are the ten lineages of elephants. Among these ten, Kālāvaka should be understood as the common lineage of elephants. The physical strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one Kālāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kālāvaka elephants is equal to the strength of one Gaṅgeyya. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyyas is equal to one Paṇḍara. The strength of ten Paṇḍaras is equal to one Tamba. The strength of ten Tambas is equal to one Piṅgala. The strength of ten Piṅgalas is equal to one Gandha elephant. The strength of ten Gandha elephants is equal to one Maṅgala. The strength of ten Maṅgalas is equal to one Hema. The strength of ten Hemas is equal to one Uposatha. The strength of ten Uposathas is equal to one Chaddanta. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to the physical power of the Blessed One. This power is also called Nārāyana-saṅghāta-bala.
294:
This power of the Buddha is also called the Buddha's power which is like the thunderbolts (vajira) that are the source of Nārāyana's strength. That power of the Buddha, in terms of the number of ordinary elephants, is equal to the strength of a thousand crore elephants. In terms of the number of men, it is equal to the strength of ten thousand crore men. This is first of all the Buddha's physical power (kāyabala).

Intellectual power (ñāṇabala), however, is already mentioned in the Pāḷi text. The Tenfold Power of Knowledge (Dasabala-ñāṇa), the Fourfold Intrepidity (Catu-vesārajja-ñāṇa) mentioned in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Unshakable Knowledge (Akampana-ñāṇa) in the eight assemblies, the Knowledge of Defining the Four Modes of Birth (Catu-yoni-pariccheda-ñāṇa), the Knowledge of Defining the Five Destinations (Pañca-gati-pariccheda-ñāṇa), the seventy-three knowledges and seventy-seven knowledges mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya—thus, these and many other knowledges are called intellectual power. In this context, only intellectual power is intended. Indeed, knowledge is called 'bala' (power) because of its unshakable nature and its nature of providing firm support.

'Āsabhaṃ ဌာနံ' refers to the noble state, the supreme state. Or, previous Buddhas are called 'Āsabha', and their state is 'āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ'. Alternatively, a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called 'usabha'. A bull that is the leader of a thousand cows is called 'vasabha'. Or, a bull that is the leader of a hundred pens is an 'usabha', and a bull that is the leader of a thousand pens is a 'vasabha'. A bull that is nobler than all cows, able to endure all dangers, white, majestic, capable of bearing great loads, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps is called 'nisabha'. In this context, that very 'nisabha' is intended as 'usabha'. This name 'nisabha' is also a synonymous term for that 'usabha'. It is called 'āsabha' because it belongs to the 'usabha'.

'Ṭhāna' refers to standing unshakably by pressing the earth with four legs. This state of the Buddha's omniscience is called 'āsabha' because it is like the standing of a noble usabha bull. Just as the usabha bull called 'nisabha', being endowed with the strength of an usabha, stands in an unshakable manner by pressing the earth with four legs, so too the Buddha, being endowed with the ten Tathāgata-powers, stands in an unshakable manner, pressing the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), such that no opposing enemy in the world with its devas can shake him. Standing thus, he claims that noble state of omniscience, reaches it, and without rejecting it, assumes it for himself. Therefore, it is said: 'He claims the supreme position (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti).'

'Parisāsu' means in the eight assemblies. 'Sīhanādaṃ nadati' means he makes a noble sound, he makes a fearless sound, or he makes a sound like a lion's roar. In this regard, there is this analogy: Just as a lion king, being endowed with lion-strength, is brave in all places and roars the lion's roar without any hair-standing (fear), so too the Buddha-lion, being endowed with the Tathāgata-powers, is brave in the eight assemblies and without any hair-standing...
295:
In the manner beginning with 'Thus is self-identity,' He utters the Lion's Roar (sīhanāda), which is endowed with the elegance of various forms of teaching. Because of such utterance, it is said, 'He utters the Lion's Roar in the assemblies.'

In the phrase 'He turns the Brahma-wheel (Brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti),' 'Brahma' means noble, most excellent, or distinguished. 'Cakka' refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). That Wheel of Dhamma is of two kinds: the Knowledge of Penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of Teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). Among them, the knowledge infused with wisdom that brings about one's own noble fruit is called the Knowledge of Penetration. The knowledge infused with compassion that brings about the noble fruit for disciples is called the Knowledge of Teaching. Of these two, the Knowledge of Penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen. It is 'arising' from the time of the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahantship, and it is 'arisen' at the moment of Fruition. Alternatively, it is 'arising' from the Tusita heaven until the Path of Arahantship at the Great Bodhi-seat, and 'arisen' at the moment of Fruition. Or, it is 'arising' from the time of Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Path of Arahantship, and 'arisen' at the moment of Fruition. The Knowledge of Teaching is also twofold: that which is turning and that which has turned. It is 'turning' until the Path of Stream-entry of Aññāsi Koṇ膽añña, and it is 'turned' at the moment of Fruition. Among these two, the Knowledge of Penetration is supramundane (lokuttara), while the Knowledge of Teaching is mundane (lokiya). Both of these are the personal knowledge (orasā-ñāṇa) of the Buddhas alone, not shared with others.

Now, to show in detail those ten powers endowed with which the Tathāgata claims the noble station of omniscience, He said: 'Monks, what are the ten? Here, monks, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible...' In that context, 'ṭhānañca ṭhānato' means the cause as the cause. It is called 'ṭhāna' (station/cause) because the effect resides there, and by depending on that cause, it arises and persists. The Blessed One understands: 'Whatever states are the productive cause (hetu) and supporting condition (paccaya) for the arising of certain states, that is the "ṭhāna" (possibility/cause) for those states. Whatever states are neither the productive cause nor the supporting condition for the arising of certain states, that is the "aṭṭhāna" (impossibility/non-cause) for those states.' Thus, He understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. In the Abhidhamma, this is explained in detail in the manner beginning with: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible?' (Vibhaṅga 809). 'Yampi' means 'by which knowledge.' 'This also, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata' means this knowledge of the possible and impossible is also called a Tathāgata-power (Tathāgata-bala). In this way, the connection of the meaning in all terms should be understood.

'Kamma-samādānānaṃ' means of the wholesome and unwholesome actions performed after undertaking them. Or, the action itself is called 'kamma-samādāna.' 'Ṭhānaso hetuso' means by way of supporting condition and root cause...
296:
...and by way of cause. Among those causes, destination (gati), substrate (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) are the 'ṭhāna' (station/condition) for the result (vipāka), while kamma is the 'hetu' (root cause). The detailed explanation of this knowledge has already appeared in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga 810) in the manner beginning with: 'Some evil undertakings of action are obstructed by the excellence of destination (gati-sampatti) and do not ripen.'

'Sabbatthagāminī' refers to the practice leading to all destinations and the practice leading to the non-destination (Nibbāna). 'Paṭipadā' means the path (kamma). 'He understands as it really is' means that even when many people kill the same living being, He knows the nature of the practices consisting of wholesome and unwholesome volitions (cetanā) in that single object without error, such as: 'This person's volition will lead to hell; this person's volition will lead to the animal realm.' The detailed explanation of this knowledge has also appeared in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga 811) in the manner beginning with: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the practice leading everywhere? Here, the Tathāgata understands: "This path, this practice leads to hell."' 

'Anekadhātu' means many elements, such as the eye-element and so on, or the sense-sphere element and so on. 'Nānādhātu' means various kinds of elements due to the different characteristics of those same elements. 'Loka' means the world consisting of aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). 'He understands as it really is' means He penetrates the nature of those elements without error. This knowledge is also detailed in the Abhidhamma in the manner beginning with: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the world with its many and various elements? Here, the Tathāgata understands the diversity of aggregates.'

'Nānādhimuttikata' means the state of having various dispositions (inclinations) such as low dispositions and so on. This knowledge is also detailed in the Abhidhamma in the manner beginning with: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the various dispositions of beings? Here, the Tathāgata understands: "There are beings with low dispositions."' 

'Parasattānaṃ' means of the noble beings. 'Parapuggalānaṃ' means of other low beings. Or, these two terms have the same meaning but are spoken in two ways according to the nature of those to be disciplined (veneyya). 'Indriyaparopariyatta' means the maturity and immaturity, the growth and decline, of the faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) and so on. The detailed explanation of this knowledge is also [found in the Abhidhamma]: 'Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the maturity and immaturity of the faculties of other beings and other persons...'
297:
The knowledge (of knowing the inclinations of beings) has already appeared in the Abhidhamma in such a way as: "Here, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of beings" (Vibh. 814), and so forth.

"Of jhānas, deliverances, concentrations, and attainments" refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first jhāna; the eight deliverances (vimokkha) beginning with "Possessing form, one sees forms"; the three concentrations (samādhi) beginning with "with initial and sustained application"; and the nine successive attainments (anupubbasamāpatti) beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna. Corruption (saṅkilesa) refers to states partaking of decline. Purification (vodāna) refers to states partaking of distinction. Emergence (vuṭṭhāna) refers to the well-practiced jhānas, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), as stated: "Purification is also emergence; emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence" (Vibh. 828).

A well-practiced lower jhāna is the proximate cause for a higher jhāna; therefore, it is said, "Purification is also emergence." However, emergence from all jhānas occurs through the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and emergence from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) occurs through the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). With reference to this emergence through the life-continuum and fruition, it is said, "Emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence." This knowledge of the corruption, purification, and emergence of these jhānas, deliverances, concentrations, and attainments has also been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma in such a way as: "Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the corruption, purification, and emergence of jhānas, deliverances, concentrations, and attainments as it really is? There are four types of meditators: here, a certain meditator, though it is an attainment (sampatti), perceives it as a failure (vipatti)," and so forth (Vibh. 828). The decision regarding the detailed explanation of all knowledges has been stated in the Sammohavinodanī, the commentary on the Vibhaṅga. The account of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) and the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) has been detailed in the Visuddhimagga. The account of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) has already been stated below.

Regarding those ten powers of knowledge (dasabalañāṇa), there is a statement by opponents (paravādī): "There is no separate knowledge called the ten powers of knowledge; this is merely a division of the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa)." That should not be regarded in that way. For the ten powers of knowledge are one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another. The ten powers of knowledge know only their respective functions, whereas the knowledge of omniscience knows those functions as well as everything else remaining.

Among the ten powers of knowledge, the first (knowledge of what is possible and impossible) knows only the cause and non-cause. The second (knowledge of the result of kamma) knows only the specific results of kamma. The third (knowledge of the way leading to all destinations) knows only the classification of kamma. The fourth (knowledge of the many and various elements) knows only the cause of the diversity of elements. The fifth (knowledge of the various inclinations) knows only the inclinations and dispositions of beings. The sixth (knowledge of the degree of faculties) knows only the sharpness or dullness of the faculties. The seventh (knowledge of corruption, etc., of jhānas, etc.) knows only the corruption and so forth of jhānas together with those jhānas themselves. The eighth (knowledge of recollection of past lives) knows only the continuity of the aggregates lived in the past. The ninth (divine eye) knows only the passing away and rebirth of beings. The tenth (knowledge of the destruction of taints) knows only the classification of the Truths. The knowledge of omniscience, however, knows what is to be known by these ten knowledges as well as what is beyond them. However, it does not perform all the functions of those ten knowledges. For that knowledge of omniscience, being a jhāna...
298:
The knowledge of omniscience is not able to reach absorption (appanā), it is not able to perform transformations as a psychic power (iddhi), and it is not able to eradicate defilements as a Path (magga).

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked this: "Is this so-called ten powers of knowledge with initial and sustained application (savitakka-savicāra), with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta), or without initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra)? Is it of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara)? Is it mundane (lokiya) or supramundane (lokuttara)?" If he knows, he will say: "In sequence, seven knowledges are with initial and sustained application; the two beyond that are without initial and sustained application." He will say: "The knowledge of the destruction of taints may be with initial and sustained application, may be with sustained application only, or may be without initial and sustained application." Likewise, he will say: "In sequence, seven knowledges are of the sense sphere, the two beyond that are of the fine-material sphere, and at the end, one (the knowledge of the destruction of taints) is supramundane." But he will say: "The knowledge of omniscience is only with initial and sustained application, and only mundane."

Thus, having understood the word-by-word commentary here, now, because the Tathāgata first of all sees, through the knowledge of what is possible and impossible, the absence of the obstruction of defilements, which is the possibility or impossibility for the attainment of the destruction of taints by beings to be led (veneyya). This is because of seeing the ground of mundane right view and because of seeing the absence of the ground of fixed wrong view. Then, through the knowledge of the result of kamma, He sees the absence of the obstruction of results (vipākāvaraṇa) by seeing the rebirth with three roots (tihetuka-paṭisandhi). Through the knowledge of the way leading to all destinations, He sees the absence of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa) by seeing the absence of kamma with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma). For those who are thus without obstructions, He sees the specific conduct through the knowledge of the many and various elements for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma accordingly, by seeing the diversity of elements. Then, through the knowledge of various inclinations, He sees their inclination (adhimutti) for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma by way of inclination even without taking up effort (payoga). Then, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma according to the capacity and strength of those whose inclinations have been thus seen, He sees the maturity or immaturity of the faculties through the knowledge of the degree of faculties, by seeing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties such as faith (saddhā). Having thus distinguished the degree of faculties, if those beings are far away, He quickly approaches them by means of specific psychic power because of His mastery in jhānas and so forth through the knowledge of jhānas, etc. Having approached them, He sees their past lives through the knowledge of recollection of past lives, and their present specific state of mind through the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) obtained through the power of the divine eye. Then, through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of taints, being free from delusion regarding the practice leading to the destruction of taints, He teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of taints. Therefore, it should be understood that these powers (bala) are taught in this sequence.
299:
## 2. Adhivuttipada Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "those teachings" (ye te dhammā) refers to the teachings of the Ten Powers (Dasabala-ñāṇa) and Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Adhivuttipadānaṃ" means the teachings of the aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), which are the basis for designations (adhivacana). In fact, "adhivutti" refers to designations (adhivacana/concepts); they are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the teaching because they serve as the foundation for the discourse. Past Buddhas have taught these very teachings, and future Buddhas will also teach these same teachings. Therefore, the teachings such as the aggregates are called "adhivuttipada" (bases of designation). Alternatively, wrong views (micchā-diṭṭhi) are called "adhivutti" because they occur by overriding the true meaning and not grasping the nature as it is; the words that indicate these wrong views are meant by "adhivuttipada." Regarding those adhivuttipada, also known as the terminology of views, "for realization through higher knowledge" means for the purpose of knowing and realizing them for oneself. "Visārado" (confident) means reaching a state of joy (somanassa) associated with knowledge. "To teach the Dhamma in such and such a way in those teachings" means to know the inclinations (āsaya) of those with wrong views or others and to teach the Dhamma in various appropriate ways. "Will know the low teaching as low" means perceiving a base or inferior teaching as an "inferior teaching." "Ñāteyya" means what should be known; "daṭṭheyya" means what should be seen; "sacchikareyya" means what should be realized. "Knowledge as it really is in those various teachings" means the knowledge of the nature (sabhāva) of those various things. By this, Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is shown. Having thus shown Omniscience, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Dasayimāni" (These ten...) wishing to show the Ten Powers (Dasabala-ñāṇa) once more. In truth, the Ten Powers are also simply the knowledge of things as they really are.

## 3. Kāya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "should one fall into a certain part" means falling into a certain category of offense (āpatti). "Anuvicca" means entering and investigating thoroughly. "Bodily misconduct" refers to the threefold bodily misconduct; "verbal misconduct" refers to the fourfold verbal misconduct. "Low envy" refers to mean jealousy (issā). "Seeing with wisdom" means seeing repeatedly and abandoning through path wisdom (magga-paññā) together with insight (vipassanā). "Ijjhati" means to be fulfilled or accomplished. "Upavāsassa" means for one who dwells relying on and approaching (a teacher or practice). "Abhibhuyya" means overpowering and crushing.
300:
(It means) overpowering and crushing. "Irīyati" means it occurs or proceeds. In this sutta, the Path along with Insight is taught.

## 4. Mahācunda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, by the phrase "I know this Dhamma," the manner of stating a claim of knowledge (ñāṇa-vāda) is expressed. By the phrases such as "one with a developed body," the manner of stating a claim of development (bhāvanā-vāda) is expressed. In the third instance, both claims are stated together; all three of these individuals claim only Arahantship. "Should speak an Aḍḍha claim" means one should speak the claim, "I am wealthy (prosperous)." "Upanīhātun" means to take out and give.

## 5. Kasiṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, they are called "kasiṇa" (entirety) because of the sense of being whole or complete. They are called "āyatana" (bases) because they are like a field (khetta) or a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) for the states that have those kasiṇa-concepts as their object; thus, they are "kasiṇāyatana." "Above" means facing the upper sky. "Below" means facing the ground below. "Across" means delimiting all around like the circumference of a field.

Some practitioners expand the kasiṇa only upwards, some downwards, and some all around. Alternatively, for various reasons, one spreads it just as one who wishes to see forms spreads light. Therefore, it is said, "One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, and across."

As for the word "adwayaṃ" (non-dual/without a second), it is said so that the single kasiṇa does not turn into something else. Just as for one who has entered water, there is only water in all directions and nothing else, in the same way, the earth kasiṇa remains only the earth kasiṇa. There is no mixing of that earth kasiṇa with other kasiṇas. This same method applies to all (other kasiṇas like the water kasiṇa, etc.).

"Measureless" (appamāṇa) is said by way of the measureless nature of the pervading (pharaṇa) of each respective kasiṇa. Indeed, one who pervades it with the mind pervades the whole; one does not take a limit such as "this is its beginning, this is its middle."

"Viññāṇa-kasiṇa" (consciousness kasiṇa) refers to the consciousness occurring in the space produced by the removal of the kasiṇa (kasiṇugghāṭima-ākāsa). In that consciousness kasiṇa, the states of being above, below, and across should be understood in the space through the removal of the kasiṇa, and in the consciousness occurring there through the power of that space. This is the summary here; however, according to the method of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā), these earth kasiṇas and so forth have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.
301:
## 6. Kāḷī Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'kumāripañhesu' means in the questions of the maidens, who were the daughters of Māra. By both terms 'atthassa patti' (attainment of the goal) and 'hadayassa santi' (peace of heart), only the fruit of Arahantship is spoken of. 'Senaṃ' (army) refers to the army of defilements such as lust (rāga) and so forth. 'Piyasātarūpaṃ' (that which is dear and pleasant) is so named because it arises in objects that are of a dear and pleasant nature. 'Ekohaṃ jhāyaṃ sukhamanubodhiṃ' means: "Having thus conquered the army of defilements, I alone, practicing jhāna, realized and experienced happiness."

'Sakkhiṃ' refers to the friend through Dhamma (dhamma-sakkhi) who has reached the state of friendship. 'Na sampajjati kenaci me' means: "I have no friendship (mittadhamma) with anyone."

'Sister, some recluses and brahmins arise taking the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa as the supreme benefit' means they arise with the thought that the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa is the most excellent and noble goal. 'Sister, as far as the limit of the earth-kasiṇa attainment goes' refers to the highest point or the ultimate boundary of the earth-kasiṇa attainment. 'The Blessed One knew that limit with higher knowledge' means the Blessed One realized the highest limit of that earth-kasiṇa attainment with the wisdom of higher knowledge (abhiññā-paññā). 'Saw the gratification (assāda)' means He saw the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). 'Saw the danger (ādīnava)' means He saw the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). 'Saw the escape (nissaraṇa)' means He saw the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). 'Saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana)' means He saw the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). 'Atthassa patti' means the reaching of the benefit known as the fruit of Arahantship because of seeing these Four Truths; 'hadayassa santi' means the peace of heart because all distress and feverish heat have been calmed.

## 7. Paṭhamamahāpañhasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'abhijānātha' means: "Live realizing and witnessing with higher knowledge." 'Abhiññāya' means having known. 'Idha' means in this Dhamma teaching. 'Dhamma teaching or Dhamma teaching' refers to the question: "What is the difference between the Dhamma teaching of the recluse Gotama and our Dhamma teaching, or our Dhamma teaching and the Dhamma teaching of the recluse Gotama?" In the second phrase, the method is the same. Thus, those wanderers (titthiyas) placed their own views on the same level as the Dispensation (Sāsana) with mere words, like broken gold in the middle. 'They did not delight' means they did not accept it, saying, "It is so." 'They did not contradict' means they did not prohibit it, saying, "It is not so." Why? Because it is said that they thought, "These wanderers are like blind people; they might speak whether they know or not," and thus they did not delight.
302:
'Na sampāyissanti' means they will not be able to answer completely. 'Uttari ca vighātaṃ' means they will encounter further distress because of not being able to answer completely. Indeed, distress arises for those who are unable to answer completely. In the phrase 'yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmiṃ', the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle (nipāta). The word 'yathā' is a causal term; it means "because they are asked a question in a matter that is not their domain." 'Ito vā pana sutvā' means having heard from this Dispensation of mine. 'Ito' (from this) means from the Tathāgata or from the disciples of the Tathāgata. 'Ārādheyya' means should satisfy; it shows that there is no other way of satisfying (ārādhanā).

'Ekadhamme' means in one thing (dhamma). This term shows the summary (uddesa). Subsequently, the phrase 'katamasmiṃ ekadhamme' shows the question. 'Sabbe sattā āhāratthitikā' (all beings subsist on nutriment) is the detailed explanation (veyyākaraṇa) here. The same method applies to the remaining summaries. In the words 'sammā nibbindamāno' and so forth, 'sammā' means being weary through the insight of weariness (nibbidānupassanā) by the proper causal method; being dispassionate through the insight of dispassion (virāgānupassanā); being liberated by making a means for liberation through the insight of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā); or being liberated by the power of decision (adhimokkha) and making a firm determination. By delimiting through arising and passing away and seeing the beginning and the end, one is 'sammā pariyantadassāvī' (one who properly sees the limit). 'Sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca' means having properly reached the true meaning with wisdom. 'Dukkhassantakaro hoti' means one becomes an end-maker of the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha).

'Sabbe sattā' refers to all beings in all existences, such as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and the one-constituent existence (ekavokārabhava). 'Āhāratthitikā' means beings who subsist on nutriment. Thus, the one thing that is the cause of the subsistence of all beings is called nutriment; (it should be known) in that one thing. Here, an objection might be raised: "Does this not contradict the Vibhaṅga passage: 'The non-percipient deities (asaññasatta) are without cause, without nutriment, without contact,' etc.?" It does not contradict. For those non-percipient beings, jhāna itself is the nutriment. If so, does it not contradict the statement: "Monks, there are these four nutriments"? This also does not contradict. In that sutta, things having the characteristic of nutriment are called nutriments in a non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense. Here, however, "cause" (paccaya) is called nutriment in a figurative (pariyāya) sense. It is appropriate to find a cause for all things. And whatever fruit that cause produces, it "brings" (āharati) that fruit; therefore, it is called nutriment (āhāra). That is why the Blessed One said: "Monks, I say that ignorance (avijjā) also has its nutriment, not that it is without nutriment."
303:
“Monks, what is the nutriment of ignorance? It should be said: the five hindrances” (A. Ni. 10.61). In this context of ‘All beings subsist on nutriment,’ this figurative nutriment is intended. When this causal nutriment is taken, all nutriments, whether figurative or non-figurative, are included.

Among those two, causal nutriment is found in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). Indeed, those who went forth into the sectarian folds before the arising of the Buddha, having performed the preliminary work on the air-kasiṇa (vāyo-kasiṇa) and produced the fourth jhāna, would emerge from that fourth jhāna and think: ‘Fie on the mind! Fie on this mind! The non-existence of the mind is indeed better. For it is depending on the mind that suffering, which has killing, binding, and so forth as its cause, arises. When there is no mind, this suffering does not exist.’ Having thus produced desire and preference for this, they die with their jhāna unimpaired and are reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings. Whatever posture was maintained by that person in the human world, they are reborn in that same posture and remain for five hundred aeons (kappas), appearing like a physical form possessed of mind. For that long duration, they are as if asleep. Causal nutriment is found even for such beings. For the very jhāna they developed to be reborn there becomes the cause for them. For example, an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels as long as the force of the bowstring lasts. Similarly, they remain as long as the cause, which is the jhāna, lasts. When that cause is exhausted, they fall like an arrow whose force is spent. At the time of their passing (cuti), their physical body disappears, and sense-sphere perception (kāmāvacara-saññā) arises; because of the arising of that perception, it is known that those devas have passed away from that body.

As for those hell-beings (nerayika) who are said to subsist neither on the fruit of exertion nor on the fruit of merit, what is their nutriment? For them, kamma itself is the nutriment. If it is asked, ‘Are there five nutriments?’, it should not be said that there are five or that there are not five; for has it not been said that ‘cause is nutriment’? Therefore, the very kamma by which they are reborn in hell is their nutriment, because it is the cause for their subsistence. With reference to this cause, it is said: ‘He does not die as long as that evil kamma is not exhausted’ (M. Ni. 3.250, 268; A. Ni. 3.36).

Even regarding the nutriment of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) in this hell, one should not dispute. For even the saliva that arises in their mouths performs the function of nutriment for them. Saliva in hell becomes a cause by being a cause for painful feeling, while in heaven it is a cause for pleasant feeling. Thus, in the sense-sphere (kāmabhava), there are four nutriments in a non-figurative sense. In the form and formless spheres (rūpa-arūpabhava), excluding the non-percipient beings,
304:
there are three nutriments for the remaining beings. For the non-percipient beings and for all other beings, it should be understood that ‘all beings subsist on nutriment’ in this manner through causal nutriment. Among those nutriments, the four nutriments or any causal nutriment is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The prior craving that produces the nutriment is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The wisdom that fully knows cessation is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Thus, the application should be made in all sections by way of the Four Truths.

## 8. Dutiya-mahāpañhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "Kajangalāyaṃ" means in the city of that name. "Kajangalā" refers to the residents of Kajangalā. "Mahāpañhesu" means in the questions that encompass great meanings. "Yathā mettha khāyati" means as it appears to me in this problem. "Sammā subhāvitacitto" means one whose mind is well-developed by the proper method of causes. In the phrase "Eso ceva tassa attho," although the Blessed One answered the questions such as ‘four things’ by way of the ‘four nutriments’ and so on, when the four nutriments are fully understood, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are already developed; and when those foundations of mindfulness are developed, the four nutriments are already fully understood. Therefore, though the phrasing (byañjana) differs through the elegance of the teaching, the meaning (attha) is one and the same. This same method applies to the faculties (indriya) and so forth. Therefore, it is said: ‘This itself is the meaning of that.’ In terms of meaning, both of these are like a piece of gold split in the middle.

## 9. Paṭhama-kosalasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "Yāvatā" means as many as. "Kāsikosalā" means the inhabitants of the Kāsi and Kosala regions. "Attheva aññathattaṃ" means for one who exists, there is certainly the nature of change. "Atthi vipariṇāmo" means there is certainly death as well. "Tasmimpi nibbindati" means he becomes weary even of that attainment of being a King of Kosala. "Agge virajjati" means he is detached even from the peak of attainment, the status of a King of Kosala. "Pagiva hīnasmiṃ" means he is already detached from the five cords of sensual pleasure of inferior, ordinary people.

"Manomayā" means beings produced by the mind of jhāna. "Vārāṇaseyyakaṃ" means cloth produced in the city of Benares (Vārāṇasī). It is said that there, the cotton is soft, the spinners and weavers are skilled, and the water is pure and smooth. "Ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ" means smooth and polished on both sides.
305:
Water is also pure and smooth. Therefore, it is smooth on both sides, and on both flanks, it appears smooth and soft. Four types of practices (perceptions) mixed with mundane and supramundane are spoken of. Among perceptions, the first is the perception of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-saññā), the second is the perception of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-saññā), the third is the supramundane perception (lokuttara-saññā), and the fourth is the perception of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-saññā). Because that perception of the sphere of nothingness is mentioned as 'foremost' (agga), and there is no designation of perception beyond that, it is called 'foremost'.

'Bāhirakānaṃ' refers to those who exist outside the Dispensation (Sāsana). 'No cassaṃ no ca me siyā' means: 'If I had not been in the past, this self-identity (attabhāva) would not exist for me now.' 'Na bhavissāmi na me bhavissati' means: 'Even if I will not be in the future, no kind of anxiety will arise for me.' 'Agge virajjati' means one is detached from the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi). This is because, in this context, the view of annihilation is considered 'foremost' due to its proximity to Nibbāna.

'Paramatthavisuddhi' means supreme purity. This is a name for the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). The sphere of nothingness is called 'foremost' because it is the proximate cause for insight (vipassanā), while the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called 'foremost' because of its long lifespan. 'Parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbānaṃ' means the supreme Nibbāna in this very self-identity (existence). 'Anupādā vimokkho' is the liberation of the mind without grasping through the four types of grasping (upādāna). This is a name for the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). 'Pariññā' means overcoming (full understanding). Therein, the Blessed One designates the full understanding of sensual pleasures through the first jhāna, the full understanding of forms (rūpa) through the immaterial attainments (arūpāvacara), and the full understanding of feelings (vedanā) through Nibbāna without grasping. For Nibbāna is called the full understanding of feelings because it is the abandoning of all feelings. 'Anupādā-parinibbānaṃ' means Parinibbāna without conditions.

The Blessed One, while teaching this sutta, saw five hundred monks oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati) and taught it to dispel their dissatisfaction. Those monks also dispelled their dissatisfaction, directed their knowledge according to the teaching, became stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and later, developing insight, reached Arahantship.

## 10. Dutiya-kosala-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, 'uyyodhika nivatto hoti' means having returned from battle. 'Laddhādhippāyo' means when King Mahākosala gave his daughter to King Bimbisāra, he gave a village named Kāsi, which yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand, situated between the two kingdoms, to his daughter...
306: When King Ajātasattu killed his father (King Bimbisāra), his mother also died shortly after due to the grief of separation from the King. Then King Pasenadi Kosala thought, 'Ajātasattu has killed his parents; this village belongs to my father,' and he initiated a conflict (war) for that village. King Ajātasattu also claimed, 'This village belongs to my mother,' and went to war for it. Thus, the uncle and nephew engaged in battle with a fourfold army. In that conflict, King Pasenadi Kosala was defeated twice by King Ajātasattu and had to retreat into the city. On the third occasion, thinking 'How can I be victorious?', he learned the method of fighting through eavesdropping (upassuti), arranged a battle array, surrounded Ajātasattu from both sides, and captured him. At that moment, because his desire for victory was fulfilled, he became known as 'Laddhādhippāyo' (one who has attained his wish). 'He went towards the monastery' means after establishing the victory camp outside the city, he thought, 'While they are decorating the city, I will go and pay homage to the Buddha. Once I enter the city, there will be delays.' Surrounded by his ministers, he went towards the monastery and entered. At what time did he enter? He entered at the time when the Buddha, after giving advice to the monks returning from their alms round, had entered the Gandhakuṭi, and the Saṅgha of monks, having received the advice, had gone to their respective places for the night and day. In the phrase 'they were walking to and fro,' at what time were they walking? They were walking to and fro to dispel the sloth and torpor (thina-middha) caused by the choice food. Or, they were monks practicing meditation during the day. For such monks, after the meal, having walked to and fro, bathed, and made the body comfortable according to the season, their minds become one-pointed (ekaggatā) while sitting and performing the recluse's duties. 'Those monks' refers to the King, who, looking around and thinking, 'Where is the Teacher? Where is the Sugata?', going from one precinct to another to ask before entering, saw the monks wearing rag-robes (pāṃsukūlika) walking on the great walkway like forest elephants, and went towards them. This statement refers to that action. 'Desiring to see' means wanting to behold the Buddha. 'Vihāra' (dwelling) refers to the Gandhakuṭi. 'Without haste' means not hurriedly, but slowly placing the feet within the space of a single step, fulfilling the duties, and not disturbing the sand which was well-swept and resembled a net of pearls or jasmine flowers. 'Ālinda' means the front porch (veranda). 'Aggaḷa' means the door-leaf. 'Having cleared the throat' means making the sound of clearing the throat. 'Knock' means to knock slightly with the tip of the fingernail near the keyhole. It is said that non-human beings knock at the very top of the door, and long-bodied creatures knock at the very bottom. Not knocking like that, but knocking near the keyhole in the middle is the proper etiquette for knocking on a door. 'The Blessed One opened the door' means the Blessed One stood up and opened the door. However, it is said that at the moment the Blessed One, who had given great gifts for many billions of aeons, extended his hand with the thought 'Let it open,' the door opened by itself as if it were improper for him to perform the act of opening the door with his own hand. Since that door opened by the power of the Blessed One's body or mind, it is appropriate to say 'The Blessed One opened the door.' 'My supreme salutation' means respectful worship with body and speech. Regarding the phrase 'knowing the favor, reciprocating the favor,' I shall speak in detail. In the past, King Pasenadi Kosala was a very corpulent person. Therefore, he used to eat a bucketful of rice. Then, the Blessed One, in order to reduce the King's daytime heaviness, came for a moment...
307:
They speak of it as the duty regarding knocking on the door. "The Blessed One opened the door" means that the Blessed One did not physically get up and open the door, but rather, while resolving "let it be opened," he extended his hand. At that moment, as if saying, "Venerable Sir, while you were giving gifts throughout many billions of aeons, you never performed the act of opening a door with your own hand," the door opened by itself. Since that door opened because of the Blessed One's mind, it is appropriate to say, "The Blessed One opened the door."

"Mettūpahāra" refers to the physical and vocal offerings associated with loving-kindness. "Kataññutā" (gratitude) refers to this: in the past, King Kosala had a stout body and would eat a bucketful (doṇapāka) of rice. Then, the Blessed One, in order to make him reduce his intake little by little every day, gave him this advice:

"For the man who is always mindful,
Knowing the measure in the food he has received,
His ailments become thin,
And he ages slowly, guarding his life."

Abiding by this advice, the King reduced his intake little by little every day until he eventually stayed at the measure of a single cupful (nāḷika) of cooked rice. His limbs also became lean and firm. Referring to that favor done by the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable Sir, I see gratitude and thankfulness."

"Ariyāya ñāya" refers to the Path together with insight (vipassanā). "Vuddhasīla" means one who has increased virtue. "Ariyasīla" means one endowed with virtues that do not belong to worldlings (puthujjanas). "Kusalasīla" means one endowed with blameless virtues. "Āraññaka" (forest-dweller) is said to show that even when he was being born, he was born in the forest; even when he was attaining enlightenment, he attained it in the forest; and even when he dwells in the Gandhakuṭi, which is like a divine mansion, he dwells only in the forest. The remaining terms are clear in meaning in every respect.

## The Third Great Chapter (Mahāvaggo Tatiyo).

## 4. The Upāli Group (Upālivagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Upāli Sutta (Upālisuttavaṇṇanā)

In the first sutta of the fourth group, regarding the words "Saṅghasuṭṭhutāya" and so on, "Saṅghasuṭṭhutā" means the excellence of the Saṅgha. Just as in the passage where it occurs as "Excellent, O King," the word "Excellent"...
308:
"Bhante" is the nature of accepting the words. For one who accepts the words of the Tathāgata, that acceptance leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time. Therefore, the training rule was laid down for the purpose of making the Saṅgha accept the words, saying, "Excellent, Venerable Sir." To clarify this meaning—that it was laid down by showing the disadvantage of not accepting and the advantage of accepting, and not by overcoming through force—he said, "Saṅghasuṭṭhutāya" (for the excellence of the Saṅgha). "Saṅghaphāsutāya" means for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the purpose of living together and dwelling in happiness.

"Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya" means for the restraint of shameless persons. "Dummaṅkū" refers to immoral persons who, even when being made to feel ashamed, reach that state with difficulty; they do not feel ashamed while committing or after having committed a transgression. The training rule was laid down for the purpose of restraining them. For if there were no training rule, they would harass the Saṅgha, saying, "What have you seen? What have you heard? What have we done? Charging us with what offense in what matter do you restrain us?" But when there is a training rule, the Saṅgha, having shown the training rule, will restrain them in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, "Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya."

"Pesalānaṃ" means for the purpose of the comfortable living of monks who love virtue. For monks who love virtue, if they do not know what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and blameless, and the boundaries and limits of the training rules, they become weary while striving to fulfill the threefold training. However, if they know what is blameworthy and blameless and the boundaries and limits, they do not become weary while striving to fulfill the training. Therefore, the laying down of training rules for those monks indeed leads to their comfortable living. Alternatively, the restraint of immoral persons is itself the comfortable living of those virtuous monks. This is because, on account of immoral persons, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā do not endure, formal acts of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma) do not take place, there is no harmony, and monks, being distracted, are unable to devote themselves to recitations and so forth. But when immoral persons are restrained, all these dangers do not exist, and thus virtuous monks dwell in comfort. In this way, two kinds of meaning should be understood in the phrase "pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya."

"Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya" means for the restraint of taints (dangers) occurring in the present life. Taints in the present life refer to specific sufferings such as being struck by hands, struck by sticks, struck by weapons, having hands or feet cut off, ill-repute, disgrace, and remorse, which are to be experienced in that very life by one who lives without restraint. It means for the purpose of closing off those dangers, for blocking the path of their arrival. "Samparāyikānaṃ" refers to taints (dangers) occurring in the future life, which one who lives without restraint...
309:
(The Blessed One prescribes the training rules) for the sake of warding off and calming the specific sufferings to be experienced in hell and other such states in the future life, which are rooted in evil kamma.

Regarding the term 'appasannānaṃ': when there is a prescription of a training rule, wise people who are not yet confident, either by knowing the prescription of the training rule or by seeing the monks practicing according to the prescription, attain confidence, thinking: 'These ascetics live far removed and restrained from those sense objects that are the causes of lust, hatred, and delusion for the majority of people in the world; indeed, they perform what is difficult to do.' This is like the Brahmins of wrong view who became confident upon seeing the volumes of the Vinaya Piṭaka. Therefore, it is said: 'For the confidence of those not yet confident.'

Regarding the term 'pasannānaṃ': those clansmen who are already confident in the Dispensation, either by knowing the prescription of the training rule or by seeing the monks practicing according to the prescription, become even more confident, thinking: 'O, how wonderful! These noble ones perform what is difficult to do, they who maintain the restraint of the Vinaya and eat only one meal a day for as long as they live.' Therefore, it is said: 'For the increase of those already confident.'

Regarding the term 'saddhammaṭṭhitiyā': the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) is threefold: the Saddhamma of scriptural study (pariyatti), the Saddhamma of practice (paṭipatti), and the Saddhamma of attainment (adhigama). Therein, the entire Word of the Buddha is called Pariyatti-saddhamma. The thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla), the virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla), concentration (samādhi), and insight (vipassanā) are called Paṭipatti-saddhamma. The nine supramundane states are called Adhigama-saddhamma. Since all this Saddhamma exists when there is a prescription of training rules, monks learn the training rules, their explanations (Vibhaṅga), and other Words of the Buddha to clarify their meaning; and by practicing according to the prescription, they fulfill the practice and attain the supramundane states to be reached through practice. Therefore, because of the prescription of training rules, the True Dhamma can endure for a long time. Thus, it is said: 'For the longevity of the True Dhamma.'

Regarding the term 'vinayānuggahāya': when there is a prescription of training rules, the fourfold Vinaya—namely, the Vinaya of restraint (saṃvara), the Vinaya of abandoning (pahāna), the Vinaya of settling (samatha), and the Vinaya of prescription (paññatti)—is supported and well-upheld. Therefore, it is said: 'For the support of the Vinaya.'

## 2. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'pārājiko' refers to one who has fallen into a Pārājika offense. 'Pārājikakathā vippakatā hoti' means that the discussion as to whether 'such and such a person has fallen into a Pārājika offense or not' has been started but not yet finished. In other sentences as well, it should be understood in this same manner.
310:
"...or not"—thus the discussion has started but is not concluded. This method applies everywhere.

## 3. Ubbāhikāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'ubbāhikāya' means for the purpose of extracting or removing from the Saṅgha to settle a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that has arisen. 'Established in the Vinaya' means being established in the characteristics of the Vinaya. 'Asaṃhīro' means not abandoning one's own view merely by the words of another. 'Paṭibalo' means being endowed with both physical strength and the strength of wisdom. 'Saññāpetuṃ' means to make known. 'Paññāpetuṃ' means to make well known or to distinguish. 'Nijjhāpetuṃ' means to make one examine. 'Pekkhatuṃ' means to make one see. 'Pasādetuṃ' means to produce inspiration that has arisen. 'Adhikaraṇaṃ' refers to the four types of legal issues, such as disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa). 'Adhikaraṇasamudayaṃ' refers to the causes that give rise to legal issues, such as the roots of disputes. 'Adhikaraṇanirodhaṃ' refers to the settling or cessation of legal issues. 'Adhikaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā' refers to the practice leading to the cessation of legal issues (adhikaraṇa-samatha) in seven ways.

## 4. Upasampadāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'anabhiratiṃ' refers to the state of being dissatisfied or bored. 'Vūpakāsetuṃ' means to dispel. 'Adhisīle' means in the higher virtue. The same method applies to 'citta' (mind) and 'paññā' (wisdom).

## 7. Saṅghabhedasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'vatthūhi' means by grounds or reasons. 'Avakassanti' means pulling the assembly, clearing them, or moving them to a suitable place. 'Apakassanti' means pulling away excessively so as to cause separation. 'Āveṇi kammāni karonti' means performing separate Saṅgha acts.

## 9-10. Ānandasuttadvaya-vaṇṇanā
39-40. In the ninth sutta, 'kappaṭṭhikaṃ' means the cause for remaining in hell for the duration of an aeon. 'Kibbisaṃ pasavati' means begetting evil or demerit. 'Āpāyiko' means one bound for the states of woe. 'Nerayiko' means one bound for hell. 'Vaggarato' means one who delights in schism.
