## 5. Akkosavagga

## 4. Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta

In the fourth sutta of the fifth chapter, "Kusinārāyaṃ" means in the city of that name. It is called Baliharaṇa because offerings (bali) for the deities are brought to this place; in that forest named Baliharaṇa. Regarding the terms "acchidda" (flawless/without holes) and "appaṭimaṃsa" (unassailable/not to be probed), if a monk's bodily conduct is such that he has been struck by someone or has undergone medical treatment, and his body is like a palm leaf eaten by termites (full of holes), or if it can be grabbed and pulled at any place (probed), then it is flawed. The opposite conduct is called "acchidda" (without holes) and "appaṭimaṃsa" (unassailable).

Speech conduct is also considered to have holes and be probe-able if it involves lying, insulting speech (omasavāda), slander (pesuñña), or baseless accusations (amūlaka-anuddhaṃsana). The opposite speech conduct is called "acchidda" and "appaṭimaṃsa." "Mettā nu kho me cittaṃ" refers to my mind of loving-kindness attained through the practice of meditation after cutting off impediments (palibodha). "Anāghātaṃ" means free from resentment, specifically resentment that has been abandoned through suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). "Kattha vuttaṃ" is a question asking in which city this training rule was spoken.

Regarding "kālena vakkhāmi" (I shall speak at the proper time), if a monk speaks after asking for permission from another monk, he is said to speak at the proper time. If he speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in places such as where lots are drawn, where gruel is served, in the hall of thought, on the alms-round path, or in the dining hall, or at a moment when the monk is surrounded by lay attendants, he is said to speak at an improper time. If he speaks with truthful words, he is said to speak "bhūtena" (truthfully). If he says, "This conduct is not suitable for you, young monk, elder, one who frequents assemblies, wearer of rag-robes, or preacher of Dhamma," he is said to speak with harsh words (pharusena). However, if he speaks based on a reason, saying, "Venerable sirs, you are elders, you frequent assemblies, you are wearers of rag-robes, you are preachers of Dhamma; this conduct is suitable for you," then...
312:
...speaking with gentle words, he is said to speak gently (saṇhena). Speaking based on a reason, he is said to speak with words connected to benefit (atthasaṃhita). "I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of anger" means he will speak after establishing a mind of loving-kindness, not with a corrupted mind.

## 5. Commentary on the Rājantepurappavesana Sutta

In the fifth sutta, "committed or will commit" means they have committed or will commit sexual misconduct. "Ratana" (gem) refers to any kind of gem, such as rubies. "Pattheti" means he desires to kill. "Hatthīsambādha" means crowded with elephants. Alternatively, there is a reading "hatthīsammadda," which means a place where there is trampling or crowding by elephants; thus, it is called "hatthīsammadda" because of the trampling by elephants in this palace. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches" means these sense objects that generate lust are fully present in that palace.

## 6. Commentary on the Sakka Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "danger accompanied by grief" (sokasabhaye) means danger arising from grief. There is also a reading "sokabhaya," which has the same meaning. The same method applies to the second term. "By any work" means by any occupation such as farming or trading. "Without falling into unwholesome states" means without committing any unwholesome act. "Nibbiseyya" means he should produce or accumulate. "Dakkho" means clever or skilled. "Uṭṭhānasampanno" means endowed with energetic effort. "Fit for speaking" means suitable for speaking. "Should live experiencing absolute happiness" means he should live experiencing absolute physical and mental happiness through wisdom.

"Impermanent" (aniccā) means they cease to exist after arising. "Empty" (tucchā) means they are devoid of essence. "False" (musā) means although they appear to be permanent, beautiful, and pleasant, they are not so; thus they are called false. "Subject to vanishing" (mosadhammā) means they have the nature of perishing. Therefore, it is shown that suffering arises depending on those (impermanent things). In this context, the word "vo" is a mere particle. "A certain Stream-enterer" (apaṇṇakaṃ vā sotāpanno) means he is definitely a Stream-enterer. Such a person also produces Jhana, or having gone to the Brahma realm, or in the six sensual heavens, he lives experiencing absolute happiness. In this sutta, the Teacher explained the virtues of the Eightfold Uposatha.
313:
## 7. Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the seventh discourse, the Mahāli Sutta: 'Micchāpaṇihitaṃ' means (a mind) that is wrongly directed. 'Adhammacariyā visamacariyā' refers to unrighteous conduct and unharmonious conduct by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha). The others (righteous and harmonious conduct) should be understood by way of the wholesome courses of action. In this sutta, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is discussed in this manner.

## 8. Pabbajita-abhiṇhasuttavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth discourse, the Pabbajita-abhiṇha Sutta: 'Pabbajitena' refers to one who has abandoned the household life and attained the state of a monk in the Dispensation. 'Abhiṇhaṃ' means frequently or repeatedly. 'Paccavekkhitabbā' means should be observed, reflected upon, and noted. 'Vevaṇṇiyaṃ' refers to the state of having an altered appearance. This altered appearance (vevaṇṇiya) is of two kinds: the altered appearance of the body and the altered appearance of the requisites. Among these, the altered appearance of the body should be understood through the shaving of the hair and beard. The altered appearance of the requisites should be understood as follows: whereas previously as a layman, one might have worn delicate clothes of various colors, eaten food of various excellent flavors from gold and silver vessels, slept or sat on noble beds and seats in splendid chambers, and prepared medicines with ghee, fresh butter, and so on; from the time of becoming a monk, one must wear clothes that are cut, sewn, and dyed with vegetable dye. One must eat mixed almsfood in an iron bowl or a clay bowl. One must sleep on mats of muñja grass and the like in dwellings such as the foot of a tree. One must sit on pieces of leather, mats, and so on. One must prepare medicine with fermented urine and the like. Thus, the altered appearance of the requisites should be understood here. For the monk who reflects in this way, anger and pride are abandoned.

'Parapaṭibaddhā me jီvikā' means 'My livelihood through the four requisites is bound up with others and dependent on others.' For the monk who reflects thus, his livelihood is purified, his almsfood is consumed with respect and reflection, and there is no such thing as the unreflective use of the four requisites. 'Añño me ākappo karaṇīyo' means 'Laypeople have a mode of walking with chests thrust out, necks held high, in a fancy manner and with unsteady steps; I must adopt a mode of conduct different from that.' He should reflect: 'I should go with restrained faculties and a peaceful mind, looking only a yoke's length ahead, with steps that are slow and measured like a water-cart on uneven ground.' For the monk who reflects thus, his deportment becomes suitable, and the three trainings (sikkhā) are fulfilled. 'Kaccinu kho' is a group of particles in the sense of investigation. 'Attā' means the mind (citta). 'Sīlato na upavadati' means not reproaching oneself on account of virtue, thinking 'Your virtue is not pure.' For the monk who reflects thus, inner shame (hiri) arises within him. That shame brings to fulfillment the restraint of the three doors. Restraint in the three doors is the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). One established in the fourfold purification of virtue develops insight and attains the fruit of Arahantship. 'Anuvicca viññū sabrahmacārī' means 'Do wise fellow-practitioners, having investigated...'
314:
...not reproach me on account of virtue, thinking 'Your virtue is impure.' For the monk who reflects thus, inner shame (hiri) arises within him. That shame brings to fulfillment the restraint of the three doors. Restraint in the three doors is the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). One established in the fourfold purification of virtue develops insight and attains the fruit of Arahantship. For the monk who reflects, 'Do wise fellow-practitioners, having investigated, not find cause to reproach me?', external dread (ottappa) is established. It should be understood in the same manner as the previous method that this dread brings to fulfillment the restraint of the three doors.

'There is diversity and separation from all that is dear and beloved' means diversity by birth and separation by death. For the monk who reflects thus, there is no lack of restraint in the three doors, and mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) is well-established. In the passage 'I am the owner of my kamma' and so on, it means: kamma is my own property, my own possession; thus 'owner of kamma'. The fruit to be given by kamma is the inheritance; the inheritance of kamma is 'kamma-inheritance', and I receive that; thus 'heir to kamma'. Kamma is my origin or cause; thus 'born of kamma'. Kamma is my relative or kinsman; thus 'related to kamma'. Kamma is my refuge or foundation; thus 'having kamma as refuge'. 'I shall be the heir of that kamma' means I shall be the one who receives the fruit given by that kamma. For one who reflects on being the owner of kamma in this way, the performing of evil no longer exists. 'In what way do the nights and days pass for me?' means reflecting: 'Do the nights and days pass for me while I am performing my duties and obligations, or while I am not? While I am reciting the Buddha's word, or while I am not? While I am performing tasks with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), or while I am not?' 'In what way do the nights and days pass for me?' has the meaning of 'How do they revolve?'. For the monk who reflects thus, heedfulness (appamāda) is fulfilled.

'Do I delight in empty places?' means reflecting: 'Do I delight in being alone in all postures in a secluded space?' For the monk who reflects thus, physical seclusion (kāyaviveka) is fulfilled. 'Superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)' refers to the states such as the jhānas of superior human beings, namely those who practice jhāna and the Noble Ones (Ariyas). Or it means states that are higher and more distinguished than the 'human states' known as the ten wholesome courses of action. The meaning is: 'Do such states exist in my internal continuity?' 'Ariyāñāṇadassanaviseso' (distinction in noble knowledge and vision): 'Knowledge' (ñāṇa) is so called in the sense of knowing through exalted (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) wisdom. 'Vision' (dassana) is so called in the sense of seeing the Dhamma directly as if seeing with the eye. Combining these two, it is called 'knowledge and vision', which is pure and noble.
315:
'Ñāṇadassana' means Noble Knowledge and Vision (ariya-ñāṇadassana). "Born of seasonal change" (utupariṇāmajā) means diseases arising from the transformation of the seasons, such as extreme heat or extreme cold. "Born of uneven care" (visamaparihārajā) means diseases born from uneven maintenance of the body, such as standing or sitting for too long. "Due to external effort" (opakkamikā) means diseases born from the efforts of others, such as assault or binding. 69-70. In the ninth sutta, "tiracchānakathā" (lowly talk) refers to talk that is contrary to the path to heaven and liberation because it does not lead out of saᅃsāra. Among those, talk concerning kings, such as "King Mahāsammata, King Mandhātu, and King Dhammāsoka possessed such great power," is called "rājakathā" (talk about kings). This same method applies to "corakathā" (talk about thieves) and so on. Among these, talk based on worldly desires, such as "Such and such a king is very handsome and beautiful to look at," is indeed lowly talk. However, talk that proceeds as "Even such a powerful king has come to destruction" stands as a subject of meditation (kammaᅩᅩhāna). Regarding thieves, talk based on worldly desires, such as "Mũladeva is so powerful, Meghadeva is so powerful," and praising their deeds as "Oh, how brave!" is lowly talk. Regarding battles, talk in the manner of enjoying the deeds in the Bhārata war and so on, such as "This person was killed by that person in this way, or pierced in that way," is lowly talk. But talk that proceeds as "They too have come to destruction" is a subject of meditation in all respects. Furthermore, regarding food and so on, it is not proper to speak with enjoyment of sensual pleasures, saying, "We ate, drank, and enjoyed food of such color, taste, and texture." However, it is proper to speak meaningfully, saying, "In the past, we gave food, drink, clothing, vehicles, flowers, and perfumes of such color and so on to virtuous persons, and we worshipped the shrine (cetiya)."

Regarding talk about relatives and so on, it is not proper to speak with enjoyment, saying, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we traveled with such magnificent vehicles."
319:
It is not proper. But it should be spoken meaningfully, saying, "Those relatives of ours have also come to destruction," or "In the past, we gave such sandals to the Saᅃgha." Talk about villages, whether it is about their being well-situated or poorly-situated, having plenty of food or being famished, or saying, "The inhabitants of such and such a village are brave and capable," is not proper if spoken with enjoyment. But it is proper to speak meaningfully, saying, "They have faith and devotion," or "They have come to destruction and passing away." The same method applies to talk about market towns, cities, and districts.

Talk about women is not proper if spoken with enjoyment regarding their complexion, figure, and so on. It is only proper to speak thus: "They have faith and devotion; they have come to destruction." Talk about heroes is not proper if spoken with enjoyment, saying, "The warrior named Nandimitta was a brave hero." It is only proper to speak thus: "He had faith; he has come to destruction." Regarding "surākathā" (talk about liquor) mentioned in the Pāᄷi, it is not proper to speak about various kinds of intoxicants with enjoyment; it is only proper to speak in terms of their danger (ādĩnava). Talk about streets is not proper if spoken with enjoyment, saying, "Such and such a street is well-situated or poorly-situated; the people are brave and capable." It is proper to speak, "They have faith and devotion; they have come to destruction." "Kumbhaᅩᅩhānakathā" refers to talk about the place where pots are made or talk about the water-front (landing place). Or it is talk about a slave girl carrying a water-pot. That too is not proper if spoken with enjoyment, saying, "She is attractive, skilled in dancing and singing." It is only proper to speak in the manner of "She has faith, she is devoted," and so on.

"Pubbapetakathā" refers to talk about deceased relatives. In that case, the judgment is the same as talk about living relatives. "Nānattakathā" refers to miscellaneous lowly talk of various natures, other than the types of talk mentioned before and after. "Lokakkhāyikā" refers to talk found in the Lokāyata and Vitaᅇᅇā treatises, such as "Who created this world? Such and such a person created it. The crow is white because its bones are white; the crane is red because its blood is red," and so on. "Samuddakkhāyikā" refers to useless talk about the ocean, such as "Why is the ocean called Sāgara? It is called Sāgara because King Sāgara dug it. It is called Samudda because he announced with a hand gesture, 'It was dug by me (samudda).'" "Bhava" means growth (prosperity), and "abhava" means decline (loss). Talk that proceeds by stating any useless reason, such as "In this way there is growth, in this way there is decline," is called "itibhavābhava-kathā."

## 1. Commentary on the Ākaṅkha Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'sampannasīlā' means those with perfected virtue or those possessed of virtue. This state of being possessed of virtue occurs due to two reasons: seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and seeing the benefits in the accomplishment of virtue. Both of these have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Regarding the term 'sampannasīlā', the Elder Sumana, a resident of Dīpavihāra, said that the Blessed One briefly referred to the fourfold purification of virtue (catu-pārisuddhi-sīla), and with the phrase 'pātimokkha-saṃvara-saṃvuta', He explained the primary virtue among them in detail.

However, his pupil, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, said: "In both places, the Blessed One spoke only of the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. Only the Pātimokkha restraint is called virtue; is there any place where the other three are called virtue?" he said with a disapproving manner. He continued: "Restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara) is merely the guarding of the six doors; purity of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi) is merely the obtaining of the four requisites in a righteous and fair manner; and [virtue] dependent on requisites (paccaya-sannissita) is merely the reflecting on and using the obtained requisites for their intended purpose. In the ultimate sense, only the Pātimokkha restraint is called virtue. If that Pātimokkha restraint is broken, it cannot be said that such a person will protect the remaining limbs, like a man whose head has been cut off. If that virtue is flawless, it is like a man whose head is not cut off, who can regain his life and restore the remaining parts to their original state. Therefore, by the term 'sampannasīlā', He referred to the Pātimokkha restraint, and using the synonym 'sampannapātimokkhā', He wished to explain it in detail, thus saying 'pātimokkha-saṃvara-saṃvuta', etc. The meaning of the terms 'pātimokkha-saṃvara-saṃvuta', etc., is as already stated.

Why is the word 'ākaṅkheyya' (if one should desire) mentioned? It is mentioned to show the benefits of virtue. If newly ordained monks or those with little wisdom should think, "The Blessed One always says, 'Fulfill virtue, fulfill virtue'; what special benefit or progress is there in fulfilling virtue?" He spoke thus to show them the benefits: "Having heard these benefits, starting from being dear and agreeable to fellow monks up to the destruction of the taints, may they fulfill their virtue." In that context, 'ākaṅkheyya' means if one should desire. 'Piyamanāpatā' means being dear and agreeable. It means being worthy of being looked upon with eyes of affection, or cultivating the mind which is the proximate cause for the arising of love, or being pervaded with a mind of loving-kindness in the hearts of fellow monks.
321:
Why is the word "ākaṅkheyya ce" (if one should desire) mentioned? It is mentioned to show the benefits of virtue. If newly ordained monks or those with little wisdom should think, "The Blessed One always says, 'Fulfill virtue, fulfill virtue'; what special benefit or progress is there in fulfilling virtue?" He spoke thus to show them the ten benefits: "Having heard these benefits, starting from being dear and agreeable to fellow monks up to the destruction of the taints, may they fulfill their virtue."

In that context, "ākaṅkheyya ce" means if one should desire. "Piyo ca assaṃ" (may I be dear) means may I be one who is looked upon with eyes of affection, one who is the proximate cause for the arising of love. "Manāpo" (agreeable) means one who increases the joy of those fellow monks, or one who is reached by their minds, or one who is pervaded with a mind of loving-kindness. "Garu" (revered) means one who is a position of respect for those fellow monks, like a stone parasol. "Bhāvanīyo" (estimable) means one who is worthy of praise such as, "Indeed, this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen." "Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī" means one should be a fulfiller of the fourfold purification of virtue alone, being endowed with it in an undiminished manner. "Ajjhattaṃ cetosamatham-anuyutto" means one who is devoted to one's own tranquility of mind (samatha). "Anirākatajjhāno" means one who has jhana that is not discarded or destroyed. "Vipassanāya" means developing insight through the seven types of contemplation. "Brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ" means one who increases [the use of] empty dwellings. Here, a monk who takes up a meditation subject through the power of tranquility and insight and enters and sits in an empty place day and night is to be understood as "one who increases empty dwellings." This is a summary here; for a detailed explanation, one who desires it should look at the commentary on the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā.

Regarding the term "lābhī" (receiver), the Blessed One does not teach the fulfillment of virtue, etc., for the sake of gains. For the Blessed One admonishes his disciples: "One should be like one whose speech is cut off in seeking food; one should not utter speech for the sake of gain." How then could He teach the fulfillment of virtue for the sake of gains? However, this was said according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of individuals. For those who might have the disposition: "If we were not troubled by the four requisites, we would be able to fulfill our virtues," He spoke thus according to their disposition. Furthermore, the four requisites are the natural benefit (sarasānisaṃsa) of virtue. This is because wise people take out grain, etc., stored in granaries and, without consuming it themselves, offer it to those who are virtuous. This was also said to show the natural benefit of virtue.

In the third turn (vāra), "yesāhaṃ" means "yesaṃ ahaṃ". "Tesaṃ te kārā" refers to the offerings of the four requisites made by those devas or humans towards me. ## 5. Commentary on Migasālāsutta

What should be said at the beginning of the fifth sutta has already been stated in the Book of Sixes (Chakkanipāta). In the passages beginning with "dussīlo hoti", "dussīlo" means one without virtue. "Cetovimutti" refers to the concentration of Fruition (phala-samādhi). "Paññāvimutti" refers to the wisdom of Fruition (phala-ñāṇa). "Nappajānāti" means not knowing by way of learning and inquiry. In the phrase "dussīlyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati", first, five types of immorality (dussīlya) are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), and ten are abandoned by the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga). At the moment of Fruition (phala-khaṇa), they are said to be abandoned. With reference to the moment of Fruition, it is said in this sutta that they "cease".

The virtue of a worldling (puthujjana) breaks due to five causes: committing a Pārājika offense, disavowing the training, joining another sect, attaining Arahatship, and death. Among these five, the first three lead to the decline of meditation (bhāvanā); the fourth cause leads to growth; the fifth cause leads neither to decline nor to growth. How does virtue break by Arahatship? The virtue of a worldling is purely wholesome (kusala), and the Path of Arahatship leads to the exhaustion of both wholesome and unwholesome kamma; thus, by that Path, that virtue is broken.

"Savenenapi akataṃ hoti" means not hearing the Dhamma that should be heard. In the phrase "bāhusaccenapi akataṃ hoti", "bāhusacca" here means energy (vīriya). It means that what should be done with energy is not done; because of not doing so, one falls away from both heaven and the Path. "Diṭṭhiyāpi appaṭividdhaṃ hoti" means not penetrating or realizing the Dhamma that should be penetrated by wisdom. "Sāmayikampi vimuttiṃ na labhati" means not obtaining the joy and gladness (pīti-pāmojja) that arises based on hearing the Dhamma at the proper time. "Hānāya pareti" means tending towards decline.

"Yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti" means knowing by way of learning and inquiry how the five types of immorality cease without remainder upon reaching the Fruition of Stream-entry. "Tassa savenenapi kataṃ hoti" means that the Dhamma that should be heard has been heard. "Bāhusaccenapi kataṃ..."

"Hoti" means that the action that should be done with energy is performed, even if it is only weak insight (vipassanā). "Diṭṭhiyāpi suppaṭividdhaṃ hoti" means that the cause is penetrated and realized even by the wisdom known as mundane wisdom (lokiya-paññā). Indeed, the wisdom of this person cleanses their virtue (sīla); through that virtue cleansed by wisdom, they reach a special distinction in the Dhamma.

"Pamāṇikā" refers to those who take the measure of persons. "Pamiṇanti" means they are worthy of comparing or measuring. "Eko hīno" means one person is inferior in qualities. "Paṇīto" means one person is superior or excellent in qualities. "Taṃ hီ" refers to making such a measure (comparison). "Abhikkantataro" means one who is better. "Paṇītataro" means one who is especially superior. "Dhammasoto nibbahati" means the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) arising courageously carries one away and leads to the noble ground (ariya-bhūmi). "Tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya" means who (other than a Noble One) could know such a reason? "Sīlavā hoti" means one is virtuous through mundane virtue. "Yatthassa taṃ sīlaṃ" means that upon reaching the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), virtue ceases without remainder; the logic for this total cessation of virtue has already been stated. In the next two factors, liberation is called the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), but in the fifth sutta, it is called the fruit of Arahantship itself. The remaining meanings should be understood according to the method already described. The sixth sutta is clear in its meaning.

## 7. Kākasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "dhaṃsī" means a destroyer of qualities. Disregarding anyone's qualities, even if caught by the hand, it drops excrement on that person's head. "Akāruṇiko" means a pitiless person. "Dubbalo" means one without strength or power. "Oravitā" means one who goes about wailing, accompanied by wailing. "Necayiko" means one who accumulates what is not beneficial.

## 9. Āghātavatthusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "aṭṭhāne" means in an inappropriate place or without cause. Indeed, in dealings with sentient beings, reasons such as "he has done me harm" may exist; however, in cases like striking against a tree stump, such a reason does not exist. Therefore, resentment toward such stumps is called resentment without cause. The remaining meanings are all very clear.

"Anayabyasanaṃ" means lack of growth and ruin. "Kiṃ nu kho" is a question asking "for what reason?"

## 5-6. Katthīsuttādi-vaṇṇanā
85-86. In the fifth sutta, "katthī hoti vikatthī" means one who has the habit of boasting and speaks openly (about oneself). "Na santatakārī" means one who does not act continuously. In the sixth sutta, "adhimāniko" means one endowed with the conceit of overestimation, thinking they have attained what they have not yet attained. "Adhimānasacco" means one who speaks of that very conceit of overestimation as the truth.

## 7. Nappiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
7. In the seventh sutta, "adhikaraṇiko hoti" means one who creates legal issues or disputes. "Na piyatāya" means not leading to the state of being loved. "Na garutāya" means not leading to the state of being respected. "Na sāmaññāya" means not leading to the state of monkhood (samaṇa-dhamma). "Na ekībhāvāya" means not leading to the state of continuous unity. "Dhammānaṃ na nisāmakajātiko" means one who does not have the nature of reflecting on or remembering the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). "Na paṭisallāno" means one who does not dwell in seclusion. "Sāṭheyyāni" means deceitful behaviors; "kူဋေယျာနိ" means fraudulent behaviors; "jimheyyāni" means crooked behaviors; "vaṅkeyyāni" means perverse behaviors.

## 8. Commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Akkosaka Sutta: In the phrase 'akkosakaparibhāsako ariyūpavādī sabrahmacārīnaṃ', the word 'sabrahmacārī' should be understood in connection with 'akkosaka' and 'paribhāsaka' as 'one who abuses fellow practitioners, one who reviles fellow practitioners.' One who accuses with the 'ultimate offense' (pārājika) with the intention of destroying the virtues of the Noble Ones is called an 'ariyūpavādī' (a reviler of Noble Ones). 'Saddhammassa na vodāyanti' means that the True Dhamma of the Dispensation, known as the threefold training, does not lead to purity for that person. In the term 'rogātaṅka', it should be understood that disease (roga) itself is called 'ātaṅka' because it causes one to live in distress and difficulty.

## 9. Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Kokālika Sutta: Regarding the statement 'The monk Kokālika approached the Blessed One'—who is this Kokālika, and why did he approach? This Kokālika was the son of the merchant Kokālika in the city of Kokālika within the Kokālika region. After ordaining, he lived in a monastery built and donated by his father and was known by the name 'Cūḷakokālika'. He was not a disciple of Devadatta. The Kokālika who was Devadatta's disciple was the son of a brahmin and was known as 'Mahākokālika'.

While the Blessed One was residing in Sāvatthī, the two Chief Disciples, along with about five hundred monks, were wandering through the countryside. As the time for the rains retreat approached, they wished to live in seclusion. They sent those monks away, took their own bowls and robes, reached that city in the countryside, and went to the monastery. There, the monk Kokālika performed the duties for the Chief Disciples. The Chief Disciples also greeted Kokālika joyfully and stayed there after obtaining a promise, saying, 'Friend, we will stay here for the three months of the rains; do not tell anyone that we are here.'

After staying for the three months of the rains, they performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony on the day of Pavāraṇā and informed Kokālika, saying, 'Friend, we are going now.' Kokālika requested, 'Venerable sirs, please stay for just one more day and depart tomorrow.' On the second day, he entered the city, called the people, and said, 'Lay followers, do you not know that the two Chief Disciples have come and are staying here? Why does no one invite these Chief Disciples with the four requisites?' The city dwellers asked, 'Venerable sir, where are the Elders? Why did you not tell us?' Kokālika replied, 'Lay followers, what is the use of telling? Do you not see the two monks sitting in the seats of the Elders? Those are the Chief Disciples.' The people quickly assembled and gathered together ghee, molasses, and the like, as well as cloth for robes. Kokālika thought, 'The Chief Disciples have very few wishes; they will not accept gains that have arisen through suggestive speech, and they will say, "Give them to the resident monk."' Thinking thus, he took the goods brought by those lay followers and went to the Elders...
327:
Kokālika thought: 'The Chief Disciples, who have very few wishes, will not accept gains obtained through suggestive speech. Since they will not accept them, they will say, "Give them to the resident monk."' Thinking thus, he took those gains and went to the Elders. As soon as the Elders saw him, they rejected them, saying, 'These requisites are not suitable for us, nor are they suitable for Kokālika,' and then they departed. Kokālika harbored a grudge, thinking, 'How is it that they do not take it themselves and also do not let it be given to me before they leave?' Those Elders went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and once again taking their own retinue, wandered through the countryside. In due course, they returned to that same city in that region. The city dwellers, recognizing the Elders, prepared offerings along with requisites, built a pavilion in the center of the city, and gave the donation. They also offered requisites to the Elders. The Elders then relinquished and handed over those items to the community of monks (Bhikkhu Saṅgha).

Seeing that they had given them away, Kokālika thought, 'These people had few wishes before, but now they have become ones of evil wishes. Even before, I think they were only pretending to be ones of few wishes, contentment, and seclusion.' He approached the Elders and said, 'Friends, you were like those with few wishes before, but now you have become evil monks.' Then, thinking, 'I will destroy their support at the very source, with the Blessed One,' he departed in great haste and approached the Blessed One. It should be understood that for this reason, Kokālika approached.

The Blessed One, seeing Kokālika coming in great haste, reflected and knew, 'This Kokālika has come wishing to abuse the Chief Disciples; is it possible to prevent him?' Then, seeing, 'It is not possible to prevent him; he has come after having already offended the Elders, and he will certainly be reborn in the Paduma Hell,' the Blessed One—in order to be free from the charge, 'The Blessed One heard him reviling persons like Sāriputta and Moggallāna but did not stop him,' and to show the great fault of slandering Noble Ones—prohibited him three times, saying, 'Do not say so.' In that context, 'Mā hevaṃ' means 'Do not say so.' 'Saddhāyika' means one who acts out of faith, one who brings inspiration, or one whose words are to be believed. 'Paccayika' means one whose words are trustworthy.

'He departed' means he departed being driven by the power of his kamma. Indeed, kamma that has found its opportunity cannot be blocked. 'Not long after he had departed' means within a short time after he had left. 'His whole body was covered' means without leaving a space even the size of a hair-tip, through boils that arose breaking through the bones of the entire body...
328:
Kokālika's body became covered with boils. Because of the power of the Buddhas, such karma was unable to bear fruit in the presence of the Buddhas; it bore fruit only as soon as he left their presence. Therefore, shortly after Kokālika had departed, the boils appeared. 'Kaḷāyamattiyo' means they were the size of chickpeas. 'Beluvasalāṭukamattiyo' means they were the size of young bael fruits. 'Pabhijjiṃsu' means they burst. When those boils burst, his whole body became like a ripe jackfruit. With his body covered in ripening sores, Kokālika lay on banana leaves at the gateway of the Jetavana monastery, like a fish that has swallowed poison. Then, people who came to listen to the Dhamma said, "How loathsome is Kokālika! Kokālika has done what is improper; by relying only on his own mouth, he has reached ruin and destruction." Hearing their voices, the guardian deities rebuked him. Hearing the voices of the guardian deities, the terrestrial deities also rebuked him. In this manner, a single cry of rebuke arose reaching as far as the Akanittha realm.

'Turū' refers to the one named Elder Tudu, who was Kokālika's preceptor. Having attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala), he was reborn in the Brahmā world. That Brahmā, starting from the terrestrial deities, heard the sound reaching the Brahmā world in succession, saying, "Kokālika has done what is improper by slandering the Chief Disciples with the ultimate matter (antima-vatthu)." Thinking, "Let not this wretched being perish while I am watching; I shall admonish him so that he may gain confidence in the Elders," he came and stood before him. Referring to his standing there, it is said, "Tudu the Pacceka-brahmā." 'Pesalā' refers to those of endearing virtue. "Friend, who are you?" Kokālika said this while sitting, opening his mottled eyes. [Tudu said,] "See how much you have offended; without seeing the great abscess on your own forehead, do you think I should be rebuked for a boil the size of a mustard seed?"

Then, knowing that Kokālika was one without vision and, like one who has swallowed poison, would not listen to anyone's words, he spoke the verse beginning with "In the mouths of men, there is a hatchet." In that context, 'kuṭhārī' (hatchet) refers to harsh speech which is like a hatchet. 'Chindati' means it cuts off the very root known as the root of merit. 'Nindiyam' refers to a person of immoral conduct who deserves blame. 'Pasaṃsati' means praising in a noble sense, saying that one is an Arahant. 'Taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyo' means slandering an Arahant who deserves praise with the ultimate matter, saying, "This person is immoral." 'Vicināti mukhena so kaliṃ' means that person seeks out that fault with his mouth.
329:
That person is said to seek out that fault with his mouth. 'Kalinā tena' means not finding happiness because of that fault. The result of praising one who deserves blame and blaming one who deserves praise is indeed the same.

'Sabbassāpi sahāpi attanā' means there is such a thing as the loss of wealth in gambling with dice, along with all one's property and oneself; such loss of wealth along with oneself is a minor fault. 'Yo sugatesu' means whoever offends with their mind against those who have gone well (the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples); this mental offense (anger) is a much greater fault than the fault of losing wealth in gambling.

Now, wishing to show the magnitude of that fault, he spoke the words beginning with 'Sataṃ sahassānaṃ'. In that Pali, 'Sataṃ sahassānaṃ' means a hundred times a hundred thousand in count. 'Chattiṃsati' means another thirty-six Nirabbuḍas. 'Pañca ca' means five Abbuḍas by count. 'Yamariyagarahī' means the hell into which one who slanders noble ones (Ariyas) falls; the meaning is that this is the extent of the lifespan in that hell.

'Kālamakāsi' means that when the preceptor (Tudu Brahmā) departed, he passed away (died). 'Padumanirayaṃ' means there is no separate hell named Paduma; rather, it is a birth in a certain place within the Great Avīci Hell where one must suffer for a duration calculated by the Paduma measure.

'Vīsati-khāriko' means that by the Magadhan measure (pattha), four patthas equal one pattha in the Kosala country. By that (Magadhan) measure, four patthas make one āḷhaka, four āḷhakas make one doṇa, four doṇas make one mānikā, and four mānikās make one khārī; 'vīsati-khāriko' refers to twenty such khārīs. 'Tilavāho' means a cartload of fine sesame seeds of the Magadhan country. 'Abbuḍo nirayo' means there is no separate hell named Abbuḍa; it is the name of the place in Avīci where one must suffer for a duration calculated by the Abbuḍa measure. The same method applies to Nirabbuḍa and so on.

The count of years here should be understood as follows: Just as a hundred times a hundred thousand is a Koṭi, so a hundred times a hundred thousand Koṭis is a Pakoṭi. A hundred times a hundred thousand Pakoṭis is a Koṭipakoṭi. A hundred times a hundred thousand Koṭipakoṭis is a Nahuta. A hundred times a hundred thousand Nahutas is a Ninnahuta. A hundred times a hundred thousand Ninnahutas is one Abbuḍa. Twenty times that Abbuḍa is a Nirabbuḍa. This method applies to all cases. The tenth sutta should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## 1-2. Kāmabhogīsutta-vaṇṇanā
91-92. In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, ‘sāhasena’ means by an act of violence or coercion. In the second sutta, ‘bhayāni’ refers to the fears that are terrors of the mind. ‘Verāni’ refers to the enmities of unwholesome states and the enemies who are individuals. ‘Ariyo cassa ñāyo’ is the Path together with insight (vipassanā). ‘Iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti’ means that when this cause, such as ignorance (avijjā), exists, this effect, such as formations (saṅkhāra), comes to be. ‘Imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati’ means that whatever state is a conascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya) for another state, with the arising of that cause, the other effect arises. ‘Imasmiṃ asati’ means that when the cause, such as ignorance, does not exist, the effect, such as formations, does not come to be. ‘Imassa nirodhā’ means that because the cause does not occur, the effect does not occur.

## 3. Kiṃdiṭṭhikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, ‘saṇṭhāpesuṃ’ means they well-established both their physical posture and their manner of speech. ‘Appasaddavinītā’ means those who are disciplined by the Teacher who speaks little and speaks only in moderation. ‘Paratoghosapaccayā vā’ means also due to the cause of another’s speech. ‘Cetayitā’ is that which is intended or conceived. ‘Maṅkubhūtā’ means having reached dejection and being devoid of splendor. ‘Pattakkhandhā’ means having drooping shoulders. ‘Sahadhammena’ means with a statement accompanied by a reason.

## 4. Vajjiyamāhitasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, ‘Vajjiyamāhito’ is the person of this name. ‘Sabbaṃ tapaṃ’ refers to all difficult ascetic practices. ‘Sabbaṃ tapassiṃ’ refers to one who follows all practices involving intense heat (asceticism). ‘Lūkhājīviṃ’ refers to one who repeatedly exerts himself in a harsh livelihood (difficult practices). ‘Gārayhaṃ’ is that which is blameworthy. ‘Pasaṃsiyaṃ’ is that which is praiseworthy. ‘Venayiko’ means one who cannot discipline himself and must be disciplined by others. ‘Apaññattiko’ means one who is unable to designate anything. Alternatively, ‘venayiko’ means one who destroys beings. ‘Apaññattiko’ means one who designates Nibbāna which is not yet realized, but is unable to designate anything regarding his own deeds, etc. ‘Na so bhagavā venayiko’ means that the Blessed One, knowing in this way according to the truth, when designating wholesome and unwholesome states, is not one to be disciplined by another, nor is he one who has learned from another. Because he designates those states starting from which a ‘being’ is designated, he is not a destroyer of beings, but is one who is well-disciplined, well-trained, and a guide for beings. Of that Blessed One...
331:
the Blessed One shows that by designating, he is indeed one who has designations. "Vimuttiṃ vimuccato akusalā dhammā" is spoken with reference to the meaning that unwholesome states increase for one who is devoted to the mind’s devotion known as wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). In the Dispensation, however, liberation (vimutti) known as the mind’s release from defilements is only a cause for wholesome states.

## 5. Uttiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "tuṇhī ahosi" (he remained silent) means he remained silent because [Uttiya] asked a question that should not be asked, while standing on the view of a "being" (satta). "Sabbasāmukkaṃsikaṃ vata me" means: "May he [Uttiya] not acquire such a low view as, 'I have asked the best of all questions, and the ascetic Gotama is confused, he does not answer; surely he is not able, he is not capable of answering.'" "Tadassa" means that such a wrong view that has arisen might be his. The reason for saying "paccantimaṃ" (border [city]) is that in the cities of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), whether the foundations of the walls, etc., are firm or weak, or even if they do not exist at all, there is no fear of robbers. Therefore, without taking such a city as an example, he spoke of a "border city." "Daḷhuḍḍhāpaṃ" means having a firm foundation for the wall. "Daḷhapākāratoraṇaṃ" means having both a firm wall and a firm gateway. Why is "ekadvāraṃ" (single gate) said? In a city with many gates, there must be many wise gatekeepers, but in a city with only one gate, one is sufficient. And there is no other equal to the Buddha in wisdom. Therefore, to illustrate the Teacher's state of being wise by way of a simile, he said "ekadvāraṃ" to show only a single gatekeeper. "Paṇ膽ito" means being endowed with wisdom. "Byatto" means being endowed with skill/proficiency. "Medhāvī" means being endowed with sagacity (medhā) known as wisdom that arises in various situations. "Anupariyāyapathaṃ" means the path named Anupariyāya (the path circling the wall). "Pākārasandhi" means the space where two bricks are separated. "Pākāravivaraṃ" means a breach in the wall. "Tadeve taṃ pañhaṃ" means asking again that same question which should be set aside (thapanīya pañha), asked in the manner of "Is the world eternal?" and so on. "Sabbo ca tena loko" shows that he asks in another way while still standing only on the view of a "being."

## 6. Kokanudasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "pubbāpayamāno" means making waterless places as before. "Kwettha āvuso" should be analyzed as "ko ettha āvuso" (Who is here, friend?). "Yāvatā āvuso" means...
332: 'Diṭṭhi' refers to all sixty-two types of views. 'Diṭṭhiṭṭhāna' refers to the eight causes of views: the aggregates (khandha), ignorance (avijjā), contact (phassa), perception (saññā), thought (vitakka), improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), bad friends (pāpamitta), and the voice of another (paratoghosa). 'Diṭṭhādhiṭṭhāna' is the foundation of views; it is so named because views exist by being established and overwhelming in that place. 'Diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna' refers to the eighteen obsessions of views. These are: view (diṭṭhi), the resort of views (diṭṭhigata), the jungle of views (diṭṭhigahana), the wilderness of views (diṭṭhikantāra), the distortion of views (diṭṭhivisūka), the agitation of views (diṭṭhivipphandita), the fetter of views (diṭṭhisaṃyojana), the barb of views (diṭṭhisalla), the congestion of views (diṭṭhisambādha), the obstacle of views (diṭṭhipalibodha), the bond of views (diṭṭhibandhana), the precipice of views (diṭṭhipapāta), the underlying tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya), the burning of views (diṭṭhisantāpa), the fever of views (diṭṭhipariḷāha), the knot of views (diṭṭhigantha), the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), the misinterpretation of views (diṭṭhābhinivesa), and the misapprehension of views (diṭṭhiparāmāsa). 'Samuṭṭhāna' is a synonym for 'diṭṭhiṭṭhāna'. As it is said: 'The aggregates are a condition for views in the sense of being their origin,' it should be understood in detail. The path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is called 'diṭṭhisamugghāta' because it completely uproots all views. 'Tamahaṃ' means 'I know all that.' 'Kyāhaṃ vakkhāmi' means 'For what reason shall I speak?' ## 7-8. Āhuneyya Sutta Ādi Vaṇṇanā 97-98. In the seventh sutta, 'sammādiṭṭhiko' means one who has a view according to reality. In the eighth sutta, 'adhikaraṇasamuppādavūpasamakusalo' means one who is skilled in calming the arising of legal issues by taking hold of the root of the four types of legal issues and calming them. ## 9. Upāli Sutta Vaṇṇanā In the ninth sutta, 'durabhisambhavāni' means difficult to attain, hard to endure; it means those with little power cannot enter into them. 'Araññavanapatthāni' means forests and forest-thickets. They are called 'arañña' (forests) because they fulfill the forest-dweller's practice. They are called 'vanapattha' (forest-thickets) because they are beyond the vicinity of the village and are not the haunts of humans. 'Pantāni' means remote, very distant places. 'Dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ' means physical seclusion (kāyaviveka) is difficult to achieve. 'Durabhiramaṃ' means not easy to delight in. 'Ekatte' means in being alone. What does it show? It shows that even if physical seclusion is achieved, it is difficult to make the mind delight there. This is because this world of beings delights only in pairs and company. 'Haranti maññe' means as if carrying away, as if devouring. 'Mano' means the mind. 'Samādhiṃ alabhamānassa' means for one who does not obtain access concentration (upacārasamādhi) or absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi). For such a monk, it shows the meaning that the forest-thickets seem to distract the mind through the sounds of grass, leaves, and wild animals, or through various terrifying objects.
333:
For one who does not obtain (concentration), what is shown? For such a monk, it is as if the forest-thickets distract the mind with various sounds of grass, leaves, wild animals, and so forth, and with various terrifying objects. "Saṃsīdissati" means he will sink down through sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka). "Upplavissati" means he will float upwards (become restless) through thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) and cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka).

"Kaṇṇasaṃdhovika" is a game played by washing the ears. "Piṭṭhisaṃdhovika" is a game played by washing the back. Among these, taking water with the trunk and pouring it into both ears is called kaṇṇasaṃdhovika; pouring it on the back is called piṭṭhisaṃdhovika. "Gādhaṃ vindati" means he finds a footing (a standing place). "Who am I, and who is the noble elephant?" means "What kind of being am I, and what is the noble elephant? I am an animal, and this elephant is also an animal; I have four legs, and he also has four legs; are we not both exactly equal?"

"Vaṅkaka" is a small toy plow for children. "Ghaṭika" is a game of hitting a short stick with a long stick. "Mokkhacika" is a game of flipping; it means the game of turning upside down by holding a stick in the air or by placing the head on the ground. "Ciṅgulaka" is a small windmill made of palm leaves etc., which rotates by the force of the wind. "Pattāḷhaka" refers to a leaf-cup; they play by measuring sand etc. with that cup. "Rathaka" is a small toy chariot. "Dhanuka" is just a small toy bow.

In the phrase "Idha kho pana vo," "vo" is a mere particle, and the meaning is "Idha kho pana." In the phrase "Iṅgha tvaṃ, Upāli, saṅghe viharāhi," "iṅgha" is a particle in the sense of urging. By this, the Buddha urges the Elder Upāli to dwell in the midst of the Saṅgha; He does not permit him to dwell in the forest. Why? It is said that if he dwelt in a forest-dwelling, he would only fulfill the burden of meditation (vāsadhura), but not the burden of scriptures (ganthadhura). However, by dwelling in the midst of the Saṅgha, he would fulfill both burdens, attain Arahantship, and become the foremost in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Then, the Teacher, seeing this benefit—that He would declare the Elder's past aspirations and past efforts in the midst of the assembly and appoint this monk to the foremost position among those who master the Vinaya—did not permit the Elder to dwell in the forest. The tenth sutta has a very clear meaning.

## 4-5. Bījasuttādivaṇṇanā
104-105. In the fourth sutta, "yathādiṭṭhi samattaṃ samādinnaṃ" means taking up everything fully and well in accordance with one's view. By the word "cetanā," only the volition arising in the three doors is taken. "Patthanā" means the aspiration: "May I be such a person." ## 6. Nijjarasuttavaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "nijjaravatthu" refers to the causes of wearing away. "Micchādiṭṭhi nijjhiṇṇā hoti" means this wrong view has already been worn away by lower insight (vipassanā). Why is it mentioned again? It is mentioned again because it has not been completely eradicated. For although it is worn away by insight, it is not completely eradicated. However, when the Path arises, it completely eradicates that wrong view and prevents it from arising again; therefore, it is mentioned again. In this way, it should be applied to all terms. In this sutta, due to the cause of right liberation (sammāvimutti), sixty-four states reach the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā). What are these sixty-four states? At the moment of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga)...
335:
...the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is fulfilled in the sense of resolution (adhimokkha); the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) in the sense of upholding; the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) in the sense of establishing; the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) in the sense of non-distraction; and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is fulfilled in the sense of seeing. Fire, poison, or weapons do not affect, penetrate, or harm the body of one who dwells in loving-kindness (metta). In this context, they also relate the story of a cow. A certain cow stood giving milk to her calf. A hunter, thinking 'I will shoot her,' aimed and released a long-handled spear.
