This happened neither by the power of access concentration (upacāra) nor by the power of absorption concentration (appanā), but solely due to the strong mind of loving-kindness toward the calf. Thus, loving-kindness possesses great majesty.

The mind of one who dwells in loving-kindness becomes concentrated quickly; there is no sluggishness for him. His facial complexion is clear, like a ripe palm fruit that has just fallen from its stalk. He dies unconfused; for one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no such thing as a confused death; rather, he passes away unconfused as if falling asleep. If he is unable to attain the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) beyond the attainment of loving-kindness (metta-samāpatti), then upon passing away from this life, he is reborn in the Brahma world (Brahmaloka) like one waking up from sleep.

## 6. Aṭṭhakanāgarasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth discourse, 'Dasama' is so named because he is counted in the tenth place, both by way of lineage and by the counting of noble families. 'Aṭṭhakanāgara' means a resident of the city of Aṭṭhakanagara. 'Kukkuṭārāma' refers to the monastery built by the merchant Kukkuṭa.

'By that Blessed One... well-proclaimed'—here is the summary of the meaning: That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and fully awakened to the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment. That Blessed One, knowing the inclinations and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of various beings, seeing all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed on the palm of the hand; furthermore, knowing through the knowledge of past lives and so on, seeing with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), knowing through the three knowledges (vijjā) or the six higher powers (abhiññā), seeing with the universal eye (samantacakkhu) which is unobstructed in all things, knowing with the wisdom capable of knowing all dhammas, [seeing] things behind walls and so forth that are beyond the visual range of all beings...
347:
When the Blessed One—who sees with an extremely pure physical eye; who knows with the wisdom of penetration based on concentration that accomplishes one's own benefit; who sees with the wisdom of teaching based on compassion that accomplishes the benefit of others; who knows the states that cause obstacles; who sees the states that lead to liberation; who is called 'Arahaṃ' because he has destroyed the enemies of defilements; and who is called 'Sammāsambuddha' because he has rightly and by himself known all phenomena—is thus praised by way of the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja) and through these four reasons, [the questioner] asks: "Is there one single Dhamma that has been declared?"

'Abhisaṅkhata' means what is made or produced. 'Abhisañcetayita' means what is thought out or intended. "Standing therein" means standing in those states of calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā). By both terms "lust for the Dhamma" (dhamma-rāga) and "delight in the Dhamma" (dhamma-nandi), the desire and lust (chandarāga) occurring in calm and insight are meant. Indeed, one who can completely and utterly eradicate all desire and lust in calm and insight becomes an Arahant; one who cannot do so becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmī). Because that person has not yet abandoned desire and lust in calm and insight, they are reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) by the volition of the fourth jhāna. This is the uniform explanation of the teachers in the commentaries.

However, a sophist (Vitandavādī) says: "Because of the words 'by that very lust for the Dhamma,' one is reborn in the Pure Abodes through an unwholesome state." He should be told: "Produce a Sutta passage [to support this]." Seeing no other, he will surely produce this very passage. Then he should be asked: "Is this Sutta one of explicit meaning (nītattha), or is it one of implicit meaning (neyyattha) to be further inferred?" He will certainly say: "It is of explicit meaning." Then he should be told: "If that is so, then one who desires the fruit of Non-returning must develop desire and lust for calm and insight; only when desire and lust are produced will the fruit of Non-returning be attained. Do not just point out whatever you like, saying 'I have found a Sutta.'" One who answers a problem should speak only after learning from a teacher and penetrating the essence of the meaning. There is no such thing as rebirth in a happy destination through an unwholesome state, nor rebirth in a state of deprivation through a wholesome state. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, gods are not known, humans are not known, nor are any other happy destinations known to arise from actions born of greed, actions born of hatred, or actions born of delusion. Rather, monks, it is hell that is known, the animal realm that is known, the realm of hungry ghosts that is known, or whatever other unhappy destinations there are, that are known to arise from actions born of greed, actions born of hatred, and actions born of delusion." (A.Ni. 6.39)

Thus should he be made to understand. If he understands, it is well. If he does not understand, that cook should be dismissed, saying, "He will drink the gruel while staying inside." Regarding the phrase "This, householder, is the one Dhamma that has been declared": it is said thus because Ānanda, who asked about one Dhamma, was answered according to his question, "This is that one Dhamma"; or because the eleven states are designated by the name 'one Dhamma' (ekadhamma); or because all the eleven states together deserve to be called 'ekadhamma' in the sense that they are the cause for the Deathless Nibbāna.

"Nidhiṃ gavesati" means searching for jars of gold and silver. "Sakideva" means it happens with only a single effort. How can eleven jars of gold be obtained with a single effort? In this world, some person might wander in the forest searching for a livelihood. Someone practicing for his own benefit sees him and asks, "Friend, why are you wandering?" He replies, "I am searching for a livelihood." Then the other says, "Friend, if so, look at this door-bolt." Just as that person, looking at that door-bolt, sees eleven jars of gold touching one another, so too is the attainment of the eleven states with a single effort.

"Other sectarians will seek wealth for the teacher" means those who learn a craft or knowledge from a teacher. While learning, they bring wealth from home and give it to the teacher either before, after, or during the training. Those who have no wealth at home seek out like-minded friends. If they have no such friends, they even wander for alms to give to the teacher. This is said in reference to such giving. The meaning is: "Even sectarians outside the Dispensation seek and give to a teacher who teaches a craft that does not lead out of the round of suffering. Why then should I not perform an act of worship for the Teacher who has taught the eleven states that lead to the Deathless Nibbāna? I shall certainly do so."

"Gives a pair of cloths to each one" means giving one pair of cloths to each person. Because such worldly usage exists, it is said "adāsi" (he gave). "Five hundred monasteries" means causing the construction of leaf-huts worth five hundred coins each.

In the seventh Sutta, the commentary is of three kinds: Ekanāḷikā, Caturassā, and Nisinnavattikā. Among these three, explaining the meaning of each word while setting aside the Pali text is called 'Ekanāḷikā'. Explaining by distinguishing the four types of cases—the unwise cowherd, the unwise monk, the wise cowherd, and the wise monk—is called 'Caturassā'. Explaining the meaning by showing the unwise cowherd and bringing it to a conclusion, then the unwise monk, then the wise cowherd, and then the wise monk to their respective conclusions is called 'Nisinnavattikā'. In this Gopālaka Sutta, this Nisinnavattikā style of explanation is the practice studied by all teachers. "Monks, with eleven factors" means with the factors of quality. "Herd" means a group of cattle. "For the sake of guarding" means for the sake of taking care of.
348:
He should be informed in this way. If he understands, let him understand. If he does not understand, he should be sent away with the words, "Go to the monastery early in the morning and drink congee."

"Householder, this Dhamma is said to be a single Dhamma." When asked about a single Dhamma, because it was taught by way of questioning as "This too is said to be a single Dhamma, and this too is said to be a single Dhamma," these eleven things are named as "a single Dhamma." Alternatively, in the sense of reaching the Deathless (Nibbāna), it is appropriate to call them all "a single Dhamma."

"Searching for the mouth of a treasure" (nidhi-mukhaṃ gavesanto) means seeking a treasure. "Only once" (sakideva) means by a single effort alone. How can eleven treasures be obtained by a single effort? Here, a certain person wanders in the forest seeking a livelihood. A benefactor sees him and asks, "Friend, why are you wandering?" He replies, "I am seeking a livelihood." The other says, "If so, friend, come and roll this stone." Having rolled it, he sees eleven pots placed one above the other or standing belly to belly. Thus, by a single effort, the eleven are obtained.

"They will seek wealth for the teacher" means that external sectarians (titthiyas) give wealth to those from whom they learn an art, either before, after, or during the course of learning, by taking it from their homes. Those who have no wealth in their homes seek it from relatives. If it is not with relatives, they seek it from those of similar status. If they still do not find it, they even go for alms and give it. This was said with reference to that.

"What about me?" means: even outsiders seek wealth for a teacher who merely gives an art in a teaching that does not lead out of saṃsāra. As for me, why should I not make an offering to the Teacher who teaches the eleven-fold practice that leads to the Deathless in such a liberating Dispensation? I will certainly do so. "He covered them with a pair of cloths each" means he gave a pair of cloths to each monk. Because the expression used here is of this nature, it is said "he covered them." "Five hundred monasteries" means he had leaf-huts worth five hundred [kahāpaṇas] built.

## 7. Gopālaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, there are three types of commentary: the one-word-based (ekanāḷikā), the four-cornered (caturassā), and the seated-concluding (nisinnavattikā). Among these, ekanāḷikā is the explanation of the meaning of each word while setting aside the Pali text. Caturassā is the explanation given by setting out four distinct cases: showing the unwise cowherd, showing the unwise monk, showing the wise cowherd, and showing the wise monk. Nisinnavattikā is the explanation that reaches the conclusion by showing the unwise cowherd, then the unwise monk, then the wise cowherd, and finally the wise monk. This kind of explanation called nisinnavattikā is the practice studied by all teachers in this Gopālaka Sutta.

"With eleven factors, bhikkhus" (ekādasahi bhikkhave aṅgehi) means with the attributes of qualities. "A herd of cattle" (gogaṇaṃ) means a group of cows. "To look after" (pariharituṃ) means to tend while wandering or to bring about the fivefold increase of cattle (conception, birth, etc.). "Unskilled in forms" (na rūpakusalo) in this world means not knowing the number and appearance of cows that are clearly shown by number and physical form. One who does not know by number does not know whether his cows are a hundred or a thousand. That foolish cowherd, not knowing the number of cows, does not know when cows are killed or run away, even after counting the herd, saying "Today this many cows do not appear." He does not wander and search between two or three villages or in the forest. Even when others' cows enter his herd, he does not count and realize "These cows are not ours." He does not drive them out by striking them with a staff. The small herd of that cowherd only goes to ruin. Like taking others' cows and wandering, the owners see them and threaten him, saying "This person has been milking our cow for so long," and take their cow away. His herd also diminishes. He is also deprived of enjoying the five cattle-products (gorasa).

Not knowing by appearance means not knowing "This many cows are black, this many are white, this many are pure white, this many are spotted, this many are brown." That foolish cowherd who does not know the appearance and form is deprived of enjoying the five cattle-products when the cows are killed or run away.

"Unskilled in marks" (na lakkhaṇakusalo) means not knowing the various marks made on the bodies of the cows with knives, spears, or brands. The cowherd who does not know those marks does not attain purity. When cows are killed or run away, he does not know "Today cows with such marks do not appear." He is also deprived of enjoying the five cattle-products.

"Not removing the eggs" (na āsayaṃ hātā): wounds occur on the bodies of cows in places struck by stumps or thorns. In those wounds, wild flies lay eggs. Those eggs are called "āsaya." One should remove those eggs with a small knife or a small stick and apply medicine. The foolish cowherd does not do so. Therefore, he is called one who does not remove the eggs. In his cows, the wounds increase and become deep. Maggots enter the insides. The cows, oppressed by the disease of the wounds, cannot eat grass or drink water as they wish. When that happens, the milk of the cows decreases. The speed of the cows diminishes. It becomes a danger to the lives of both the cows and the owner. Thus, his herd diminishes and he is deprived of the five cattle-products.

"Not dressing the wound" (na vaṇaṃ paṭicchādetā) means one should dress the wounds of cows caused by knives or sticks by applying medicine or by binding them with a new or old cloth. The foolish cowherd does not do so. Then, pus and blood leak from the cows' wounds. Because those cows rub against each other, wounds occur in other cows as well. When this happens...
349:
## 
Showing the unskilled cowherd, showing the unskilled monk, showing the skilled cowherd, and showing the skilled monk—this teaching arranged in four groups is called Caturassa (four-sided). Showing the unskilled cowherd to the end, showing the unskilled monk to the end, showing the skilled cowherd to the end, and showing the skilled monk to the end is called Nisinnavattikā (a discourse set in motion while seated). This method is the one practiced by all teachers in this Dispensation.

"Monks, with eleven factors" means with eleven categories of faults. "Gogaṇa" means a herd of cattle. "Pariharituṃ" means to wander while taking care of them. "Phātiṃ kātuṃ" means to make them increase or prosper. "Idha" means in this world. "Not knowing forms (rūpaññū)" means not knowing the physical appearance of the cows, either by number or by color. Not knowing by number means not knowing whether one has a hundred or a thousand of one's own cows. When cows are stolen or run away, that cowherd, even if he knows by counting the herd that "so many cows are not seen today," does not wander and search between two or three villages or in the forest. Even when others' cows enter his own herd, although he counts the herd and knows "these many cows are not ours," he does not strike them with a stick and drive them out. The cows he has lost remain lost. He wanders taking others' cows. When the owners of the cows see this, they threaten him, saying, "This man has been milking our cows for so long," and take their cows away. His own herd also declines and perishes, and he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow (pañca-gorasa). Not knowing by color means not being able to distinguish: "This many cows are white, this many are red, this many are black, this many are yellow, this many are spotted, this many are brown." When cows are stolen or run away... (etc.) ... he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow.

"Not skilled in marks" means not knowing the various marks made on the bodies of the cows, such as bows, weapons, spears, and so forth. When cows are stolen or run away, because he does not know "cows with such-and-such marks are not seen today" and does not search for them, he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow.

"Does not remove fly-eggs (maggots)" means that wounds often occur on cows in places where they have been struck by stumps, thorns, and so forth. Bluebottles lay eggs in those wounds; these are called āsāṭika (fly-eggs/maggots). Those eggs must be removed with a small stick or a small knife and medicine must be applied, but the foolish cowherd does not do so. Therefore, it is said: "Does not remove fly-eggs..."
350:
(The cowherd) is one who does not habitually remove (the maggots in the wound). The wounds of those cows grow and become deep; the maggots enter the belly. The cows, being overcome by disease, are unable to eat as much grass as they want or drink water. Then, the milk of the cows is cut off, the speed of the bulls declines, and for both, there is a danger to life. In this way, his herd of cattle also declines... (etc.) ... and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

He is one who does not habitually cover the wound. A wound that has arisen on the cows in the manner already mentioned should be covered by applying medicine and binding it with bark or a piece of cloth. The foolish cowherd does not do so. Then, putrid pus flows from the wounds of those cows, and those cows rub against one another. Because of such rubbing, wounds also arise in other cows. In this way, the cows, being overcome by disease, are unable to eat as much grass as they want... (etc.) ... and he is excluded.

He is one who does not habitually make smoke. During the rainy season, when gnats, mosquitoes, and so forth are abundant, when the herd of cattle has entered the pen, smoke should be made here and there. The unskilled cowherd does not do so; the herd of cattle, being harassed all night by gnats and so on, does not get to sleep, and the next day they lie down and sleep under trees and such in the forest. They are unable to eat as much grass as they want... (etc.) ... and he is excluded.

He is one who does not know the ford (watering place). He does not know whether the ford is even or uneven, or whether it has crocodiles or not. He makes the cows go down at a place that is not a ford. In an uneven ford, the feet of those cows who step on stones and such are broken. When they go down into a deep ford where there are crocodiles, crocodiles and such seize the cows, and it comes to the point where it must be said, "Today so many cows are lost, today so many cows are lost." In this way, his herd of cattle also declines... (etc.) ... and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

He is one who does not know what has been drunk and what has not been drunk. He does not know what has been drunk or what has not yet been drunk. A cowherd should know: "This cow has drunk, this cow has not yet drunk; this cow got a turn at the watering ford, this cow has not yet gotten a turn." But this man, having guarded the herd in the forest during the day, drives them to a river or a lake, thinking, "I will give them water to drink." At that ford, the great bulls, the young bulls, the strong cows, and the weak and old cows
351:
The strong bulls, using their horns or their flanks, push the other cows aside to make a way for themselves. They enter the upper waters and drink as much as they desire. The remaining weak cows, unable to find an opening, stand on the bank and drink water mixed with mire, or they do not get to drink at all. Then, the cowherd beats them on their backs and drives them back into the forest. In that forest, the cows that have not yet drunk water become parched with thirst and are unable to eat as much grass as they need. When this happens, the milk of the cows is cut off, and the speed and strength of the bulls decline... they become excluded from their own welfare.

'Does not know the path' means not knowing: 'This path is level and safe; this path is uneven, worrisome, and dangerous.' That cowherd avoids the level and safe path and leads the herd of cattle onto the other uneven path. On that path, the cows are oppressed by the scent of lions, tigers, and so on, as well as by the danger of thieves. Like frightened wild animals, they stand with their necks raised. They do not eat as much grass as they need, nor do they drink water. When this happens, the milk of the cows is cut off... they become excluded from their own welfare.

'Not skilled in pastures' means that a cowherd must be skilled in pastures; he must know the five-day rotation or the seven-day rotation. Having grazed the herd in one direction, he should not graze them in that same spot again the next day. This is because a place grazed by a large herd becomes as bare as the surface of a drum, devoid of grass, and the water becomes turbid. Therefore, he should only graze them there again on the fifth or seventh day. Within this period, the grass grows back and the water becomes clear. This foolish cowherd, however, does not know this five-day or seven-day rotation and keeps them in the same guarded spot day after day. Then his herd does not get green grass; eating dry grass, they drink water mixed with mire. When this happens, the milk of the cows is cut off... they become excluded from their own welfare.

'One who milks without leaving a remainder' means that a wise cowherd, as long as the flesh and blood of the calf can be sustained, should leave one or two teats and milk with a remainder. This foolish cowherd milks without leaving even a little for the calf. The suckling calf, parched with thirst for milk and unable to stand, falls trembling before its mother and dies. The mother cow, seeing her young calf, thinks, 'My little son did not get to drink his mother's milk'...
352:
"...due to the grief for her calf, she is unable to eat as much grass as she needs or drink water. The milk in her teats is cut off. In this way, his herd of cattle also declines... (in detail) ...and he is excluded from the five dairy products.

They are called 'Gopitara' (fathers of the cattle) because they provide a foundation for the cows. They are called 'Gopariṇāyaka' (leaders of the cattle) because they lead the cows wherever they wish. 'Does not honor those cows with extra respect' means: a wise cowherd honors such bulls with extra respect. He gives them excellent gruel, rice, and so on. He decorates them with five-finger marks of perfume. He decks them with flowers. He fits gold or silver casings onto their horns. At night, he lights a lamp and lets them sleep under a canopy.

This foolish cowherd, however, does not perform even one of these honors. The bulls, not receiving extra respect, do not protect the herd and do not ward off dangers. In this way, his herd of cattle declines and he is excluded from the five dairy products.

'In this' means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Does not know form' means not knowing form—which is described as 'the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements'—in two ways: by number or by origin (samuṭṭhāna).

Not knowing by number means: not knowing the twenty-five groups of form mentioned in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali, namely: the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, visible-form-base, sound-base, odor-base, flavor-base, tangible-base, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, bodily intimation, vocal intimation, the space element, the water element, lightness of form (lahutā), malleability (mudutā), wieldiness (kammaññatā), accumulation (upacaya), continuity (santati), decay (jaratā), impermanence of form (aniccatā), and physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra āhāra).

Just as that cowherd does not know the form (the count) of the cows by number, this monk is similar to him. That monk, not knowing form by number, is unable to complete the meditation subject by grasping form, defining mentality, grasping mentality and form, discerning the causes, and applying the characteristics (of existence).

Just as the herd of that cowherd does not increase, in the same way, in this Dispensation, he does not increase in virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Just as that cowherd is excluded from the five dairy products, in the same way, this monk is excluded from the five aggregates of Dhamma: the aggregate of virtue of an adept (asekha), the aggregate of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

What is meant by 'not knowing by origin' is..."
353:
Not knowing by way of origin (samuṭṭhāna) means: not knowing that "this much matter (rūpa) arises from one cause, this much matter arises from two causes, this much matter arises from three causes, this much matter arises from four causes, and this much matter does not arise from any cause at all." For example, just as that cowherd does not know the form of the cows by their color, this monk is similar to him. Because he does not know matter by way of its origin, he cannot reach the end of his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) through the practices of grasping matter, discerning mentality, grasping mentality and matter, noting the causes, and applying the three characteristics, and thus he becomes an outsider [to the Dispensation].

Not being skilled in characteristics means: not knowing that "a fool is characterized by his deeds, a wise man is characterized by his deeds," and thus not knowing that wholesome and unwholesome kamma are the characteristics that mark the wise and the fool. Because he does not know this, he does not avoid fools and does not associate with the wise. Because he does not avoid fools and does not associate with the wise, he does not know what is allowable and unallowable, wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, grave offenses and light offenses, curable offenses and incurable offenses, and what is a cause and what is not. Because he does not know these, he cannot take up a meditation subject and develop it. Just as that cowherd's herd does not grow, so he cannot grow in this Dispensation through the aforementioned virtue (sīla) and so forth. Like that cowherd who is an outsider to the five kinds of dairy products, this monk is an outsider to the five aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha).

Not removing fly eggs means: not dispelling sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) and so forth, as it is said, "a sensual thought that has arisen." That monk, without removing these unwholesome thoughts which are like fly eggs, wanders about under the influence of those thoughts and thus cannot take up a meditation subject and develop it. Just like that cowherd... he becomes an outsider.

Not covering wounds means: taking up signs (nimitta) in all sense objects in the manner described as "having seen a form with the eye, he grasps at its signs." Just as that cowherd does not cover the wounds [of the cows], so this monk does not fulfill restraint (saṃvara). Wandering about with his sense doors open, he cannot take up a meditation subject and develop it... he becomes an outsider.

Not making smoke means: just as that cowherd does not make smoke, this monk does not make the smoke of Dhamma teaching; he does not give Dhamma talks, recite in the sarabhañña style, give a talk to those sitting nearby, or perform the thanksgiving (anumodanā). Because of this, people do not know him as "one of great learning (bahussuta) or one of virtue." Because those people do not know whether he has virtues or not, they do not support him with the four requisites. Being weary due to the lack of requisites, he cannot recite the Buddha's words, fulfill his major and minor duties, or take up a meditation subject and develop it... he becomes an outsider.
354:
Not knowing the watering place (tittha) means not approaching learned (bahussuta) monks who are like watering places. Because he does not approach them, he does not repeatedly ask or inquire, "Venerable sir, how should this phrasing be placed? What is the meaning of this statement? What does the Pali say in this instance? What does the meaning illustrate in this instance?" and thus he does not make himself know. Because he has not inquired, those learned monks do not reveal the meaning that has not yet been revealed, they do not analyze and show it, they do not make clear what is not yet clear, and they do not clarify what is obscure. Regarding the various things that are grounds for doubt, they cannot dispel even a single doubt. Indeed, doubts themselves are called "things that are grounds for doubt." The meaning is that they cannot remove even one of those doubts. Without approaching the watering place of the learned in this way, he is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it while still possessed of doubt. Alternatively, just as that cowherd does not know the watering place, so this monk does not know the watering place of the Dhamma. Because he does not know, he asks questions in an inappropriate field; approaching an Abhidhamma expert, he asks about what is allowable or unallowable (Vinaya matters); approaching a Vinaya expert, he asks about the discernment of mentality and matter (Abhidhamma matters). Those monks, being asked about things outside their field, are unable to answer. That monk, having doubts himself, is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it... he becomes an outsider to the Dispensation.

Not knowing the drinking water means that just as that cowherd does not know which water the cows should or should not drink, this monk does not know or obtain the joy (pāmojja) associated with the Dhamma. He does not obtain the benefits based on the ground of merit consisting in hearing the Dhamma. Even when he goes to the place of Dhamma preaching, he does not listen respectfully, but instead falls asleep while sitting, talks, or becomes distracted. Such a monk who does not listen to the Dhamma respectfully is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it... he becomes an outsider.

Not knowing the path means that just as that cowherd does not know the path from what is not the path, this monk does not know the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is, thinking, "This is the mundane (lokiya) path, this is the supramundane (lokuttara) path." Because he does not know, he remains attached to the mundane path and is unable to produce the supramundane path... he becomes an outsider.

Not being skilled in the pasture means that just as that cowherd does not know the grazing grounds visited every five or seven days, this monk does not know the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) as they truly are, thinking, "These are mundane, these are supramundane." Because he does not know, he is unable to let his knowledge range over subtle objects; remaining attached to mundane foundations of mindfulness, he is unable to produce the supramundane foundations of mindfulness... he becomes an outsider.
355:
‘One who milks dry without remainder’ means one who, not knowing moderation in receiving offerings, milks (receives) everything without leaving anything behind. In the Niddesavāra (Exposition Section), however, it is said ‘they bring forth and invite,’ meaning they bring offerings and make an invitation. Here, there are two kinds of invitations: verbal invitation (vācābhihāra) and material invitation (paccayābhihāra). Verbal invitation means people go to the presence of a monk and invite him, saying, “Venerable sir, please tell us what you need.” Material invitation means people take requisites such as robes, or ghee, fresh butter, molasses, milk, etc., and go to the presence of a monk, saying, “Venerable sir, please take as much as you need.”

In such invitations, a monk ‘not knowing moderation’ means he does not know the proper amount regarding those requisites. It means that he does not take what is appropriate according to the method: “The donor’s wealth must be known, the power of the gift must be known, and one’s own capacity must be known,” but instead takes everything that is brought. Consequently, the people become dissatisfied and no longer bring offerings to invite him. That monk, being exhausted for lack of the four requisites, is unable to take up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and develop it... and thus becomes an outsider to the Dispensation.

‘They are not honored with extraordinary honor’ means that the cowherd does not honor the senior monks (Theras) with extraordinary honor, such as bodily acts of loving-kindness (mettā-kāyakamma) performed both in their presence and in their absence, just as he would not honor the great bulls. Because of this, the senior monks, thinking, “These monks do not show us respect and esteem,” do not support the junior monks (Navakas) with the two kinds of support (saṅgaha); they support them neither with the support of Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgaha) nor with the support of material things (āmisa-saṅgaha). Even when the juniors are struggling for robes, alms-bowls, food, or lodgings, the seniors do not look after them. They do not teach them the Pāḷi, the Commentaries (Atthakathā), the structure of Dhamma discourses, or the profound texts.

The junior monks, not receiving these two kinds of support from the senior monks in any way, are unable to remain established in this Dispensation. Just as the cowherd’s herd of cattle does not increase, in the same way, they do not increase in virtue (sīla) and so forth. And just as that cowherd is deprived of the five products of the cow, in the same way, they are deprived of the five aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha). The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by applying the opposite meaning to what was said for the dark side (kaṇhapakkha).

## Second Anussati Vagga.
## The explanation of the Book of the Elevens of the Manorathapūraṇī,
## the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is finished.
356:
## Concluding Remarks

By this much—

Being requested by the wise Elder Bhadanta Jotipāla, who formerly lived with me in cities such as Kañcipura.

And also during the time of residing in the Mahāvihāra in the noble island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka), while enjoying the True Dhamma just as one enjoys a tree with ripe fruit, being requested by the wise Elder Jīvaka, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the Three Piṭakas and possesses a pure livelihood.

I, desiring the long endurance of the noble Dispensation, began this commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which contains subtle and profound Dhamma discourses.

This [commentary], taking the essence of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, is completed with a Pāḷi text measuring ninety-four recital sections (bhāṇavāras).

Since my heart’s desire to explain all the Agamas (Nikāyas) has been fulfilled, this commentary is therefore named ‘Manorathapūraṇī’ (The Fulfillment of Wishes).

Since I have also composed the Visuddhimagga, measuring fifty-nine recital sections, for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the Agamas.

Therefore, together with that [Visuddhimagga], according to the method of counting verses, this commentary should be known to have one hundred and fifty-three recital sections.

Measuring one hundred and fifty-three recital sections, clarifying the tradition of the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra, may the merit accumulated by me in composing this [work] by taking the essence of the original commentaries, cause all people in the world to be forever happy.
357:
This Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, was composed by the Elder who is adorned with supremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy; who is endowed with a collection of virtues such as morality (sīla), conduct, integrity, and gentleness; who is capable of diving into the depths of his own and other doctrines; who is possessed of mature wisdom; who has the power of unimpeded knowledge in the Teacher’s Dispensation consisting of the three Baskets (Tipiṭaka) of scriptures together with the Commentaries; who is a great grammarian; who is endowed with the beauty of sweet and noble speech that flows happily from the perfection of the vocal organs; who speaks what is appropriate and relevant; who is the most excellent of speakers; who is a great poet; who is surrounded by the various analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); who is adorned with virtues such as the six direct knowledges (abhiññā); who is well-established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma); who is a lamp for the lineage of the Elders; who is an ornament to the lineage of the residents of the Mahāvihāra; who possesses vast and pure wisdom; and who was given the name ‘Buddhaghosa’ by his venerable teachers—

As long as the name ‘Buddha’ of the Pure-minded One,
Who is the Foremost of the world, the Great Sage,
Continues to exist in the world,

May this commentary remain in the world,
Showing the way to mental purity
To the sons of good family
Who seek liberation from the world.

## The Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya
## named Manorathapūraṇī is completed in every respect.
